## Microsoft Dynamics 365
98100 subscribers
11 likes

### Description
807 views
Posted: 12 Sep 2025
In this exclusive AI in Action special series, Microsoft Corporate Vice President of AI Business Solutions Jonathan Hunt and Microsoft Corporate Vice President for Business Applications & Agents Bryan Goode sit down with leading consultancy partners to explore how AI is driving new opportunities for businesses around the world. Together, they unpack the top AI trends in the market, including how these partners are leveraging Microsoft's AI technology to drive innovation and transformation within their own businesses as well as across client engagements. In this episode, Bryan Goode interviews Naresh Khanduri, Executive Vice President, CoE Lead (DCX-NA) of Capgemini. Together, they explore the strategic partnership between Capgemini and Microsoft, and how Capgemini is leveraging Copilot and Dynamics 365 for rapid business impact. The discussion highlights the strong alignment when it comes to practical solutions for customers across sales, service, and software engineering. 
Want to learn more? View more of AI in Action here: https://msft.it/6055skgRJ


### Transcript:
[ Music ] BRYAN GOODE: Alright, Naresh. Thank you so much for
joining me today. NARESH KHANDURI:
Thank you, Bryan. Thank you for having me here. BRYAN GOODE: Yes, it's
great to have you. Well, look, AI's driving
new opportunities for business around the world. Can you tell me a little bit
about what you're seeing in terms of the opportunity
and some of the challenges that customers are facing? NARESH KHANDURI: Well,
so last two years, we are on this hyper
growth of AI: generative, agentic, and everything. I think our customers are
seeing a lot more value. Being service provider, we see
value in delivering and driving that value to our clients. But particularly in customer
experience and engagement space, the expectations has been high,
and obviously the outcomes that we have delivered over
the last two years has been exceptional. From transforming
how our clients look at their sales processes, how they service
their end consumers, that has drastically changed. I would say first
six months probably, everybody was a
little bit worried. Will it work or not? But last year, year and a half,
has been a phenomenal journey. People are seeing the result; businesses are
seeing the result. They have been able to serve
their end clients far better. We definitely see that
it is a new world out of this (inaudible)
help our clients and help serve them better. BRYAN GOODE: That's great. And how are you thinking about
solving some of those challenges and serving those businesses
together with Microsoft? NARESH KHANDURI: How we
are deploying Microsoft in conjunction with
what we already have, this will make the workforce
part far more efficient. So all the sales
agents or salespeople in the team use all
the Microsoft tooling. So how do we use the power
of the Copilot and augment that with (inaudible)
and augment that with the remaining
pieces from the Azure system. So it's a really good
transformation story, if you will. BRYAN GOODE: Sure. NARESH KHANDURI: Microsoft
brings us not only hyper skilling, but a platform
to solve a client problem. We can do hyper skilling in
many ways, but then solving that customer problem becomes
easier with the equal system that we have with Microsoft. And the speed at
which we can deliver. The challenging part of these
technologies is we don't have time to wait for three years. You need to deliver
it in three months, six months, and
do it repetitive. So it's great. BRYAN GOODE: And how are you
using Microsoft's AI solutions as part of your own
delivery to your clients? NARESH KHANDURI: So we
use a lot of Copilot, but it helps our salespeople. It helps us be more efficient. It helps us understand
things much more faster. Another thing that I
personally feel good about is, it's tricky at times
to have all the people around in the same call. How do you ensure everybody
has the same information base to operate from? To build a solution
for our clients, you need a solution architect,
you need a designer, you need a process person. And when you are having
those briefing discussions, can you get all five
experts at same time? Most probably it's
a tricky situation. And once we enable the Copilot
parts of it, it becomes easier to manage the knowledge, share
the knowledge, work on it. It's good. BRYAN GOODE: That's great. And how would you say that Microsoft's AI vision is
differentiated, and how does that align with
Capgemini's vision for AI? NARESH KHANDURI: So I'll start
with how our vision was, and we failed to
(inaudible) align with the way we were thinking. So if you see about 2022,
Aiman made a statement on saying AI's not
just one part of it. You need AI to do
customer experience. You need AI to
build base models. You need AI to do
software engineering. So while everybody
says AI has one shot, it depends where
you are deploying. Which part of business
are you deploying it for? So when you're solving
a customer problem, it becomes gen AI for CX. When you are doing
software engineering, then you need gen AI for
software engineering. In that way, we're
quite aligned. So if you see in the biz apps
business, it helps us say no, we are helping
business applications. But when you go down to
solving a developer's problem, oh I am doing Copilot
for a developer. So it was quite aligned to
our strategy of saying oh, you said these are four
or five big domains that are business (inaudible). What's the technology partner
who supports that vision? It got augmented by having the
right tooling from Microsoft. So kind of aligned a lot with the way we were
thinking (inaudible). BRYAN GOODE: That's great. Well, thank you so much
for your partnership. I've loved to get to know you,
Naresh, and really look forward to what we can do together in
the future for our customers. NARESH KHANDURI: Yes. BRYAN GOODE: Appreciate it. NARESH KHANDURI: Thank you. [ Music ]

Key points discussed:
- The last two years have seen hyper growth in generative and agentic AI, with customers seeing significant value, particularly in customer experience and engagement, sales processes, and service transformation.
- After initial skepticism for the first six months, the last year and a half has been a phenomenal journey with businesses seeing real results.
- Capgemini deploys Microsoft Copilot augmented with Azure systems to make sales teams and workforces far more efficient.
- Microsoft provides hyper-skilling and a platform to solve client problems, with speed being critical—solutions need to be delivered in 3-6 months repetitively rather than over years.
- Copilot helps Capgemini manage and share knowledge across solution architects, designers, and process experts, ensuring all team members have the same information base.
- Khanduri highlights alignment with Microsoft's AI vision, referencing a 2022 statement by Capgemini's Aiman about AI being applied differently across domains (customer experience, base models, software engineering) rather than being a one-size-fits-all solution.

# Use Cases for AI

by **[Sarah Saunders](/alumni#author-sarah-saunders)**

on [AI](/tags/index.html#AI "Posts tagged with AI"), [Machine Learning](/tags/index.html#Machine Learning "Posts tagged with Machine Learning"), [Development](/tags/index.html#Development "Posts tagged with Development"), [Testing](/tags/index.html#Testing "Posts tagged with Testing")

Estimated reading time 15 minutes

# Use Cases for Generative AI

For the past year, almost every week the Software Engineering world is asked about Artificial Intelligence (AI). “What should Capgemini’s AI offerings be?”, “Aren’t you worried about the role of Capgemini software engineers now that AI can write code?” Specifically in these cases, the questions are around Generative AI. To put that in context, here is a recap of some terms used to describe different implementations of AI.

### Machine Learning

A nice dictionary definition of machine learning from [Oxford Languages](https://languages.oup.com/) is: “the use and development of computer systems that are able to learn and adapt without following explicit instructions, by using algorithms and statistical models to analyse and draw inferences from patterns in data.” The difference between a basic decision tree and machine learning is that with machine learning, a person didn’t sit down and define a set of if-statements for the machine to follow to make decisions (as used, for instance, in the NHS [Map of Medicine](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2004/dec/map-medicine) from 2007). Instead, they provided a set of inputs and expected outputs and let the machine’s algorithms figure out how to get from input to output. You could describe it as a bottom-up approach to problem solving rather than a top-down approach. This evokes the differences between [Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton) and [Leibnitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_Wilhelm_Leibniz) in their attempts to describe the physical world in the 17th century. Newton’s laws are built more like a decision tree, describing the results of forces on objects, whereas Leibnitz’s “monads” are more like the algorithms in machine learning where small, simple rules build up together to create the complex forces we see in action. They are both very useful tools in describing and learning about the physical world but may result in different predictions of varying accuracy. Machine learning algorithms are loosely based on the [neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuron) in the brain. Each “artificial neuron” is a function that receives one or more inputs, applies weights to these inputs, and sums them to produce an output. Chained together into a “Neural Network” these small functions can complete amazing tasks such as image recognition, text generation and predictive analytics. Machine learning is incredibly useful and can benefit a wide range of industries from healthcare to travel to finance.

### Generative AI

Dictionaries are not so hot on defining generative AI. Perhaps the best example is from [Merriam Webster](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/generative%20AI): “artificial intelligence that is capable of generating new content (such as images or text) in response to a submitted prompt (such as a query) by learning from a large reference database of examples”. The important difference here is the generation of new content. There are still machine-learning algorithms at play, but the ask is that they produce something new. The output of a generative AI query isn’t pulled from a list, it isn’t copied from an article. It is created by the neural network. You MAY get a text answer that is the same as an existing article, but it will have been probabilistically generated using an algorithm that, in simple terms, says “what word is most likely to come next in this phrase”, for example. Asking the same question twice will not produce the same output. With machine learning, the output you get is usually a probability – for example, a handwriting recognition system would give a probability percentage that a given input image contains certain words. As such, it isn’t ever completely wrong, because it doesn’t give a definitive answer. Generative AI will look at the various probable outputs and choose one by applying a separate decision algorithm. In this way, it is possible to get answers that are just plain wrong.

### General AI

Wikipedia says General AI “is a type of AI that matches or surpasses human capabilities across a wide range of cognitive tasks.” To put it simply, General AI does not exist. We don’t currently accurately define human capabilities, so trying to decide whether a machine can exceed them is impossible!

## Examining the Use Cases

As mentioned above, Machine Learning solutions are proving vastly useful in automating complex tasks that must make deductions based on huge quantities of data. A notable example is evaluating patient [CT scan data in search of cancerous growths](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43856-022-00199-0). The algorithm does not replace the oncologist, but assists to alleviate an otherwise “repetitive, tedious and burdensome” task. The outputs are not treated as gospel truth, but help the oncologist choose where to focus their time and efforts.

There has understandably been much buzz and excitement about the amazing capabilities of Generative AI this past year, with the broader uptake of [ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt/) and [Dall-e](https://openai.com/index/dall-e-2/), for example. Now that the dust has settled, a closer evaluation of Generative AI use cases is required.

Remember this diagram for blockchain use cases? Perhaps it’s time for something similar for Generative AI use cases?

The key thing to remember about Generative AI is that the answers it generates are not necessarily correct, and are not even [intended](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11023-022-09602-0) to be correct. When architecting a solution that involves Generative AI, the pertinent questions are:

* Does it matter if this generated answer is wrong?
* Do I require the same answer to the same question if I ask it twice?

If the answer to either of these questions is YES, then you cannot use a standard Generative AI solution without some significant [tuning](https://www.forbes.com/sites/forbestechcouncil/2023/10/10/the-power-of-fine-tuning-in-generative-ai/) which in itself removes the “generative-ness” of your solution.

There are still plenty of scenarios where the answer to the above questions is NO. With a focus on Microservice Development, we will look at the use cases that have been put forward for enhancing the software development lifecycle:

### User Interface Design

When designing a human-computer interface to improve the user experience, there are best practices but there is no wrong answer. As such, it is a viable candidate for applying Generative AI - the role of an [Agile Software Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agile_software_development) in interface design is to iteratively put suggestions forward to the system user for their consideration. AI tools could accelerate prototypes, and assist the designer in breaking out of their habitual designs and trying something new. Already, design tools such as [Figma](https://www.figma.com/) and [V0 by Vercel](https://v0.dev/) have started to put this into practice.

### Automated Testing

A software test suite should allow all routes through the system to be automatically checked when a change is added, to ensure that no previous logic has been broken by the new addition. Defining “all routes” isn’t as straightforward as you may think. There is a great testing joke:

> A tester walks into a bar and orders a beer.  
>  Then they order null beers.  
>  Then they order 99999 beers.  
>  Then they order ytugihoij^%&\*( beers.  
>  Then they order a bear.  
>  A customer walks into a bar and asks where the toilets are. The bar explodes.

Turning up the “[temperature](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/how-should-i-set-the-temperature-parameter)” on Generative AI and asking it to generate some test cases, and getting some random test cases generated which a tester might not have considered, could be useful. A similar principle is applied to testing technical architectures in Barry O’Reilly’s [Residuality Theory](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877050922004975), whereby he suggests imagining random events to test the robustness of a software architecture. For example, if you architect for the scenario that giant lizards might crawl out of the River Thames and set fire to London, your application will consequently be able to survive events such as power blackouts or train strikes! Generative AI could be used to produce those off-the-wall architectural scenarios that help improve your overall application stability over time.

### Writing Code

There has been a lot published around the ability of Generative AI to [write code](https://youtu.be/qbIk7-JPB2c?t=1771). With applications such as Github Copilot and Azure Copilot being very easy to integrate into a developer’s workflow (or to use standalone as a pseudo developer), this would appear to be a central use case for Generative AI, and some believe that Generative AI will replace the software engineer’s role imminently. What we have seen with Capgemini software projects does not align with this, however – it is not possible to provide a junior developer with a Copilot license and expect them to perform like a senior developer, let alone enabling businesses to create software themselves without a software engineer present at all. There are a few big and obvious reasons for this:

1. It only saves time spent writing code  
    Developers spend surprisingly small amounts of time actually writing code There are [various studies](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/uploads/prod/2019/04/devtime-preprint-TSE19.pdf) showing percentages between 9% and 67% of time is spent “coding”, depending on the definition, the seniority of the developer, the workplace environment. Either way, there is a lot of time that a developer spends on tasks that Generative AI code assistants are not designed to help with. Github proudly announced huge [productivity gains](https://github.blog/2022-09-07-research-quantifying-github-copilots-impact-on-developer-productivity-and-happiness/) of 55% when using Copilot, but saving 55% of the 9% of time you actually spend coding isn’t as impressive - plus, most of the examples I have seen of using Copilot focus on reducing boilerplate or writing simple games, and these use-cases are not particularly relevant to the typical task list of a senior software engineer.
2. It takes value away from the development lifecycle  
    An often-quoted example of Generative AI writing code is the creation of unit tests. The best practice when developing code is to employ [Test-Driven Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test-driven_development) (TDD), an architectural approach which forces the developer to consider their code interfaces before they even write their method implementations. Relying on Generative AI to write unit tests implies they will be written after the code, hence not following TDD practices. A counter-argument is where a team inherits a codebase which does not have high unit test coverage. Is it safe to allow Generative AI to create the tests? Again, let’s go back to the initial ask - Does it matter if this generated answer is wrong? Yes it does matter. The only thing worse than no tests is incorrect tests! It is possible to generate unit tests for an existing code framework [using rules](https://symflower.com/en/) rather than Generative AI. In fact, for many Generative AI use cases this is true – a rules-based or machine learning result from a query is more useful than a generated result. What we find with many Generative AI use cases is that the useful component is very often the natural language “chatbot” interface and the way it can translate a natural language query into a search term, rather than the generated result.
3. It’s most useful for the people who don’t want it  
    It is worth considering who will find a Generative AI code assistant most useful. Senior developers are less likely to use it to generate much code, as they have already found ways to avoid boilerplate, and the difficult work of fine-tuning or bug-fixing a code base is less likely to bring useful suggestions from Copilot. It is still incredibly useful though and can save many hours of trawling the Internet. Below is a real-world example of a conversation held with Azure Copilot. The software engineer has identified an issue with the code, and uses Copilot to find a way to code a specific fix. Interestingly many of the most useful applications of Generative AI coding appear to be helping humans to write [regular expressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression)!

As you can see from the prompt engineering, considerable knowledge is needed to get the code that is required to fix a problem in a code base. Further knowledge is needed to check whether the required answer is relevant. And user beware - if you lose your chat history in Copilot (as will happen with Microsoft Copilot in “Data Protection” mode) of course you cannot get the same answer a second time by asking the question again, and this can result in many frustrating lost hours trying to find what you briefly saw via an internet search instead! So much for time saving!

When interviewed, most senior software engineers will talk about their problem-solving mindset. They enjoy problem solving, and will actively look for problems to solve. As such, a tool which does the “fun bit” of problem solving for them is not going to have a great take-up. Regular expressions aside, it is junior developers who will be most likely to take up Generative AI and use it as a crutch. And here we must go back to our initial check: Does it matter if the code they generate is wrong? In our software supply chain pipelines we usually have built-in checks to ensure compilation, look at code quality and mandate test coverage, so some “wrong” code will be weeded out by the pipelines, but there is still a huge risk that a junior developer is shipping code the impact of which they do not really understand. Currently, hackers have to go to great lengths to get unknown code into production code-bases, now it seems we are embracing a tool that will do it for them. Care must be taken here.

1. It’s only as good as the average of the code it learns from  
    The data set used by Generative AI to produce code is often all open source code bases. This is a huge dataset and fairly comprehensive – many, many programmers have contributed to open source projects. Therefore, we have literally created the world’s most average programmer. This is rarely the target that a business sets for its IT divisions… And indeed, [reports](https://www.gitclear.com/coding_on_copilot_data_shows_ais_downward_pressure_on_code_quality) are now proving that a code base maintained with Generative AI degenerates in quality over time.
2. It’s just another programming language to learn  
    There have always been layers of abstraction between humans and machines, be it 10 strings on an abacus to represent decimal numbers, typewriter keys operating little letter printers, or an [IDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_development_environment) auto-completing your code bracket pairs. Even Java code compiling to JVM bytecode which is turned into operating-system-specific instructions by the [JVM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_virtual_machine), or NoCode/LoCode drag-and-drop integrations. Most of the text-based layers of abstraction have been called “programming languages” and in that way, is Generative AI very different? It is still part of the chain between the human ideation of the software, and the executable software itself. If we all become expert prompt engineers and lose the ability to write Javascript code from scratch, is that any different from losing the ability to write C++ code because we write Javascript and get Google’s [V8 engine](https://v8.dev/) to turn it into C++ for us? Software engineering is still the same skill, but the language used is now the language of prompt engineering. The only difference is in the fact that the Generative AI answer varies over time and hence the process of debugging could get pretty interesting .

In conclusion, there are fewer use cases than one might think for Generative AI, and whilst it will be a great tool for developers and will probably be as game-changing as IDEs were in the 1990s, it isn’t quite the end to software engineering that people are predicting - developers, don’t go hanging up your boots just yet.

### Content Generation

One of the often-touted use cases of Generative AI, within and without the Software Development community, is its ability to generate content for blogs and articles. (Perhaps it is also able to read said content and “like” it?) As an example, we can compare the content of this article with the content generated when we ask Microsoft Copilot to write it, using this prompt:

“Write 2000 words on the use cases for Generative AI in the software development lifecycle. Include a definition of machine learning, generative AI and general AI in the first section. Use a formal but friendly tone. Write with the persona of a cautious software engineer.”

## Copilot

> Certainly! Let’s delve into the fascinating world of Generative AI and its impact on the software development lifecycle. As a cautious software engineer, I’ll guide you through the nuances while maintaining a friendly tone.
>
> Before we explore the use cases, let’s clarify some terms:
>
> 1. Machine Learning (ML): ML is a subset of artificial intelligence (AI) that enables systems to learn from data and improve their performance over time. It involves algorithms that automatically learn patterns and make predictions based on examples.
> 2. Generative AI (GenAI): GenAI goes beyond traditional ML by creating new content rather than just predicting existing patterns. It generates novel outputs, such as text, images, or code, based on input data or prompts.
> 3. General AI (AGI): AGI refers to an AI system with human-like cognitive abilities, including reasoning, problem-solving, and creativity. While AGI remains an aspiration, > GenAI represents a step toward achieving it.
>
> ### Code Generation and Assistance:
>
> * GenAI tools like ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot assist developers by suggesting code snippets, improving productivity, and reducing manual coding efforts.
> * However, it’s essential to recognize that GenAI isn’t a silver bullet. It complements human expertise rather than replacing it entirely.
>
>   ### Content Creation:
> * GenAI can create documentation, blog posts, and other textual content. It helps developers communicate effectively and maintain consistent documentation.
>
>   ### Test Script Generation:
> * Beyond user stories and test cases, GenAI can generate test scripts and scenarios.
> * It identifies edge cases, executes automated tests, and logs defects, enhancing software quality.
>
>   ### Unit Test Cases:
> * GenAI assists in writing unit test cases, ensuring robust code coverage.
> * Developers benefit from faster test case creation and improved code reliability.
>
>   ### Source Code Generation:
> * While GenAI isn’t writing entire applications (yet!), it can generate boilerplate code, saving time during initial setup.
> * Developers remain responsible for critical design decisions.
>
> 1. Quality Control:
>    * Always review GenAI-generated content critically. It’s a tool, not a replacement for human judgment.
>    * Verify that the code aligns with best practices, security guidelines, and project requirements.
> 2. Ethical Implications:
>    * GenAI learns from existing data, which may contain biases. Be cautious about perpetuating bias in your code.
>    * Regularly assess the ethical impact of GenAI-generated content.
> 3. Balancing Speed and Quality:
>    * GenAI accelerates development, but don’t sacrifice quality for speed.
>    * Maintain a balance—use GenAI where it enhances productivity without compromising reliability.
>
> Generative AI holds immense promise for software development. By understanding its capabilities, limitations, and ethical considerations, cautious engineers can leverage it effectively. Remember, GenAI is a valuable ally, but it’s our collective wisdom that truly drives innovation in the software development lifecycle. As a cautious software engineer, I’ve emphasized practical insights while maintaining a friendly tone. If you have any further questions or need clarification, feel free to ask! 😊 Source: Conversation with Copilot, 19/06/2024  
>  References given:
>
> 1. [Generative AI and the software development lifecycle](https://www.thoughtworks.com/insights/articles/generative-ai-software-development-lifecycle-more-than-coding-assistance)
> 2. [Automating the Software Development Life Cycle with Generative AI](https://www.architectureandgovernance.com/artificial-intelligence/automating-the-software-development-life-cycle-with-generative-ai/)
> 3. [How Generative AI is Reshaping the Software Development Lifecycle: From …](https://geekyants.com/blog/from-concept-to-code-how-generative-ai-is-reshaping-the-software-development-lifecycle)
> 4. [IMPACT OF GENERATIVE AI ON THE SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT LIFE CYCLE (SDLC)](https://ijcrt.org/papers/IJCRT2308145.pdf)

Not bad, Copilot! However it’s only 500 words. No amount of re-prompting and scolding would generate more. Seems you still can’t beat humans for their sheer ability to vacillate!

Please follow these guidelines to create your summary:

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

Present your summary in the following format:

```
{
   "summary": "Your summary here, structured with appropriate paragraphs or bullet points as needed",
   "key_excerpts": "First important quote or excerpt, Second important quote or excerpt, Third important quote or excerpt, ...Add more excerpts as needed, up to a maximum of 5"
}
```

Here are two examples of good summaries:

Example 1 (for a news article):
```json
{
   "summary": "On July 15, 2023, NASA successfully launched the Artemis II mission from Kennedy Space Center. This marks the first crewed mission to the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. The four-person crew, led by Commander Jane Smith, will orbit the Moon for 10 days before returning to Earth. This mission is a crucial step in NASA's plans to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon by 2030.",
   "key_excerpts": "Artemis II represents a new era in space exploration, said NASA Administrator John Doe. The mission will test critical systems for future long-duration stays on the Moon, explained Lead Engineer Sarah Johnson. We're not just going back to the Moon, we're going forward to the Moon, Commander Jane Smith stated during the pre-launch press conference."
}
```

Example 2 (for a scientific article):
```json
{
   "summary": "A new study published in Nature Climate Change reveals that global sea levels are rising faster than previously thought. Researchers analyzed satellite data from 1993 to 2022 and found that the rate of sea-level rise has accelerated by 0.08 mm/year² over the past three decades. This acceleration is primarily attributed to melting ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. The study projects that if current trends continue, global sea levels could rise by up to 2 meters by 2100, posing significant risks to coastal communities worldwide.",
   "key_excerpts": "Our findings indicate a clear acceleration in sea-level rise, which has significant implications for coastal planning and adaptation strategies, lead author Dr. Emily Brown stated. The rate of ice sheet melt in Greenland and Antarctica has tripled since the 1990s, the study reports. Without immediate and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, we are looking at potentially catastrophic sea-level rise by the end of this century, warned co-author Professor Michael Green."  
}
```

Remember, your goal is to create a summary that can be easily understood and utilized by a downstream research agent while preserving the most critical information from the original webpage.

args.summary:
This article by Sarah Saunders (Capgemini) examines the practical use cases for Generative AI in software development, offering a cautious engineer's perspective on both the capabilities and limitations of these tools.

**Definitions of AI types:**
- **Machine Learning (ML):** Systems that learn and adapt without explicit instructions, using algorithms to analyze patterns in data. It's a bottom-up approach where machines figure out how to get from input to output (e.g., CT scan analysis for cancerous growths in healthcare).
- **Generative AI:** AI that generates new content (images, text) in response to prompts, learned from large reference databases. The output is probabilistically generated, so asking the same question twice won't produce the same answer, and answers can be "just plain wrong."
- **General AI:** AI that matches or surpasses human capabilities across cognitive tasks. This does not currently exist.

**Key evaluation questions for Generative AI use cases:**
- Does it matter if the generated answer is wrong?
- Do you require the same answer when asking the same question twice?
- If YES to either, standard Generative AI can't be used without significant tuning.

**Examined use cases:**
1. **User Interface Design:** Viable use case since design has no wrong answers; tools like Figma and V0 by Vercel already use this. AI can accelerate prototypes and help designers break habitual patterns.
2. **Automated Testing:** Can be useful to generate random/off-the-wall test cases (by raising "temperature") that testers might not consider; similar to Barry O'Reilly's Residuality Theory.
3. **Writing Code:** The author is skeptical about this being as transformative as predicted. Key reasons:
   - Code writing only takes 9-67% of developer time (GitHub claimed 55% productivity gains, but saving 55% of the small portion of time spent coding isn't as impressive).
   - Using AI for unit tests conflicts with Test-Driven Development (TDD) practices; "The only thing worse than no tests is incorrect tests."
   - Most useful for junior developers who shouldn't rely on it as a crutch; risks shipping code whose impact isn't understood.
   - Trained on open source codebases, it creates "the world's most average programmer"; reports show AI-maintained codebases degenerate in quality over time.
   - It's just another programming language/abstraction layer to learn (prompt engineering).
   - The most useful applications involve helping with regular expressions.
4. **Content Generation:** The author demonstrates that Copilot can generate a reasonable but only 500-word article when asked for 2000 words, concluding AI can't yet match humans "for their sheer ability to vacillate."

**Conclusion:** There are fewer use cases than one might think for Generative AI. While it will be a great tool (potentially as game-changing as IDEs in the 1990s), it isn't the end of software engineering. The author includes a real-world example of using Azure Copilot for bug fixing and warns about risks including lost chat history and security concerns with AI-generated code.

This article from Google Cloud's Transform blog (published April 12, 2024, last updated April 22, 2026) presents a catalog of 1,302 real-world generative AI use cases from leading organizations. Authored by Matt Renner (President and Chief Revenue Officer, Google Cloud) and Matt A.V. Chaban, the piece was first published at Next '24 and has grown significantly, reflecting the transition into "the era of the agentic enterprise." The use cases are organized by 11 major industry groups and six agent types: Customer, Employee, Creative, Code, Data, and Security. This edition includes 301 new entries (denoted with asterisks).

The article highlights five key trends identified using Gemini Enterprise and the latest Gemini Pro models:
1. The shift from AI assistants to agentic teams, where specialized agents orchestrate entire workflows autonomously (e.g., supply chain agents triggering financial forecasting agents).
2. Natural language interfaces unlocking legacy IT systems (40-year-old SAP instances, mainframes, and COBOL codebases) without migration.
3. Gen media as a low-marginal-cost factory, with tools like Veo 3 and Imagen 4 enabling hundreds of personalized creative variations in hours.
4. Multimodality digitizing the physical world (monitoring factory floors, shelf inventory via robotics, athlete biomechanics from smartphone footage).
5. Cybersecurity moving to agentic auto-remediation, where AI agents automatically write detection rules, isolate compromised workloads, and deploy "honeytokens."

The article includes detailed case studies across industries. In Automotive & Logistics, examples include Continental (in-vehicle speech solutions), General Motors' OnStar virtual assistant, MercedesBenz (MBUX Virtual Assistant via Gemini), Volkswagen (myVW app with multimodal camera features), and LUXGEN (chatbot reducing customer service workload by 30%). Employee agents include Toyota (over 10,000 man-hours saved annually), Uber, and Valeo (deploying Gemini to 100,000-person workforce with 35% of code AI-generated). Data agents include BMW (SORDI.ai digital twins, SLMs for vehicles), Geotab (analyzing billions of data points daily from 4.7 million vehicles), UPS (digital twin of its distribution network), Moglix (4X sourcing efficiency improvement), and Domina (80% better real-time data access). Security examples include BMW (95% reduction in critical issues via Wiz).

In Business & Professional Services, customer agents include Deloitte's "Care Finder" (finding providers in under a minute vs. 5-8 minute calls), Intuit (TurboTax autofill across ten tax forms), Wagestream (handling 80%+ internal customer inquiries), and atmira (114 million monthly requests, 30-40% better recovery rates). Employee agents include Altumatim (eDiscovery from months to hours with 90%+ accuracy), Harvey (Gemini 2.5 Pro document reviews), KPMG (90% Gemini Enterprise adoption with 100+ agents in first month), Benifex (Project Brain multi-agent system on 20+ years of benefits data), Instalily (cutting diagnosis time from 15 minutes to under 10 seconds, 98% lower serving costs), and Gelato (ticket assignment accuracy from 60% to 90%). Creative agents include AdVon Commerce (93,673-product catalog processed in under a month, $17M revenue lift in 60 days), Comeen (multilingual subtitles in 40 languages), and Hotmob (33% productivity boost). Code agents include Capgemini, Infosys (equipping 100,000+ developers with Gemini Enterprise), and TCS.

Agility: With compute in-house, experimentation and scaling become faster and more controlled. 3️⃣ The Q2 Context — Caution + Momentum TCS’s management struck a confident tone: ✅ Faster client decision-making ✅ No new macro threats ✅ Improving demand visibility The message: short-term moderation, but long-term conviction. 4️⃣ Why This Matters Differentiation: Owning AI infrastructure builds defensible advantage in a crowded sector. args.summary:
This LinkedIn feed page contains a collection of posts about the Indian IT sector's transformation toward AI in 2025-2026, covering hiring trends, financial results, and strategic pivots. Key topics include:

**Capgemini India Hiring (2025):** Capgemini India announced plans to hire 40,000-45,000 professionals in 2025 with a focus on AI-skilling. About 35-40% of roles are earmarked for experienced professionals, with collaboration across 50+ campuses. Candidates are advised to focus on ML, LLMs, data engineering, and generative AI tools. Recommendations for candidates include skill alignment, domain integration, balancing technical depth with agile mindset, and networking.

**Top 10 IT Company News (October 2025):** Key headlines include: Infosys facing a ₹415 crore GST show-cause notice over inflated export turnover; TCS reporting muted single-digit Q2 growth due to weak demand from North America/Europe; HCLTech expanding AI services for BFSI/healthcare; Wipro restructuring leadership with new CTO and AI strategy head; Tech Mahindra partnering with NVIDIA for GenAI models; LTIMindtree winning a $100M deal from a European bank; Persistent Systems acquiring a US cloud firm; Mphasis launching a quantum computing lab; Zoho hitting $1 billion revenue milestone; and TCS/Infosys/Wipro facing GenAI talent crunch.

**TCS vs HCLTech Q2 Comparison:** TCS Q2 FY26: Revenue ₹65,280 crore (↑1.6%), Net Profit ₹12,590 crore (↑5.7%), Margin 24.4%, Deal wins $7-9B expected. HCLTech Q1 FY26: Revenue ₹30,349 crore (↑8.2%), Net Profit ₹3,843 crore (↓9.7%), Margin 16.3%, Deal wins $1.81B. TCS protects margins with slow growth while HCLTech chases revenue with lower margins. Job market data shows 80,000+ roles eliminated across IT sector, TCS cutting 2% workforce (~12,000 people), but AI/ML roles up 41%, and 75% of AI roles pay 28% more than traditional IT roles. AI architect salaries range ₹21-44 lakhs. Tier-2/3 cities are becoming hiring hubs.

**TCS AI Infrastructure Pivot:** TCS announced a $5-6 billion (some posts say $6.5-7 billion / ₹55,000 crore) capex plan to build 1 GW of data-centre capacity, signaling a shift from people-led services to AI-powered infrastructure. TCS reported a net headcount drop of 19,755 employees in Q2 FY26 (sharpest fall since 2008), which some call restructuring and others call silent layoffs. The pivot is described as moving from "billing hours to building horsepower" and from "code export to compute independence."

**TCS UK Expansion:** TCS announced plans to create 5,000 new jobs in the UK over the next three years and launched an AI Experience Zone and Design Studio in London (modeled on PacePort centers). TCS supports ~42,000 jobs in the UK, contributed £3.3 billion to the UK economy in FY2024, and paid over £780 million in taxes. The announcement came during UK PM Keir Starmer's business delegation visit to TCS's Banyan Park campus in Mumbai.

**Indian IT Sector Silent Transformation (October 2025):** Infosys revenue ₹44,990 crore (up 8.55% YoY); TCS ₹65,300 crore (up 5.3% YoY); midcaps like Mphasis and Persistent growing 11-14%. AI deal inquiries up 25% YoY; 50,000+ job exits in 2025 with 250,000 employees being reskilled in AI/cloud. Cloud services now 18% of revenue (up from 14%); cybersecurity growing 22% YoY. Analysts project FY26 growth of 2-5%, FY27 growth of 6-8%, with 30% of new spending going to AI/cloud.

**Wipro Overview (FY25):** Revenue ₹890.9 billion (~US$10.4 billion), Net Profit ₹131.4 billion (+18.9% YoY), Operating Margin 17.1%, Operating Cash Flow 128.2% of net income. Vertical mix: BFSI 34.3%, Consumer 19.1%, Healthcare 14.1%, Manufacturing & Energy 17.2%, Technology & Communications 15.3%. Trained 87,000+ employees in Generative AI during FY25. Large deal bookings were US$5.4 billion. Shifting to consulting-led, AI-driven model under Chairman Rishad Premji.

**Other Hiring News:** Nagarro plans to hire 1,000 more professionals in India over 12-18 months (already has 13,000 employees in India and 700 open positions). Alvarez & Marsal plans to double India headcount to 2,000 by 2028. These announcements come amid projections of a hiring slowdown in October-December quarter.

**Infosys & Hiring Amid Automation:** Analysts note Infosys and other Indian IT firms continue hiring even as automation expands, with a "humans working with machines" narrative. For fresh talent, AI fluency and adaptability are key entry credentials.

## Main article

Capgemini CEO Aiman Ezzat said the French IT company is “clearly pivoting” to facilitate artificial intelligence adoption, which will fuel sales this year.

Revenue in 2026 will grow 6.5% to 8.5%, the company said in a statement on Feb. 13. That compared to the 7.2% average analyst forecast compiled by Bloomberg.

Capgemini offers software, cloud services, engineering and outsourcing services to corporate clients and has been partnering with firms like Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and compatriot Mistral to offer AI products to its business users. Still, companies selling specialized software and consulting services have been targeted in a broad selloff in businesses seen as vulnerable to AI innovation.

“In 2026, our growth will be fueled by AI-led transformation programs, Intelligent Operations where we are signing some large deals, and sovereignty where demand is significantly increasing,” Ezzat said in the statement.

Capgemini shares rose 1.5% to €101.20 at 9:09 a.m. in Paris trading. The stock has dropped about 29% so far this year.

Revenue grew 1.7% to €22.5 billion ($26.7 billion) in 2025, compared to analyst estimates for €22.3 billion. Net income for the period declined 4.2% from a year earlier to €1.6 billion.

The French company is also dealing with an economic slowdown that’s forcing customers to hold off on new spending. Ongoing uncertainty around tariffs and trade as well as high interest rates are making companies more cautious about investing in technology and IT.

While demand was “subdued in some markets” last year, the company said customers were focused on adding AI tools to their businesses and Paris-based Capgemini is seeing “growing momentum” in demand from the defense industry and for sovereign technology.

Capgemini said this month it plans to sell its US-based unit [Capgemini Government Solutions](https://www.staffingindustry.com/news/global-daily-news/capgemini-to-sell-us-subsidiary-with-ice-contract-after-criticism-in-europe)due to scrutiny and critics over its contracts with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

(This article first appeared in SIA’s Global Daily News on Feb.13.)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On March 25, 2025, Deloitte announced the significant scaling of its Global Artificial Intelligence (AI) Simulation Center of Excellence (CoE), building on its global investment of US$3 billion in Generative AI (GenAI) through fiscal year 2030. The CoE was first launched in Bengaluru, India to serve Deloitte's global network, aiming to accelerate clients' decision-making, mitigate risks, and maximize ROI. It leverages real-time insights, advanced visualizations, simulations, scenario modeling, digital twins, and multi-agent systems.

The Simulation CoE is newly integrated into existing Deloitte Experience Centers to offer immersive client experiences and augments Deloitte's Global GenAI Market Incubator. The CoE focuses on four simulations designed to help executives accelerate and improve decision-making and serves as a dynamic hub orchestrated with regional centers globally. Deloitte has applied the CoE to create enterprise simulations for the power and utilities sector, addressing use cases such as real-time monitoring, preventive maintenance, and hazard sensing.

Deloitte provides leading professional services to nearly 90% of the Fortune Global 500 and thousands of private companies, spans more than 150 countries and territories, and employs over 470,000 people worldwide, building on its 180+ year history.

## Deloitte's 2025 Tech Value Survey: AI Dominance and Portfolio Imbalance

**Published:** 2025 (fielded May–June 2025)

**Authors:** Tim Smith, Gregory Dost, Garima Dhasmana, Parth Patwari, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, Iram Parveen

**Overview:** This report, based on a survey of nearly 550 business and technology leaders across five industries (consumer; energy/resources/industrials; financial services; life sciences/healthcare; technology/media/telecom), analyzes how AI investments are consuming an outsized share of digital budgets, potentially leaving other critical technology areas underfunded.

### Key Findings:

**1. AI is Dominating Digital Budgets:**

--- SOURCE 2: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation ---
URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This McKinsey Global Survey article, published November 5, 2025, examines the state of AI adoption across organizations. Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, while revenue benefits are reported in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development.

The survey identifies "AI high performers" (about 6% of respondents who attribute 5%+ EBIT impact and report significant value) as distinguished by several factors: they are more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; more likely to set growth and/or innovation objectives (not just efficiency); nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows (identified as one of the strongest contributing factors via a relative weights analysis of 31 variables); three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to have senior leaders demonstrating ownership and commitment; more likely to have defined human-validation processes; and more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI (one-third of high performers do so, versus about three-quarters scaling AI overall). Successful practices align with McKinsey's Rewired research across six dimensions: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption/scaling.

On workforce impact, expectations vary: 32% of respondents expect enterprise-wide workforce decreases of 3% or more in the coming year, 43% expect no change, and 13% expect increases. A median of 17% of respondents report declines in function workforce sizes in the past year due to AI, but a median of 30% expect decreases next year. Larger organizations and high performers are more likely to expect meaningful workforce changes. Most organizations hired for AI-related roles in the past year, with software and data engineers most in demand.

Risk mitigation efforts are becoming more common. Respondents report acting to manage an average of four AI-related risks today versus two in 2022. Fifty-one percent of respondents from organizations using AI report at least one negative consequence, with nearly one-third reporting consequences from AI inaccuracy—the most commonly experienced and mitigated risk. Explainability is the second-most-reported risk but is not among the most commonly mitigated. High performers report more negative consequences (particularly IP infringement and regulatory compliance) but also protect against more risks.

The survey was in the field June 25 to July 29, 2025, with 1,993 respondents from 105 nations, weighted by GDP contribution. Thirty-eight percent work for organizations with over $1 billion in annual revenues. Authors include Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, and Tara Balakrishnan from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey.
</summary>

"Three years since the introduction of gen AI tools triggered a new era of artificial intelligence, nearly nine out of ten survey respondents say their organizations are regularly using AI—but the pace of progress remains uneven."

--- SOURCE 1: IBM Introduces Granite 3.0: High Performing AI Models Built for Business - Oct 21, 2024 ---
URL: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2024-10-21-ibm-introduces-granite-3-0-high-performing-ai-models-built-for-business

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On October 21, 2024, IBM announced the release of Granite 3.0, its most advanced family of AI models, at its annual TechXchange event in Armonk, NY. The third-generation Granite flagship language models outperform or match similarly sized models from leading providers on many academic and industry benchmarks while showcasing strong performance, transparency, and safety. Released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, the models are unique in combining performance, flexibility, and autonomy for enterprise clients.

The Granite 3.0 family includes: (1) 8B and 2B language models designed as "workhorse" models for enterprise AI tasks including RAG, classification, summarization, entity extraction, and tool use; (2) Granite 3.0 1B-A400M and 3B-A800M Mixture of Experts (MoE) models for low-latency and CPU-based deployments; (3) updated pre-trained Granite Time Series models trained on 3x more data that outperform 10x larger models from Google and Alibaba; and (4) new Granite Guardian 3.0 8B and 2B safety models providing the most comprehensive risk and harm detection capabilities available, including RAG-specific checks (groundedness, context relevance, answer relevance).

Key benchmark results: The Granite 3.0 8B Instruct model leads on average against state-of-the-art similar-sized open-source models from Meta and Mistral on Hugging Face's OpenLLM Leaderboard, on IBM's AttaQ safety benchmark, and across enterprise tasks of RAG, tool use, and cybersecurity. Models were trained on over 12 trillion tokens across 12 natural languages and 116 programming languages using a novel two-stage training method. By end of 2024, the 8B and 2B models are expected to support 128K context windows and multi-modal document understanding.

IBM announced the models would be available on HuggingFace under Apache 2.0 license, with instruct variants commercially available on watsonx.ai (including IP indemnity), NVIDIA NIM microservices, Google Cloud's Vertex AI, Ollama, and Replicate. IBM also announced the next generation of watsonx Code Assistant, IBM Granite.Code VS Code extension, new watsonx.ai developer tools, and AI agent chat features for watsonx Orchestrate (Q1 2025). IBM Consulting Advantage was expanded with Granite 3.0 as the default model, empowering 160,000 consultants.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
IBM's third-generation Granite flagship language models can outperform or match similarly sized models from leading model providers on many academic and industry benchmarks, showcasing strong performance, transparency and safety.
</key_excerpts>

This research note analyzes IBM's launch of its Granite 3.0 family of large language models (LLMs), marking a strategic departure from the industry trend of massive general-purpose models. IBM focuses instead on smaller, more efficient, and cost-effective models tailored to specific enterprise needs, aimed at leveraging the 99% of enterprise data that remains untapped by internet-trained models.

**Key Strategic Points:**
- IBM released Granite 3.0 under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, allowing full commercial rights, transparency, and community collaboration (contrasting with models like Meta's Llama, which have certain commercial-use restrictions).
- At IBM's February 2025 Investor Day, CEO Matt Hicks touted an AI TAM approaching $1T by the end of the decade, focusing on three pillars: Cost reduction, Complexity reduction (smaller, easier-to-deploy LLMs with built-in security), and Expertise (embedding domain expertise into AI workflows). **Granite 3.0 Model Family:**

- **Granite Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Models**: Efficient inference, low latency, suitable for CPU and edge deployments.
- **Granite Time Series Models**: State-of-the-art zero/few-shot forecasting, outperforming models ten times larger.

**Performance and Cost:**
- The 8B Instruct model leads or matches similar-sized models from Meta and Mistral on Hugging Face's OpenLLM Leaderboard.
- Granite models offer cost reductions of up to 90% compared to larger models like GPT-4 and Llama 3.1, with comparable performance in enterprise tasks.

**Integration and Adoption:**

**Future Vision:** IBM emphasizes the progression from AI assistants to autonomous AI agents capable of complex reasoning, multi-step problem-solving, tool use, and multi-agent orchestration, with plans for pre-built domain-specific agents and integration with platforms like Adobe Firefly and Salesforce.

This IBM Think article (published 19 August 2024, by Keith O'Brien and Amanda Downie) explores the use of artificial intelligence in talent acquisition—the use of AI in sourcing and hiring new employees. It highlights how organizations can use machine learning, generative AI, natural language processing (NLP), and automation to improve hiring workflows, save money, and find better candidates.

**Why it's important:** Hiring managers can use AI to meet three key goals: improve the candidate experience (via chatbots and demonstrating tech-forward workflows), enhance recruitment strategies (freeing HR professionals for strategic initiatives), and foster happier employees (by automating manual tasks).

**Key use cases:** 1) Idea and script generation, 2) Candidate screening (analyzing public info like social media for red flags), 3) Rapid employee onboarding, 4) Customized job postings (automating creation of tailored versions), and 5) One-way video interviews (with care needed to explain the process to candidates).

**Strategies:** 1) Audit roles and tasks, 2) Identify the right tools (coordinating with IT and HR), 3) Build for responsible AI (considering reputational, ethical, and legal ramifications), 4) Test and learn (to identify biases), and 5) Debrief and review with a natural cadence of assessments.

**Benefits:** Reduced recruiting and hiring costs (e.g., AI scheduling interviews, scanning resumes), quicker hiring decisions (reduced time-to-hire via automated resume screening and candidate matching), improved candidate engagement (personalized recommendations, predictive analytics), and improved quality of hires (aiding retention and identifying what attracts top employees).

**Challenges:** Inherited bias (carried over from human-built systems), increased startup costs (offset by long-term efficiency gains), decreased human connection (AI should be an enhancement, not a replacement), and prospect/employee concerns (61% of Americans are unaware organizations use AI in hiring, per Forbes October 2023).

**Future outlook:** AI will become a more powerful force as language models improve, with AI increasingly handling job postings and resume screening. Organizations must ensure systems are free from bias and set up to identify diverse candidates.
</summary>

URL: https://capgemini.github.io/ai/use-cases-for-ai

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Sarah Saunders (Capgemini) examines the practical use cases for Generative AI in software development, offering a cautious engineer's perspective on both the capabilities and limitations of these tools.

**Definitions of AI types:**
- **Machine Learning (ML):** Systems that learn and adapt without explicit instructions, using algorithms to analyze patterns in data. It's a bottom-up approach where machines figure out how to get from input to output (e.g., CT scan analysis for cancerous growths in healthcare).
- **Generative AI:** AI that generates new content (images, text) in response to prompts, learned from large reference databases. The output is probabilistically generated, so asking the same question twice won't produce the same answer, and answers can be "just plain wrong."
- **General AI:** AI that matches or surpasses human capabilities across cognitive tasks. This does not currently exist.

**Key evaluation questions for Generative AI use cases:**
- Does it matter if the generated answer is wrong?
- Do you require the same answer when asking the same question twice?
- If YES to either, standard Generative AI can't be used without significant tuning.

**Examined use cases:**
1. **User Interface Design:** Viable use case since design has no wrong answers; tools like Figma and V0 by Vercel already use this. AI can accelerate prototypes and help designers break habitual patterns.
2. **Automated Testing:** Can be useful to generate random/off-the-wall test cases (by raising "temperature") that testers might not consider; similar to Barry O'Reilly's Residuality Theory.
3. **Writing Code:** The author is skeptical about this being as transformative as predicted. Key reasons:
   - Code writing only takes 9-67% of developer time (GitHub claimed 55% productivity gains, but saving 55% of the small portion of time spent coding isn't as impressive).
   - Using AI for unit tests conflicts with Test-Driven Development (TDD) practices; "The only thing worse than no tests is incorrect tests."
   - Most useful for junior developers who shouldn't rely on it as a crutch; risks shipping code whose impact isn't understood.
   - Trained on open source codebases, it creates "the world's most average programmer"; reports show AI-maintained codebases degenerate in quality over time.
   - It's just another programming language/abstraction layer to learn (prompt engineering).
   - The most useful applications involve helping with regular expressions.
4. **Content Generation:** The author demonstrates that Copilot can generate a reasonable but only 500-word article when asked for 2000 words, concluding AI can't yet match humans "for their sheer ability to vacillate."

**Conclusion:** There are fewer use cases than one might think for Generative AI. While it will be a great tool (potentially as game-changing as IDEs in the 1990s), it isn't the end of software engineering. The author includes a real-world example of using Azure Copilot for bug fixing and warns about risks including lost chat history and security concerns with AI-generated code.
</summary>

Do I require the same answer to the same question if I ask it twice? If the answer to either of these questions is YES, then you cannot use a standard Generative AI solution without some significant tuning.", "The only thing worse than no tests is incorrect tests!", "What we find with many Generative AI use cases is that the useful component is very often the natural language 'chatbot' interface and the way it can translate a natural language query into a search term, rather than the generated result.", "Therefore, we have literally created the world's most average programmer. Happy to share our Q3 2025 revenues, announced this morning. The Group delivered a strong Q3, better than expected, thanks to the relevance of our AI-powered business and technology partner positioning and the targeted actions initiated a year ago, in a demand environment that is largely unchanged. Revenue growth improved in all regions, with a significant acceleration in North America. Demand continued to be driven by [#Cloud](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fcloud&trk=public_post-text), [#Data](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fdata&trk=public_post-text) and [#AI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fai&trk=public_post-text), with a strong focus on efficiency and optimization. We are accelerating the integration of [#GenAI](https://www.linkedin.com/signup/cold-join?session_redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.linkedin.com%2Ffeed%2Fhashtag%2Fgenai&trk=public_post-text) across our service portfolio to enable clients to achieve tangible business value. This is reflected in robust deal wins in generative and agentic AI. With the acquisition of [WNS](https://www.linkedin.com/company/wns-global-services?trk=public_post-text) now complete, we lead in the fast-growing Intelligent Operations market addressing client demand for agentic AI-powered business operations. On the back of this strong performance, we raise our growth target for 2025 and narrow our operating margin target. args.summary: Aiman Ezzat, CEO of Capgemini Group, announced the company's Q3 2025 results on LinkedIn. The Group delivered a strong Q3, better than expected, with revenue growth improving in all regions, including a significant acceleration in North America, despite a largely unchanged demand environment. Demand continued to be driven by Cloud, Data, and AI, with a strong focus on efficiency and optimization. Capgemini is accelerating the integration of GenAI across its service portfolio, reflected in robust deal wins in generative and agentic AI. With the acquisition of WNS now complete, Capgemini leads in the fast-growing Intelligent Operations market. Based on this strong performance, the company raised its 2025 growth target to between +2.0% and +2.5% (at constant currency) and narrowed its operating margin target to between 13.3% and 13.4%. Q3 revenue rose by 2.9% in constant currency terms. Olaf Pietschner (CRO Asia Pacific & Middle East) noted that the Asia-Pacific and Latin America region (9% of 2024 Group revenues) increased by +13.6%. Comments on the post were largely positive from employees and leadership, praising the WNS integration, GenAI momentum, and strong results, though one employee commented that employee issues are not being addressed alongside company revenue gains.

# IT Giant Capgemini Will Invest $2.2 Billion in Generative AI

July 28, 2023, 8:14 PM UTC

![Yun Park](https://bwrite-static.bloombergindustry.com/dims4/default/ed08a9d/2147483647/brightness/4x0/brightness/0x-1/crop/4672x4672+0+0/resize/80x80%3E/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fbloomberg-bna-brightspot.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2F84%2Fe0%2Fbba2cb9244bb90fba4c29f22c22b%2Fypark-bloombergindustry.com.jpg)

Yun Park

Reporter

[![](https://news-cdn.bindg.com/indg/images/20_AUTO_icon-X-black.webp "Tweet Yun Park")](https://twitter.com/@yunpark_)

Global IT and consulting giant Capgemini announced major investment in a portfolio of generative AI services on Friday, noting increasing client demands in recent months.

The Paris-based company will spend 2 billion euros ($2.2 billion) on artificial intelligence over three years “to build its leadership in this breakthrough technology, that must be deployed responsibly, reliably, and sustainably,” CEO Aiman Ezzat said in an earnings release. “We are developing a portfolio of industry-specific offers and signing strategic partnerships, notably with Google Cloud and Microsoft, while training most of our workforce through our Data & AI Campus to fully leverage the power of generative AI in our operations.”

Capgemini will provide generative AI services for strategy, customer experience, software engineering, and enterprise, it [said in a separate release](https://aboutblaw.com/9E1)[.](https://aboutblaw.com/9E1) It has delivered generative AI projects in life science, consumer products & retail, and financial services for the past few years. The group is currently working with Heathrow Airport to deliver AI-based e-commerce and passenger services.

Under the new portfolio, four generative AI assistants will serve to enhance customer experience, the company said. They include a synthetic design assistant for hyper-personalized customer experience, personalized chatbots for customer self-service, a content and knowledge assistant for customer care services, and a product and offers knowledge assistant for sales team performance.

* **Growth at constant exchange rates**[**\***](#_ftn1) **of +0.2% in H1 and +0.7% in Q2**

***Paris, July 30, 2025 –*** The Board of Directors of Capgemini SE, chaired by Paul Hermelin, convened yesterday in Paris to review and adopt the accounts[[1]](#_ftn2) of [Capgemini](https://www.capgemini.com/) Group for the first half of 2025.

Aiman Ezzat, Chief Executive Officer of the Capgemini Group, said: *“The Group’s performance continued to improve in Q2. Momentum was positive in North America, the UK and APAC & LatAm and stable in Continental Europe, including France. Our bookings were solid, with a strong book-to-bill ratio of 1.08, and the operating margin was stable at 12.4%. In a challenging environment, our performance in H1 demonstrates the resilience of the Group’s operating model.*

*Client demand continues to be driven by efficiency and cost optimization. We benefit from good traction in cloud, data & AI and digital core and have built a strong pipeline in generative and agentic AI, which accounted for more than 7% of Group bookings in Q2. On this front, we launched our* [*Resonance AI Framework*](https://www.capgemini.com/news/press-releases/capgemini-unveils-strategic-ai-framework-to-turn-enterprise-ambition-into-measurable-business-impact/) *and further enhanced our AI offerings and partnerships with major players such as Mistral AI and SAP. Demand is increasing in the emerging areas of defense and sovereignty, as well as in digital business process services primarily driven by intelligent operations.*

*Going into Q3, we see some stability in the environment, while we retain our cautious stance to account for the uncertainty created by geopolitical tensions and a slow economy. In this context and on the strength of this resilient H1 performance, we narrow the range of our constant currency growth outlook for the year to between -1 and +1%.”*
