# How to Accelerate Progress on AI

# How to Accelerate Progress on AI

Our rapid internal deployment offers useful lessons for our clients.

![](/contentassets/a245f6a5741744129de8b26b5f6661db/32883_ai-at-bainnb007401-1-1.jpg?width=110&height=110&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Brief

###### How to Accelerate Progress on AI

A dedicated issue of *Time* magazine. A massive installation at the Museum of Modern Art. Even a prime-time special hosted by Oprah. No doubt the speed at which [artificial intelligence](/fr-ca/insights/what-is-artificial-intelligence/) has leaped from technological advance to cultural phenomenon is unprecedented.

But CEOs could be forgiven for experiencing a certain cognitive dissonance regarding these developments, because many businesses today are moving more slowly than they’d like in deploying AI. By now, most company leaders don’t need to be convinced that AI has the potential to transform how work gets done and even how companies are organized. But the challenge of “crossing the chasm” from hype to results requires commitment and innovation.

We know, because we’ve crossed it. At Bain offices around the world, all 18,000 team members have access to AI tools, and 12,000 are actively using them to address in minutes a variety of manual tasks that once took hours or even days. That means they can devote more time to analyzing and applying the strategic insights that deliver real value to clients.

What’s perhaps most remarkable—*and instructive*—about our journey is how quickly AI has become ubiquitous across our organization.

What’s perhaps most remarkable—and instructive—about our journey is how quickly AI has become ubiquitous across our organization. As one example, within two weeks of making ChatGPT Enterprise available to everyone at Bain, we achieved 60% adoption among our consulting and expert delivery teams.

Yes, two weeks. So it is possible to get results from AI quickly—if you approach deployment the right way. Here are three things we’ve learned that can help boost the velocity of your AI initiatives.

### 1. Involve your employees

### We quickly achieved high adoption by designing AI pilots to be core to what our teams do

adoption

Like most companies exploring the power of AI, we began with pilots. But we designed these pilots to be core to what our teams do. Launching in our Seattle and Washington, DC, offices, we quickly achieved 80% adoption by building ChatGPT Enterprise tools that could produce Python code for data analysis and automate complex Excel processes. Consultants instantly saw the labor-saving value of these tools and how they freed up capacity to deliver differentiated insights.

The success of those pilots prompted our senior leadership team to orchestrate a comprehensive rollout of ChatGPT Enterprise, which, as noted, gained 60% adoption among our consultants in just two weeks. In a sense, this rapid adoption was a two-way street: We provided upskilling via training sessions and resources (see below), while many of our consultants, inspired by the tools’ ease of use, quickly became power users and stepped up to train others and further explore what the tools can do.

Bain employees have used ChatGPT Enterprise to create *more than 2,000 MyGPTs* customized for specific tasks.

In fact, employee innovation has been a pillar of our success. Our rapid adoption of AI hearkens back to the spread of kaizen across the manufacturing sector, when companies learned that employees on the front lines were best positioned to recommend new ways of working. To date, Bain employees have used ChatGPT Enterprise to create more than 2,000 MyGPTs customized for specific tasks. # Widening talent gap threatens executives’ AI ambitions – Bain & Company

* March 04, 2025
* min read

Press release

###### Widening talent gap threatens executives’ AI ambitions – Bain & Company

* 44% of executives say a lack of in-house expertise is slowing AI adoption
* Demand for AI skills has grown 21% annually since 2019 amid an AI talent shortage likely to persist through 2027
* Compensation for AI skills continues to increase, growing 11% annually since 2019

**NEW YORK – March 4, 2025 –** Businesses are facing a growing shortage of skilled professionals as they race to implement AI. New [research from Bain & Company](/insights/ai-the-ambitions-are-bold-but-the-talent-is-scarce-snap-chart/) reveals AI-related job postings have surged by 21% annually since 2019, with compensation growing 11% annually over the same period. Yet the number of qualified candidates has not kept pace, creating a widening talent gap that is slowing AI adoption.

“AI is at the forefront of corporate transformation, but without the right talent, businesses will struggle to move from ambition to implementation,” said [Sarah Elk](/our-team/sarah-elk/), Americas head of [AI, Insights, and Solutions](/vector-digital/ai-insights-and-solutions/) at Bain & Company. “Executives see the growing AI talent gap as a major roadblock to innovation, limiting businesses’ ability to scale and compete in an AI-driven world. Companies navigating this increasingly competitive hiring landscape need to take action now, upskilling existing teams, expanding hiring strategies, and rethinking ways to attract and retain AI talent.”

Bain’s study finds nearly half (44%) of executives cite a lack of in-house AI expertise as a key barrier to implementing generative AI. This talent gap is expected to persist through at least 2027, with its impact varying in severity across global markets:

* **United States: 1 in 2 AI jobs could be left unfilled by 2027.** Bain projects AI job demand could reach up to more than 1.3 million in the US over the next two years, while supply is on track to hit less than 645,000—implying the need to reskill up to 700,000 US workers.
* **Germany could see the biggest AI talent gap, with around 70% of AI jobs unfilled by 2027.** With an estimated 62,000 AI professionals available to fill 190,000 – 219,000 job openings in 2027, there is a clear opportunity for reskilling employees in Germany.
* **United Kingdom may see talent shortfalls of more than 50%,** with just 105,000 AI workers available to fill up to 255,000 AI jobs in 2027.
* **India’s AI sector could surpass 2.3 million job openings by 2027** while the AI talent pool is expected to grow to around 1.2 million, presenting an opportunity to reskill more than 1 million workers.
* **Australia could see a shortfall of more than 60,000 AI professionals by 2027,** with just 84,000 AI specialists available to fill up to 146,000 jobs.

args.summary:
This PRNewswire press release from March 4, 2025 announces new research from Bain & Company revealing a widening AI talent gap that is threatening executives' AI ambitions.

Key findings from the research:
- 44% of executives cite a lack of in-house AI expertise as a key barrier to implementing generative AI
- AI-related job postings have surged by 21% annually since 2019
- Compensation for AI skills has grown 11% annually over the same period
- The AI talent shortage is expected to persist through at least 2027

Regional projections for 2027 include:
- United States: 1 in 2 AI jobs could be left unfilled; demand could reach over 1.3 million jobs while supply tracks below 645,000, implying a need to reskill up to 700,000 workers
- Germany: Expected to see the biggest AI talent gap, with around 70% of AI jobs unfilled; only about 62,000 AI professionals available to fill 190,000–219,000 openings
- United Kingdom: Talent shortfalls of more than 50%, with just 105,000 AI workers to fill up to 255,000 AI jobs
- India: Could surpass 2.3 million AI job openings while the talent pool grows to ~1.2 million, presenting an opportunity to reskill over 1 million workers
- Australia: Shortfall of more than 60,000 AI professionals, with 84,000 specialists available to fill up to 146,000 jobs

Sarah Elk, Americas head of AI, Insights, and Solutions at Bain & Company, emphasized that executives must take action by upskilling existing teams, expanding hiring strategies, and rethinking how to attract and retain AI talent. The press release also includes media contact information and background on Bain & Company, a global consultancy operating across 65 cities in 40 countries.

# AI, Insights, & Solutions (AIS)

# AI, Insights, & Solutions (AIS)

Join AI, Insights, & Solutions (AIS), a multidisciplinary team of experts who bring technical and business acumen to solve transformative challenges across industries. AIS drives innovation by integrating AI and data-driven solutions for real impact. From launching new ventures to reimagining user experiences and building tech-enabled products, you’ll help shape what’s next. Be part of a team that turns strategy into breakthrough results.

Data science & machine learning (ML)

Build advanced models, prototypes, and AI solutions. Work with large datasets and complex systems to develop scalable, repeatable solutions.

AI & engineering

Design, build, and optimize AI-powered platforms and digital transformation solutions that enhance performance and drive business impact.

Innovation & digital experience design

Create and scale digital businesses, products, and experiences that blend strategy, technology, and human-centered design.

Advanced analytics experts

Develop AI-driven analytics strategies, build predictive models, and drive high-value insights that help clients make informed decisions.

Insights & primary research

Uncover behaviors, trends, and business drivers using qualitative and quantitative research, data science, and market intelligence to inform strategic decisions.

Product management

Bridge consulting and technical teams to turn business needs into scalable solutions. Lead high-impact product development while growing technical and business expertise.

## Integrated AI expertise powering business transformation and breakthrough results

AI, Insights, & Solutions combines technical expertise with business acumen to help clients solve their most pressing challenges. Our collaborative culture enables an end-to-end approach to digital transformation, strengthened by strategic investments and industry partnerships. We lead AI-driven transformation, enabling clients to innovate, scale, and integrate [AI](/insights/what-is-artificial-intelligence/) into their operations.

Our experts—strategists, engineers, data scientists, designers, and product managers—work in integrated teams to develop data-driven solutions. One day, you might build production-grade code for a luxury retailer shifting to direct-to-consumer; the next, [deploy AI-powered simulation tools](/careers/impact-stories/athena-pathway/) to enhance a high-performance sailing team’s training. We design machine learning models, cloud platforms, and automation tools that drive lasting impact—delivering seamless, personalized customer experiences at scale.

We also shape Bain’s proprietary products and internal capabilities, constantly evolving our toolkit to stay at the forefront. With experience in startups, innovation labs, and venture-backed companies, our team strengthens the entrepreneurial spirit embedded in Bain’s culture. If you’re looking for a place to push boundaries and be part of a team that supports your growth, this is it.

## What our people love about working on this team

![](/contentassets/7d2f08d0567a4671a61a0ea9caede29a/value_prop_icon.png?width=50&height=50&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Enable leading companies to win with AI

Build generative AI capabilities and end-to-end solutions, unlocking value for clients across industries.

![](/globalassets/careers/images/value_prop_icon.png?width=50&height=50&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Launch new ventures

Help leading companies transform their futures by designing new experiences, digital products, and businesses.

![](/contentassets/7d2f08d0567a4671a61a0ea9caede29a/value_prop_icon.png?width=50&height=50&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Learn from the best

Get mentored by current and future leaders in their field and develop sharp business acumen and communication skills.

![](/contentassets/7d2f08d0567a4671a61a0ea9caede29a/value_prop_icon.png?width=50&height=50&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Have an impact

You’ll work on high-value problems. Our projects tend to be the CEO’s top concern and your discoveries will guide major businesses and societal organizations.

![](/contentassets/c246786342cf4976bef57553a8a46aaa/value_prop_icon.png?width=50&height=50&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Develop skills in multiple areas

You’ll get to work on many projects across a variety of industries. We find that’s the key to recognizing patterns and making discoveries.

![](/globalassets/careers/images/value_prop_icon.png?width=50&height=50&rmode=crop&rsampler=bicubic&compand=true)

Well-earned balance

Here, you’ll get to pursue and balance purpose, fun, recognition, and growth in a uniquely collaborative environment.

URL: https://www.deloitte.com/global/en/about/press-room/global-gen-ai-simulation-center-of-excellence.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On March 25, 2025, Deloitte announced the significant scaling of its Global Artificial Intelligence (AI) Simulation Center of Excellence (CoE), building on its global investment of US$3 billion in Generative AI (GenAI) through fiscal year 2030. The CoE was first launched in Bengaluru, India to serve Deloitte's global network, aiming to accelerate clients' decision-making, mitigate risks, and maximize ROI. It leverages real-time insights, advanced visualizations, simulations, scenario modeling, digital twins, and multi-agent systems.

The Simulation CoE is newly integrated into existing Deloitte Experience Centers to offer immersive client experiences and augments Deloitte's Global GenAI Market Incubator. The CoE focuses on four simulations designed to help executives accelerate and improve decision-making and serves as a dynamic hub orchestrated with regional centers globally. Deloitte has applied the CoE to create enterprise simulations for the power and utilities sector, addressing use cases such as real-time monitoring, preventive maintenance, and hazard sensing.

Deloitte provides leading professional services to nearly 90% of the Fortune Global 500 and thousands of private companies, spans more than 150 countries and territories, and employs over 470,000 people worldwide, building on its 180+ year history.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Global AI Simulation Center of Excellence will help revolutionize the way clients approach strategy development," says Deloitte Global Strategy, Risk & Transactions leader Nicolai Andersen. "This innovative CoE couples the power of GenAI with data to deliver customized recommendations for each client, providing leaders with actionable insights rather than relying on predictions from traditional approaches.", "Deloitte's Simulation CoE in India bolsters the ability to advise clients globally—moving from discussing potential impacts to actively demonstrating how adjusting variables affects business outcomes," says Sanghamitra Pati, Managing Director, AI and Engineering, Deloitte Consulting India Private Limited., Deloitte today announced the significant scaling of its Global Artificial Intelligence (AI) Simulation Center of Excellence (CoE), building on its global investment of US$3 billion in Generative AI (GenAI) through fiscal year 2030.

<summary>
This LinkedIn feed page centers on a post by Joseph Pavalon, Strategy Partner at Deloitte Consulting, announcing Deloitte's significant scaling of its Global Artificial Intelligence Simulation Center of Excellence. The announcement builds on Deloitte's global investment of $3 billion in Generative AI through fiscal year 2030. The Simulation CoE was launched first in Bengaluru, India to serve Deloitte's global network and is designed to accelerate return on investment for clients by creating real-time business insights and innovation.

## Deloitte's 2025 Tech Value Survey: AI Dominance and Portfolio Imbalance

**Published:** 2025 (fielded May–June 2025)

**Authors:** Tim Smith, Gregory Dost, Garima Dhasmana, Parth Patwari, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, Iram Parveen

**Overview:** This report, based on a survey of nearly 550 business and technology leaders across five industries (consumer; energy/resources/industrials; financial services; life sciences/healthcare; technology/media/telecom), analyzes how AI investments are consuming an outsized share of digital budgets, potentially leaving other critical technology areas underfunded.

### Key Findings:

**1. AI is Dominating Digital Budgets:**
- 74% of surveyed organizations invested in AI and gen AI over the past year — nearly 20 percentage points higher than the next most popular technologies (data management, cloud, IoT, ERP at ~55% and below).
- More than half of respondents allocate 21% to 50% (average 36%) of digital initiative budgets to AI — about US$700M for a company with US$13B revenue.
- Digital budgets rose from 7.5% of revenue (2024) to 13.7% (2025). If growth continues at this pace, budgets could reach 32% of revenue by 2028.
- Cybersecurity investment is lagging: only 25% to 32% invested in identity management, zero trust, or federated security.
- Emerging areas: 39% invested in agentic AI, 23% in robotics.

**2. Value Creation is Real but Fragmented:**
- 84% of AI/gen AI investors report gaining ROI. However, a cited MIT study found only 5% of gen AI pilots deliver sustained value at scale.
- Over 95% say digital initiatives lifted market cap or return on equity.
- Nearly 60% believe 21% to 50% of enterprise value remains latent.
- Paradox: AI investors were less likely to see significant market cap gains (43%) than those investing in data (65%) or security (66%).
- Data monetization strategy adoption grew from 16% (2023) to 65% (2025).

**3. C-Suite Alignment is Critical:**
- CFOs, CIOs, and CTOs often define success differently (ROI vs. EBITDA vs. KPIs), creating misalignment.
- Strategy innovation leaders — organizations that implement 4+ of 7 strategic innovation actions — outperform peers across all value measures and attribute over 40% of enterprise value to digital initiatives.

**4. Persistent Challenges:**
- Top barriers: misaligned incentives, legacy systems, lack of technical expertise (grew from 52% to 58%), security concerns, lack of strategy, insufficient funding.
- 60% cite data privacy/security as a major hurdle to AI automation.
- Success hinges on three factors: cyber strategy, tech strategy alignment, and dedicated leadership.

### Recommendations:
- Raise digital budgets to match ambition.
- Establish spending minimums for foundational technologies (platforms, data architecture, identity/zero trust, ERP) so AI doesn't starve the portfolio.
- Measure value beyond ROI — use a shared value scorecard.
- Align leadership incentives around enterprisewide outcomes.
- Shift from AI pilots to learning-capable systems integrated into core workflows.

Regulations like the European AI Act's "human-in-the-loop" principle emphasize human accountability. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from IoT Analytics (published March 4, 2025, by analyst Joaquin Fernandez) identifies the leading generative AI companies across three market segments, based on the firm's 263-page Generative AI Market Report 2025–2030 (published January 2025). The research included interviews with 50+ experts and analysis of 530+ generative AI projects.

KEY MARKET DATA:
- The combined generative AI software and services market (foundation models, model management platforms, and services, excluding applications like ChatGPT) surged from $191 million in 2022 to $25.6 billion in 2024.
- The data center GPU market grew from $17 billion (2022) to $125 billion (2024).

MARKET 1: DATA CENTER GPUs
- NVIDIA dominates with 92% market share, achieving record annual data center GPU revenue of just over $115 billion in 2024 (up 142% YoY). Its strengths are advanced GPUs (H100, Blackwell architecture) and the CUDA ecosystem, considered its biggest moat.
- AMD is NVIDIA's first real challenger, growing 179% between CY2023 and CY2024 to reach 4% market share (up from 3%). AMD shipped an estimated 307,000 MI300X GPUs to Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle by December 2024, and offers cheaper accelerators (Instinct MI325) and the ROCm 6.2 platform as a CUDA alternative.
- Emerging players: Huawei secured 2% market share with Ascend AI chips using its proprietary Da Vinci architecture; US startups Cerebras (wafer-scale processors for training) and Groq (ultra-low-latency inference chips) are also innovating.

MARKET 2: FOUNDATION MODELS AND MODEL MANAGEMENT PLATFORMS (reached $11 billion in 2024, excluding ChatGPT)
- Microsoft leads with an estimated 39% market share, driven by Azure AI integration with OpenAI models. Microsoft announced $80 billion in AI infrastructure investment for 2025, on top of its existing $10 billion investment in OpenAI.
- AWS holds 19% market share via Bedrock and SageMaker platforms (offering its NOVA models plus those from Anthropic, AI21 Labs, Cohere, etc.). AWS invested $4 billion in Anthropic in November 2024 (making Anthropic its primary training partner) and plans over $100 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2025.
- Google holds 15% market share, focusing on developer innovation via Vertex AI (offering Gemini and third-party models). Google announced a $75 billion AI investment for 2025 and a $1 billion new investment in Anthropic (January 2025).
- OpenAI holds 9% share of the platform market (excluding ChatGPT revenue). It was nearing a $40 billion primary investment (as of February 2025) bringing its valuation close to $300 billion, with a strategy focused on pursuing AGI.
- Emerging players: China's DeepSeek disrupted the market with its efficient, low-cost R1 model, causing concerns along the AI value chain; Hugging Face (US) and Mistral AI (France) are promoting open-source AI.

MARKET 3: GENERATIVE AI SERVICES (highly fragmented)
- Accenture leads with 7% market share, backed by a $3 billion AI investment; its GenAI services revenue grew 390% YoY by end of 2024. It deployed 14 million AI training hours and partners with OpenAI, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Google.
- Deloitte holds 3% share, with $3 billion in genAI investments pledged through FY2030 plus $1 billion for AI-enabled delivery. It delivered over 700 generative AI projects by June 2024 and partners with NVIDIA, Google, AWS, and Oracle.
- IBM holds 2% share, centered on its watsonx platform, focusing on automation, hybrid cloud, responsible AI, and open-source Granite models.
- Others: McKinsey (2%), BCG (2%), Cognizant (1%), and Capgemini (1%). Strategy firms (McKinsey, BCG, Bain) hold disproportionately high share because AI initiatives are mostly CEO-driven.

OUTLOOK: The market is highly dynamic—even Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned the AI hype may resemble the 1999 Dot-Com bubble. DeepSeek's R1 briefly overtook ChatGPT as the top Apple App Store download (as of Feb 27, 2025, ChatGPT reclaimed the spot). NVIDIA's stock was down over 13% since the start of 2025 as of March 3, 2025.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Motley Fool financial analysis article (published October 22, 2025) examining whether the expanded partnership between Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) and Accenture (NYSE: ACN) represents a "game-changer" for AI adoption and investors.

**Key Context and Deal Details:**
- Nvidia and Accenture are expanding their existing partnership to accelerate enterprise AI adoption, combining Nvidia's gold-standard AI chips with Accenture's global IT consulting network.
- Late last year, they launched the Accenture Nvidia Business Group, training 30,000+ subject matter experts to help clients "reinvent processes and scale enterprise AI adoption with AI agents."
- They introduced the Accenture AI Refinery platform, powered by Nvidia's AI Foundry, AI Enterprise, and Omniverse, allowing users to create and deploy custom large language models (LLMs) with domain-specific knowledge. The platform is available across all public and private cloud platforms.
- More recently, the AI Refinery was deployed in Europe to meet demand for sovereign AI (a nation's ability to produce AI using its own infrastructure, data, workforce, and business networks). Accenture estimates Europe will represent 30% of the global sovereign AI market by 2030.

**Financial Performance:**
- Accenture (fiscal 2025 Q4, ended Aug 31): Revenue grew 7% year-over-year to $17.67 billion; EPS of $2.25 rose 15%; new bookings of $21.3 billion. Early AI investments helped drive strong results.
- Nvidia (fiscal 2026 Q2, ended Jul 27): Revenue climbed 56% year-over-year to $46.7 billion; EPS of $1.08 jumped 61%, despite a moratorium on chip sales to China.

**Analyst Assessment:**
- Accenture offers more than 53,000 consultants trained on Nvidia technology and serves 9,000+ clients across 120+ countries.
- From an investment standpoint: Accenture trades at ~16 times next year's earnings (attractive valuation) but has declined 36% over the past year due to economic uncertainty. Nvidia trades at a premium multiple of 28, befitting its industry-leading position.
- Author Danny Vena concludes that while both companies benefit—Nvidia from additional chip sales and Accenture from AI services demand—the deal does not rise to the level of a "game-changer," though it is still a clear winner.

**Why it's important:** Hiring managers can use AI to meet three key goals: improve the candidate experience (via chatbots and demonstrating tech-forward workflows), enhance recruitment strategies (freeing HR professionals for strategic initiatives), and foster happier employees (by automating manual tasks).

**Key use cases:** 1) Idea and script generation, 2) Candidate screening (analyzing public info like social media for red flags), 3) Rapid employee onboarding, 4) Customized job postings (automating creation of tailored versions), and 5) One-way video interviews (with care needed to explain the process to candidates).

**Strategies:** 1) Audit roles and tasks, 2) Identify the right tools (coordinating with IT and HR), 3) Build for responsible AI (considering reputational, ethical, and legal ramifications), 4) Test and learn (to identify biases), and 5) Debrief and review with a natural cadence of assessments.

**Benefits:** Reduced recruiting and hiring costs (e.g., AI scheduling interviews, scanning resumes), quicker hiring decisions (reduced time-to-hire via automated resume screening and candidate matching), improved candidate engagement (personalized recommendations, predictive analytics), and improved quality of hires (aiding retention and identifying what attracts top employees).

**Challenges:** Inherited bias (carried over from human-built systems), increased startup costs (offset by long-term efficiency gains), decreased human connection (AI should be an enhancement, not a replacement), and prospect/employee concerns (61% of Americans are unaware organizations use AI in hiring, per Forbes October 2023).

**Future outlook:** AI will become a more powerful force as language models improve, with AI increasingly handling job postings and resume screening. Organizations must ensure systems are free from bias and set up to identify diverse candidates.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Use Cases for AI - Capgemini Software Engineering ---
URL: https://capgemini.github.io/ai/use-cases-for-ai

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Sarah Saunders (Capgemini) examines the practical use cases for Generative AI in software development, offering a cautious engineer's perspective on both the capabilities and limitations of these tools.

**Definitions of AI types:**
- **Machine Learning (ML):** Systems that learn and adapt without explicit instructions, using algorithms to analyze patterns in data. It's a bottom-up approach where machines figure out how to get from input to output (e.g., CT scan analysis for cancerous growths in healthcare).
- **Generative AI:** AI that generates new content (images, text) in response to prompts, learned from large reference databases. The output is probabilistically generated, so asking the same question twice won't produce the same answer, and answers can be "just plain wrong."
- **General AI:** AI that matches or surpasses human capabilities across cognitive tasks. This does not currently exist.

**Key evaluation questions for Generative AI use cases:**
- Does it matter if the generated answer is wrong?
- Do you require the same answer when asking the same question twice?
- If YES to either, standard Generative AI can't be used without significant tuning.

**Examined use cases:**
1. **User Interface Design:** Viable use case since design has no wrong answers; tools like Figma and V0 by Vercel already use this. AI can accelerate prototypes and help designers break habitual patterns.
2. **Automated Testing:** Can be useful to generate random/off-the-wall test cases (by raising "temperature") that testers might not consider; similar to Barry O'Reilly's Residuality Theory.
3. **Writing Code:** The author is skeptical about this being as transformative as predicted. Key reasons:
   - Code writing only takes 9-67% of developer time (GitHub claimed 55% productivity gains, but saving 55% of the small portion of time spent coding isn't as impressive).
   - Using AI for unit tests conflicts with Test-Driven Development (TDD) practices; "The only thing worse than no tests is incorrect tests."
   - Most useful for junior developers who shouldn't rely on it as a crutch; risks shipping code whose impact isn't understood.
   - Trained on open source codebases, it creates "the world's most average programmer"; reports show AI-maintained codebases degenerate in quality over time.
   - It's just another programming language/abstraction layer to learn (prompt engineering).
   - The most useful applications involve helping with regular expressions.
4. **Content Generation:** The author demonstrates that Copilot can generate a reasonable but only 500-word article when asked for 2000 words, concluding AI can't yet match humans "for their sheer ability to vacillate."

**Conclusion:** There are fewer use cases than one might think for Generative AI. While it will be a great tool (potentially as game-changing as IDEs in the 1990s), it isn't the end of software engineering. The author includes a real-world example of using Azure Copilot for bug fixing and warns about risks including lost chat history and security concerns with AI-generated code.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

URL: https://thecuberesearch.com/real-time-breaking-analysis-ibm-think-2025-arvind-krishnas-enterprise-ai-playbook

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by David Vellante (published May 6, 2025 on theCUBE Research) provides real-time breaking analysis of IBM Think 2025, focusing on CEO Arvind Krishna's Enterprise AI playbook.

**Key Highlights:**
- **Watsonx Orchestrate**: Catalog of 150+ pre-built agents covering HR, sales, procurement, IT ops, and customer service; users can build custom agents in under 5 minutes. IBM's "client zero" claimed 125K labor hours/quarter saved in case summarization and 2× that in HR.
- **Granite small-parameter models (3B–20B)**: IBM argues these domain-tuned models meet or beat 300-500B parameter models at 100–1,000× lower cost. The article cites a 7–10× cost delta per 1K tokens in production, based on IBM benchmarking analysis.
- **Hybrid cloud + open-source model zoo** (Granite, Llama, Mistral) for security and sovereignty, focused on on-premise and regulated industries.
- **WebMethods Hybrid Integration + HashiCorp stack** addresses integration debt with a unified family for APIs, file transfers, and workflows.
- **Watsonx.data lakehouse** plus pending Datastax acquisition adds vector search for RAG workloads.

**Strategic Positioning:**
- IBM advocates "Small is the New Smart" - positioning itself as an anti-hype vendor against ever-larger parameter counts.
- The Orchestrate + WebMethods combo is positioned as IBM's answer to Microsoft Copilot + Power Automate.
- Three vectors of openness: model optionality, hybrid tooling (Red Hat OpenShift, HashiCorp), and partner solutions (Oracle HR, Salesforce, Ferrari F1, Sevilla FC, Lumen).
- Commercial traction: "300+ engagements" last quarter and "over $3 billion" in AI business book; IBM's client-zero achieved $3 billion in cumulative cost takeout from automation.

**IBM Z17 Mainframe:**
- Positioned as an AI-first transaction engine, not a legacy drag.
- Over 70% of the world's structured financial data lands on mainframes at some point.
- Embedded Telum and Spire AI cores eliminate the air gap between production data and AI models.
- Claims 450 billion inference operations capability; bets regulated industries will keep transaction logic in data centers vs. hyperscaler cloud backhauling.

**Implications:**
- For CIOs: Granite provides lower-risk GenAI on-ramp aligned with sovereign-data constraints.
- For NVIDIA/frontier-model vendors: reinforces demand for more efficient models to lower GPU cluster costs.
- IBM positions itself as "a sort of Switzerland of agent integration" - an open alternative to vertically integrated AWS/Microsoft stacks.

**Bottom Line**: IBM has crystallized a coherent AI thesis based on smaller, domain-tuned models on an open hybrid-cloud fabric, aiming to unlock the "99 percent of enterprise data still untouched by GenAI." Success depends on execution in integration speed and cost transparency over the next two quarters of Watsonx bookings and Granite adoption.
</summary>

"IBM's public dismissal of 'massive, general-purpose' models was perhaps the sharpest edge of the keynote. IBM open-sourced a family of Granite language and code models (available under Apache 2.0 licenses on Hugging Face and GitHub). These code models range from 3B to 34B parameters, offer both base and instruction-following variants, are trained on 116 programming languages, and consistently reach state-of-the-art performance among open-source code LLMs—often outperforming open-source code models twice their size. The 20B parameter Granite base code model powers watsonx Code Assistant (WCA) and was tuned for natural language to SQL generation, achieving top accuracy and efficiency scores on the BIRD leaderboard.

IBM and Red Hat launched InstructLab, a first-of-its-kind model alignment technique enabling continuous, incremental contributions to base models—similar to decades of open-source software development. This is integrated with watsonx.ai and the new Red Hat Enterprise Linux AI (RHEL AI) solution. IBM Consulting launched a practice to help clients use InstructLab with proprietary data.

**New watsonx Assistants and Tools:**
- watsonx Code Assistant for Enterprise Java Applications (planned October 2024)
- watsonx Assistant for Z (planned June 2024)
- Expansion of watsonx Code Assistant for Z Service with code explanation (planned June 2024)
- New generative AI data products: Data Product Hub (June 2024), Data Gate for watsonx (June 2024), and updates to watsonx.data
- Expanded NVIDIA GPU offerings (L40S and L4 Tensor Core GPUs) with RHEL AI and OpenShift AI support

**AI-Powered Automation:**
IBM previewed IBM Concert (general availability June 2024), a generative AI-powered "nerve center" tool providing insights across application portfolios to identify, predict, and suggest fixes. The synergy between these acquisitions and IBM's existing portfolio should lead to innovative solutions ranging from data migration and integration to advanced analytics and machine learning, including enhanced hybrid cloud capabilities and real-time data processing.

**Role of Business Insights:** Kevin Ameche, president of RealSTEEL, noted that data integration is a mandatory step for many IBM customers to extract, load, transform, and deliver trusted data in real-time for AI use. Real-time data integration allows organizations to access and analyze data as it is generated for timely decision-making. IBM also supports AI and machine learning initiatives through platforms like IBM Cloud Pak for Data and IBM Cloud Pak for Integration, which include automation capabilities, process mapping, AI, and predictive analysis.

**Enhancing Watson:** Alex Sheplyakov, CTO at WiserBrand, said the acquisitions align with IBM's 2023 announcement of three main development areas: IBM Watsonx.ai, IBM Watsonx.data, and IBM Watsonx.governance. IBM Watsonx.ai demonstrates IBM's long-standing commitment to AI (including a partnership with Hugging Face for sensitive models and datasets), while Watsonx.data and Watsonx.governance focus on optimizing data collection and ensuring reliable work processes. The integration of StreamSets and webMethods is expected to enhance these areas, offering more comprehensive solutions for data management and governance, as IBM seeks to capture a larger share of the rapidly growing AI market.

These new assets will likely be integrated with IBM's existing AI and cloud services, creating a more cohesive and powerful offering for clients," Wood added. URL: https://investors.capgemini.com/en/publication/2025-h1-results

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 30, 2025, Capgemini SE announced its H1 2025 financial results, demonstrating resilience in a challenging economic environment. The Group reported revenues of €11,107 million for the first half, down -0.3% year-on-year on a reported basis but up +0.2% at constant exchange rates, with Q2 returning to positive growth at +0.7%. The operating margin remained stable at 12.4% (€1,377 million). Other financial highlights include operating profit of €976 million (down -15%), net profit Group share of €724 million (down -13%), basic EPS of €4.26, and normalized EPS of €6.00 (up +2%). Organic free cash flow was €60 million, down from €163 million in H1 2024.

Bookings totaled €11,993 million in H1 (up +2.1% at constant exchange rates) with a strong book-to-bill ratio of 1.08. CEO Aiman Ezzat noted continued momentum in cloud, data & AI, and digital core, with generative and agentic AI accounting for more than 7% of Group bookings in Q2. The Group launched its Resonance AI Framework and enhanced partnerships with Mistral AI and SAP.

Regional performance at constant exchange rates varied: North America grew +1.6% (margin improved to 16.3%), UK & Ireland grew +6.0% (margin fell to 18.1%), France declined -5.0% (margin improved to 10.0%), Rest of Europe declined -2.3% (margin fell to 10.4%), and Asia-Pacific & Latin America grew +8.7% (margin of 10.1%). By business line, Strategy & Transformation grew +1.3%, Applications & Technology grew +2.6%, and Operations & Engineering declined -1.5%.

The Group announced the acquisition of WNS (NYSE: WNS) announced July 7, 2025, for $76.50 per share, aimed at creating a global leader in Agentic AI-powered Intelligent Operations. The deal is expected to be accretive to normalized EPS by 4% before synergies in 2026 and 7% post-synergies in 2027, with closing expected by end of 2025. Capgemini secured €4.0 billion in bridge financing for the transaction. A new multi-year share buyback program of €2 billion was also approved.

The Group updated its 2025 financial targets: revenue growth narrowed to -1.0% to +1.0% at constant currency (from -2.0% to +2.0%), operating margin unchanged at 13.3% to 13.5%, and organic free cash flow unchanged at approximately €1.9 billion. Headcount stood at 349,400 as of June 30, 2025, with offshore employees comprising 59% of the total. Net debt was €2.8 billion at end of H1 2025. In sustainability, Capgemini updated its ESG policy (adding a 9th priority on ethics and 14 objectives), maintained its Ecovadis Platinum rating (87/100), remained on the CDP A-List, and received recognitions for disability inclusion and gender equality. The payment of H1 2025 dividends was €578 million (€3.40 per share) for fiscal year 2024.

--- SOURCE 2: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation ---
URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This McKinsey Global Survey article, published November 5, 2025, examines the state of AI adoption across organizations. Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, while revenue benefits are reported in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development.

The survey identifies "AI high performers" (about 6% of respondents who attribute 5%+ EBIT impact and report significant value) as distinguished by several factors: they are more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; more likely to set growth and/or innovation objectives (not just efficiency); nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows (identified as one of the strongest contributing factors via a relative weights analysis of 31 variables); three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to have senior leaders demonstrating ownership and commitment; more likely to have defined human-validation processes; and more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI (one-third of high performers do so, versus about three-quarters scaling AI overall). Successful practices align with McKinsey's Rewired research across six dimensions: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption/scaling.

On workforce impact, expectations vary: 32% of respondents expect enterprise-wide workforce decreases of 3% or more in the coming year, 43% expect no change, and 13% expect increases. A median of 17% of respondents report declines in function workforce sizes in the past year due to AI, but a median of 30% expect decreases next year. Larger organizations and high performers are more likely to expect meaningful workforce changes. Most organizations hired for AI-related roles in the past year, with software and data engineers most in demand.

Risk mitigation efforts are becoming more common. Respondents report acting to manage an average of four AI-related risks today versus two in 2022. Fifty-one percent of respondents from organizations using AI report at least one negative consequence, with nearly one-third reporting consequences from AI inaccuracy—the most commonly experienced and mitigated risk. Explainability is the second-most-reported risk but is not among the most commonly mitigated. High performers report more negative consequences (particularly IP infringement and regulatory compliance) but also protect against more risks.

The survey was in the field June 25 to July 29, 2025, with 1,993 respondents from 105 nations, weighted by GDP contribution. Thirty-eight percent work for organizations with over $1 billion in annual revenues. Authors include Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, and Tara Balakrishnan from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey.

URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bain_%26_Company

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Bain & Company is a privately held American management consulting firm headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, and is one of the "Big Three" management consultancies (alongside McKinsey and BCG). Founded in 1973 by Bill Bain (former Group Vice President of Boston Consulting Group) and Patrick F. Graham, the firm was spawned from an internal competition at BCG in which Bain led the winning "blue team"; most of that team followed him when he left. The firm grew rapidly through word-of-mouth, reaching $150 million in revenues by 1986 and 800 staff by 1987.

Corporate history: Bain faced turmoil in the late 1980s, including a PR crisis over its work with Guinness (following the Guinness share-trading fraud scandal, though Bain itself was not charged), financial problems from leveraged ESOP buyouts, and layoffs of about 30% of staff. Mitt Romney was brought back as interim CEO in January 1991 and saved the firm from bankruptcy by renegotiating debt, restructuring ownership, and convincing founding partners to give up $100 million in equity. Orit Gadiesh became chairman (a role she has held since) and Thomas Tierney became worldwide managing director in 1993, helping the firm rebound with 25% annual growth from 1992–1999. Recent leaders include managing directors John Donahoe, Robert Bechek, and Manny Maceda; Christophe De Vusser became global CEO in July 2024, the first European to hold the post. In 2025 the firm reported revenue of $14 billion and 22,000 employees, having ~64 offices worldwide. Bill Bain spun off Bain Capital (an investment firm led by Mitt Romney) in 1984.

Controversies: Bain was embroiled in a major scandal in South Africa involving its 2015 consulting work with the South African Revenue Service (SARS), where it billed $11 million for work later deemed bad advice. The Zondo Commission found Bain worked with President Jacob Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to facilitate the takeover of SARS, partly to prevent corruption investigations, and that Bain tried to bribe a former employee (Athol Williams) to "bury the truth." Consequences included: Bain's resignation from Business Leadership South Africa (Jan 2022); a three-year ban from UK government contracts (Aug 2022, later overturned/lifted in March 2023); and a 10-year ban from South African state contracts (Sept 2022). In July 2025, Bain announced it was winding down its consulting operations in South Africa entirely.

Consulting services: Bain primarily advises Fortune 500 CEOs on private equity investments, M&A, corporate strategy, finance, and operations. It developed the Net Promoter Score (sold since 2006), has a large private equity practice (by 2018 over 3x the size of its nearest PE consulting competitor, representing 25% of global business), created the Bridgespan Group for nonprofits, and pledged $1 billion in pro bono consulting by 2025. It also does "AI diligence work" using vibe coding to create prototype replications of commercial software to inform M&A decisions.

Reception and culture: A Price Waterhouse audit found Bain client market value increased 456% from 1980–1989 vs. 192% for the Dow. Bain operates on a non-competition model requiring long-term client engagement, which critics say can make the firm "unfirable." Known for secrecy (dubbed the "KGB of Consulting"), employees sign confidentiality contracts, and clients are given codenames. Bain consistently ranks among top workplaces (Glassdoor, Consulting Magazine) and has a highly ranked LGBT employee group called Pride. Employees are sometimes called "Bainies."
</summary>

According to the report, “[Reinventing Enterprise Operations with Gen AI](https://www.accenture.com/us-en/insights/strategic-managed-services/reinvent-operations-with-genai?c=acn_glb_aipoweredoperatmediarelations_14200178&n=mrl_0924)*,”* the number of companies that have fully modernized, AI-led processes has nearly doubled from 9% in 2023 to 16% in 2024. Compared to peers, these organizations achieve 2.5x higher revenue growth, 2.4x greater productivity and 3.3x greater success at scaling generative AI use cases.

Findings also assessed that these “reinvention-ready” companies are moving faster and are amplifying the impact of generative AI across the business. Enabled by a digital core, these organizations have already developed generative AI use cases in IT (75%), marketing (64%), customer service (59%), finance (58%), R&D (34%) and other core functions.

![](./media_11fc3bd605d337e209404282a41cf00db21458b5b.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

![](./media_11fc3bd605d337e209404282a41cf00db21458b5b.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

While the research indicates that some companies have moved to the highest level of operations maturity, nearly two thirds (64%) still struggle to change the way they operate. For example, they lag behind on building a robust data foundation: 61% report that their data assets are not ready for generative AI yet and 70% find it hard to scale projects that use proprietary data.

The deep dependency on people is often overlooked: 82% of companies at the early stage of operations maturity have not applied a talent reinvention strategy, planned to meet workforce needs, or acquired new talent or training to prepare workers for generative AI-led workflows. In fact, many executives (78%) indicate that AI and generative AI are advancing too fast for their organization’s training efforts to keep pace.

“Most executives understand the urgency of reinventing with generative AI, but in many cases their enterprise operations are not ready to support large scale transformation,” said Arundhati Chakraborty, group chief executive of Accenture Operations. “Generative AI is more than the technology. It is a driver of a mindset change that impacts the entire enterprise. It requires organizations to have a strong digital core, data strategy and a well-defined roadmap to change the way they operate. Additionally, an end-to-end perspective leveraging talent, leading practices and effective collaboration between business and technology teams is essential for intelligent operations.”

The report highlights four key actions business leaders should take to advance their operations maturity:

Explore the report in Accenture’s thought leadership app, Foresight, and get a personalized feed of recent latest insights, data, case studies and more at <http://www.accenture.com/foresight>.

**About the Research**  
For the report, “Reinventing Enterprise Operations with Gen AI,” Accenture surveyed 2,000 executives across 12 countries and 15 industries. The latest research assessed the progression of business operations maturity across four criteria: Reinvention-ready, Insight-driven, Automated and Foundational —each underpinned by more advanced ways of working with data, automation, common AI and generative AI. The study then combined survey responses with externally validated data across multiple dimensions of value, including financial, experience, sustainability, talent, inclusion and diversity, innovation and agility.

The revenue growth comparison was done by leveraging financial performance data for companies in our survey (for companies with available data and after performing appropriate data quality assurance). For each intelligent operations group, Accenture looked at overall revenue in a given fiscal year and, based on this metric, calculated the group revenue growth ratio.

Accenture is a leading global professional services company that helps the world’s leading organizations build their digital core, optimize their operations, accelerate revenue growth and enhance services—creating tangible value at speed and scale. We are a talent- and innovation-led company with 774,000 people serving clients in more than 120 countries. Technology is at the core of change today, and we are one of the world’s leaders in helping drive that change, with strong ecosystem relationships. We combine our strength in technology and leadership in cloud, data and AI with unmatched industry experience, functional expertise and global delivery capability. Our broad range of services, solutions and assets across Strategy & Consulting, Technology, Operations, Industry X and Song, together with our culture of shared success and commitment to creating 360° value, enable us to help our clients reinvent and build trusted, lasting relationships. # Implementing Generative AI in Manufacturing: A Multi-Use Case Study

Accenture·2023

[View original source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z3wsKHw4qZo)

Accenture's Industry X division conducted extensive experiments with generative AI in manufacturing settings throughout 2023. They developed and validated nine key use cases including operations twins, virtual mentors, test case generation, and technical documentation automation. The implementations showed significant efficiency gains (40-50% effort reduction in some cases) while maintaining a human-in-the-loop approach. The study emphasized the importance of using domain-specific data, avoiding generic knowledge management solutions, and implementing multi-agent orchestrated solutions rather than standalone models.

## Industry

## Technologies

[amazon\_aws](/llmops-tags/amazon-aws)[compliance](/llmops-tags/compliance)[document\_processing](/llmops-tags/document-processing)[documentation](/llmops-tags/documentation)[error\_handling](/llmops-tags/error-handling)[fallback\_strategies](/llmops-tags/fallback-strategies)[google\_gcp](/llmops-tags/google-gcp)[guardrails](/llmops-tags/guardrails)[human\_in\_the\_loop](/llmops-tags/human-in-the-loop)[internet\_of\_things](/llmops-tags/internet-of-things)[legacy\_system\_integration](/llmops-tags/legacy-system-integration)[microsoft\_azure](/llmops-tags/microsoft-azure)[monitoring](/llmops-tags/monitoring)[multi\_agent\_systems](/llmops-tags/multi-agent-systems)[orchestration](/llmops-tags/orchestration)[poc](/llmops-tags/poc)[prompt\_engineering](/llmops-tags/prompt-engineering)[regulatory\_compliance](/llmops-tags/regulatory-compliance)[reliability](/llmops-tags/reliability)[scalability](/llmops-tags/scalability)[security](/llmops-tags/security)

## Overview

This case study comes from a PTC Talks webinar featuring Jonathan Tipper (Generative AI Lead for Industry X at Accenture) and Jan Nicholls (EMEA Manufacturing Practice Lead at Accenture). The session, held in early 2024, provides insights into how Accenture has been approaching generative AI for manufacturing clients through their Industry X practice—a 26,000-person global team focused on digitizing engineering and manufacturing operations.

The presentation represents a consulting perspective on LLMOps for manufacturing, showcasing validated use cases developed through rapid experimentation rather than a single production deployment. While the content is inherently promotional for Accenture’s services, it offers valuable insights into real-world challenges and lessons learned when deploying LLMs in industrial contexts.

## Context and Approach

Accenture’s Industry X practice has been applying generative AI to manufacturing since ChatGPT’s emergence in late 2022. Their approach follows a three-phase methodology: Explore, Experiment, and Execute. The presenters emphasized the “Experiment” phase as particularly critical for manufacturing, arguing that unlike creative industries where generative AI applications may be more obvious, manufacturing use cases require rigorous validation before scaling.

The team conducts experiments in four to six week cycles at relatively low investment, measuring impact not just on direct processes but also on people, data, and architecture. They reference Harvard research on the “technological frontier”—the concept that AI excels at some difficult tasks while failing at seemingly easy ones, making upfront experimentation essential.

## Validated Use Cases

The presentation covered nine validated use cases that emerged from their experimentation program, categorized into three capability areas:

### Content Generation

The first category focuses on generative AI’s core strength: creating new content. Two prominent examples include test case generation for software-defined vehicles and technical publication generation for automotive. In the test case generation scenario, the system takes requirements (in text or image prototype form), generates test cases, and then produces test scripts. For technical publications, the solution ingests vehicle features and details, applies proper structure and formatting, and generates documentation. Both applications demonstrated 40-50% reductions in manual effort, freeing workers for higher-value activities.

### Data Interaction and Insights

The second category addresses a persistent challenge in manufacturing: getting actionable insights from industrial data. Since manufacturing data typically isn’t in the public domain and thus wasn’t part of LLM training data, Accenture developed approaches to make this proprietary data accessible through conversational interfaces.

One example involves dynamic digital dashboards that respond to natural language queries about KPIs, OEE metrics, and trends. Another integrates a copilot assistant into Accenture’s operations twin (digital twin for operations), enabling users to perform root cause analysis and identify trends by “talking to your factory.” These applications leverage retrieval and contextual integration rather than relying solely on the LLM’s parametric knowledge.

### Workflow-Integrated Copilots

The third category emphasizes human augmentation through copilots embedded directly into existing tools and workflows. Examples include integration with standard operating procedures, log books, model-based systems engineering (MBSE) tools, and PTC Codebeamer for requirements quality checking. The Codebeamer integration performs requirements quality checks natively within the tool, applying ISO standards and compliance requirements through generative AI.

The virtual mentor for manufacturing represents their most adoption-focused solution, providing shop floor operators with a copilot that synthesizes standard operating procedures, log books, and tribal knowledge on the fly based on their current position in the assembly process.

## Technical Architecture Considerations

### Model Selection and Multi-Agent Systems

The presenters noted that they don’t select a single platform or model provider. Instead, they evaluate different models during each experiment based on client needs and use case requirements. They mentioned OpenAI, Meta’s open-source offerings, and hyperscaler platforms (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) as common options.

A key theme was the shift toward “multi-modal, multi-agent solutions.” Jonathan Tipper characterized ChatGPT as “so 2022,” predicting that 2024 would see significant growth in agent-based architectures. These agents function as “specialized virtual team members” that perform tasks, coordinate with each other, and return results to human users. This architectural pattern enables tackling complex problems that simple chatbots cannot address.

### Offline and Local Deployments

A significant production consideration for manufacturing is network connectivity—operators often work in environments without internet access. Accenture confirmed they have developed offline, local deployment options, either in customer data centers or directly on-machine. These deployments rely on open-source, deployable models rather than cloud-based APIs, with different architectural patterns to accommodate air-gapped environments while maintaining data integrity and system-level integration.

This capability is particularly relevant for aerospace, defense, and other sectors with strict data sovereignty requirements, where cloud model access may not be acceptable.

## Lessons Learned and LLMOps Best Practices

The presentation outlined four key learnings from their experimentation program:

### Start with Your Own Data

This includes not just industrial sensor data but also processes, workflows, standards, operating procedures, log books, and tribal/expert knowledge. The emphasis on “tribal knowledge trapped within expert individuals” suggests significant effort goes into knowledge capture and structuring before LLM integration can succeed.

### Avoid the Knowledge Management Trap

While it’s tempting to deploy a general-purpose enterprise knowledge management chatbot, the presenters explicitly advised against this approach. LLMs are “not natively good” at solving broad knowledge management challenges without substantial surrounding infrastructure. Instead, they recommend focusing on specific use cases that radically augment existing high-value activities, driving adoption through workflow integration rather than general-purpose search.

### Embrace Multi-Agent Orchestration

Rather than single chatbots, the architecture should support multiple specialized agents coordinating to solve complex problems. This requires thinking bigger about the problems being tackled and designing systems that can grow in capability over time.

### Maintain Human-in-the-Loop

All demonstrated solutions involve human oversight and collaboration. Test case generation, technical publication creation, and copilot interactions all position the AI as an augmentation tool rather than a fully automated system. The presenters stated explicitly: “These aren’t fully automated running and unsupervised—not yet, not this year.” Trust-building through human verification is essential for adoption.

## Risk Management and Responsible AI

The presentation acknowledged substantial risks with generative AI: unreliable results, confidence calibration issues, model bias, liability questions, compliance concerns, and workforce impact. Accenture references their “Responsible AI” program, which they’ve operated since 2016, as a framework for addressing these concerns. In manufacturing contexts, where outputs may affect safety-critical systems or regulatory compliance, these considerations are particularly important.

## Results and Value Claims

The reported value metrics vary significantly by use case:

* 40-50% effort reduction for technical publication and test case generation
* Up to 80% reduction in time for converting functional requirements into MBSE models
* Various efficiency improvements in inspection, maintenance planning, and cycle time

The presenters appropriately cautioned that value depends heavily on industry, current maturity level, data foundation, and existing automation. They explicitly recommend honest measurement during experimentation rather than assuming value will materialize.

## Failed Experiments and Honest Assessment

When asked about failed experiments, Jonathan Tipper mentioned engineering drawing interpretation as an example where early 2023 capabilities were insufficient. While models could process vector-based drawings to some degree, they couldn’t match the expertise of experienced human engineers. He noted that many experiments produced “cool demos” that weren’t actually valuable enough for daily workflow adoption—an important distinction for production deployments where adoption is the ultimate success metric.

## Limitations and Considerations

This case study represents a consulting firm’s perspective on generative AI for manufacturing. While the experiences described appear genuine, the presentation is inherently promotional, and specific client names or detailed implementation architectures aren’t disclosed. The metrics cited are from experiments rather than long-running production systems, and the four-to-six-week experimentation cycles, while practical for rapid learning, may not capture challenges that emerge only at scale or over extended periods.

The emphasis on rapid technological change—with acknowledgment that answers would differ “in three months time”—also suggests that some recommended approaches may have already evolved since the January 2024 presentation.

[### Agentic AI Copilot for Insurance Underwriting with Multi-Tool Integration

Snorkel·2025

Snorkel developed a specialized benchmark dataset for evaluating AI agents in insurance underwriting, leveraging their expert network of Chartered Property and Casualty Underwriters (CPCUs). The benchmark simulates an AI copilot that assists junior underwriters by reasoning over proprietary knowledge, using multiple tools including databases and underwriting guidelines, and engaging in multi-turn conversations. The evaluation revealed significant performance variations across frontier models (single digits to ~80% accuracy), with notable error modes including tool use failures (36% of conversations) and hallucinations from pretrained domain knowledge, particularly from OpenAI models which hallucinated non-existent insurance products 15-45% of the time.

Smartling operates an enterprise-scale AI-first agentic translation delivery platform serving major corporations like Disney and IBM. The company addresses challenges around automation, centralization, compliance, brand consistency, and handling diverse content types across global markets. Their solution employs multi-step agentic workflows where different model functions validate each other's outputs, combining neural machine translation with large language models, RAG for accessing validated linguistic assets, sophisticated prompting, and automated post-editing for hyper-localization. The platform demonstrates measurable improvements in throughput (from 2,000 to 6,000-7,000 words per day), cost reduction (4-10x cheaper than human translation), and quality approaching 70% human parity for certain language pairs and content types, while maintaining enterprise requirements for repeatability, compliance, and brand voice consistency.

We see this new age of technology as an opportunity to inject trust in AI in a systematic manner so that businesses and people can realize its incredible reinvention potential. AI: A Declaration of Autonomy Is trust the limit of AI's limitless possibilities?
Welcome to our Technology Vision for 2025. This 25th edition of our annual technology trends report arrives at a watershed moment for technology and humanity. As more and more leaders embrace the need to continuously reinvent using tech, data and AI, they, now more than ever, need a deep understanding of AI. Why? Because the rate of AI’s technology diffusion is unprecedented and the pace is only increasing—creating new opportunities for reinvention across the enterprise—including new ways of achieving efficiencies, operating the core of businesses, new business models and new ways of engaging with customers.
We view AI as the new digital because, like digital, it is both a technology and a new way of working. We believe it will be used in every part of the enterprise and it will have a network effect on everything and everyone involved. Its impact is already real, and as companies continue to scale AI—and use generative AI as a catalyst for reinvention—it will solve new problems, create new inventions, change how we work and live, and transform industries and governments. Accenture research shows that only 36% of executives say their organizations have scaled gen AI solutions, and just 13% report achieving significant enterprise-level impact. We are actively equipping them to do it faster and more safely as we see 2025 as the year of scaled AI. This year’s Technology Vision explores a future when AI transitions from being an automation enabler to acting autonomously on behalf of people--equipping them with the capability to perform new tasks and perform others better than ever. Consider the possibilities and opportunities to reinvent as AI finds its way into new and unfamiliar territories. To truly understand and take advantage of this potential, enterprises will be creating their own, unique AI cognitive digital brains that will completely reshape the role technology plays across their enterprise and with their people. This will dramatically upend how enterprise tech systems are designed, used and operated; act as a brand ambassador; and inhabit in the physical world by powering robotic bodies. And when AI is spread across an organization, it enables people and AI to bring out the best in each other.
Leaders are aware of the challenges to creating this future, which include high up-front investments in their core technologies, data centricity and quality, and talent and new skills. And chief among these challenges is trust. Our research finds that 77% of executives believe unlocking the true benefits of AI will only be possible when it’s built on a foundation of trust. Leaders must build trust in digital systems and the AI models, with customers and the workforce by ensuring accuracy, predictability, consistency and traceability over and above the responsible use of AI. People’s trust in AI that it will perform as expected and justly—beyond any technical aspect— is an essential component that we must get right. The rush of an AI race is undeniable. We’ve seen it before. In 1997, Garry Kasparov lost a six-game chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue.1 It was the first time a computer ever beat a chess grandmaster, after decades of testing machine capability against humans using this game. The victory set off a storm of excitement and questions about AI and the future. Now, a new race is underway. Many companies building today’s cutting-edge AI models have their sights set on Artificial General Intelligence (AGI).2,3 And like before, the race has captivated business leaders, governments, and the world at large. But it’s a red herring—a distraction most business leaders can’t afford. Someday, AGI will be hugely consequential, but today it’s still far away with deep technical and ethical challenges to address. Instead, it’s vitally important that leaders see the far more pressing matter already here: the generalization of artificial intelligence, which will bring a new level of autonomy and capability to enterprises’ systems, workforces, and operations long before AGI comes into play.
The Generalization of AI To understand this generalization of AI, one simply needs to look around and see how rooted AI is becoming in our lives. It’s been nearly 30 years since Kasparov’s game, and now models that could make Deep Blue look like an average player are sitting in everyone’s pockets. The Turing Test, once considered the loftiest benchmark for machine intelligence, is effectively broken every day by conversations people have with Large Language Model (LLM)-backed customer service bots and sales agents. Today’s AI models have shrugged off the deep but specific and linear approaches of the past and are demonstrating more autonomy than ever—in how they learn, approach tasks, and in what they ultimately can do. And they’re bringing this autonomy to work, where 75% of knowledge workers report using generative AI; to how we interact with technology, as a coding copilot and by expanding voice assistant capabilities; and to nearly everything else, from robotics, to cars, to health care.4,5,6,7,8,9,10 Highly capable advanced AI Introduction AI: A Declaration of Autonomy Is trust the limit of AI's limitless possibilities?

This is the real disruption to focus on. Because right now, even as executives race to implement this new generation of AI, few are looking past the separate pieces to truly understand the scope of what they are actually building: AI “cognitive digital brains” that will completely reshape the role technology plays across the enterprise and people’s lives. What leaders have to fully grasp is that the singularly most important feature of AI is its ability to learn. When AI becomes generalized, and as enterprises diffuse it across the business and people adopt it into their lives, it has the potential to become much more than just the new features and capabilities it provides. Enterprises aren’t merely empowering the workforce, creating a new channel for customer service, or automating parts of their operations. They are taking a technology that comes with broad general knowledge and is intrinsically defined by its ability to learn and they are teaching it about parts of the business. And when people use it, they’re further teaching it about their likes, preferences, and needs. If built intentionally, enterprises can take all the distributed AI efforts they are pursuing and build a cognitive digital brain. They can hard-code workflows, institutional knowledge, value chains, social interactions, and so much other crucial data about businesses and the world into a system that can understand—and increasingly act—at a higher level than ever before. What can a person do with this power? What can a business do deploying it across the workforce? What will the world look like as wide proliferation brings it to every dimension of our lives? It seems inevitable that as leaders start to combine their AI generalization efforts, they will soon enhance and empower individuals, drive and help operate enterprises, radically reshape industries and even uplift nation states. Take Insilico Medicine, a pharmaceutical company, which used generative AI to go from discovery to phase one trials of a drug in under 30 months, around half the time it usually takes.11 They used one model fine tuned on omics and clinical data to identify potential targets for drug therapy. To develop possible drug compositions, they used a generative chemistry engine that consisted of 500 predictive and pre-trained models. For Insilico, AI is at the very heart of what they do—shaping the very business and industry around it. A Cognitive Digital Brain at Every Level It can be difficult to see this trend; at every layer of scale it manifests slightly differently. But across the board, this next stage for AI will infuse enhanced capability and increased autonomy into everything it touches. For individuals, the cognitive digital brain will operate as a co-pilot or sidekick, something that will understand their job, learn their preferences, and get to know them through its interactions, in service of helping them be an enhanced version of themselves. For businesses, it might seem more like a central nervous system—an evolution of the enterprise architecture into something that can capture the collective knowledge of the business, its unique differentiators, and its culture and persona, and become a key orchestrator (and even autonomous operator) for parts of it. industries, it may look like the common framework and communications protocol between companies in an industry, or engines codifying the grand challenges that shape an industry—models that will help grow our understanding of things like physics, genetics, movement, and more.
