## 2. Leading companies are already ahead with gen AI

The survey results show that AI high performers—that is, organizations where respondents say at least 20 percent of EBIT in 2022 was attributable to AI use—are going all in on artificial intelligence, both with gen AI and more traditional AI capabilities. These organizations that achieve significant value from AI are already using gen AI in more business functions than other organizations do, especially in product and service development and risk and supply chain management. When looking at all AI capabilities—including more traditional machine learning capabilities, robotic process automation, and chatbots—AI high performers also are much more likely than others to use AI in product and service development, for uses such as product-development-cycle optimization, adding new features to existing products, and creating new AI-based products. These organizations also are using AI more often than other organizations in risk modeling and for uses within HR such as performance management and organization design and workforce deployment optimization.

> AI high performers are much more likely than others to use AI in product and service development.

Another difference from their peers: high performers’ gen AI efforts are less oriented toward cost reduction, which is a top priority at other organizations. Respondents from AI high performers are twice as likely as others to say their organizations’ top objective for gen AI is to create entirely new businesses or sources of revenue—and they’re _most_ likely to cite the increase in the value of existing offerings through new AI-based features.

As we’ve seen [in previous years](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai-in-2022-and-a-half-decade-in-review), these high-performing organizations invest much more than others in AI: respondents from AI high performers are more than five times more likely than others to say they spend more than 20 percent of their digital budgets on AI. They also use AI capabilities more broadly throughout the organization. Respondents from high performers are much more likely than others to say that their organizations have adopted AI in four or more business functions and that they have embedded a higher number of AI capabilities. For example, respondents from high performers more often report embedding knowledge graphs in at least one product or business function process, in addition to gen AI and related natural-language capabilities.

While AI high performers are not immune to the challenges of capturing value from AI, the results suggest that the difficulties they face reflect their relative AI maturity, while others struggle with the more foundational, strategic elements of AI adoption. Respondents at AI high performers most often point to models and tools, such as monitoring model performance in production and retraining models as needed over time, as their top challenge. By comparison, other respondents cite strategy issues, such as setting a clearly defined AI vision that is linked with business value or finding sufficient resources.

The findings offer further evidence that even high performers haven’t mastered best practices regarding AI adoption, such as machine-learning-operations (MLOps) approaches, though they are much more likely than others to do so. For example, just 35 percent of respondents at AI high performers report that where possible, their organizations assemble existing components, rather than reinvent them, but that’s a much larger share than the 19 percent of respondents from other organizations who report that practice.

Many [specialized MLOps technologies and practices](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/exploring-opportunities-in-the-generative-ai-value-chain)may be needed to adopt some of the more transformative uses cases that gen AI applications can deliver—and do so as safely as possible. Live-model operations is one such area, where monitoring systems and setting up instant alerts to enable rapid issue resolution can keep gen AI systems in check. High performers stand out in this respect but have room to grow: one-quarter of respondents from these organizations say their entire system is monitored and equipped with instant alerts, compared with just 12 percent of other respondents.

## 3. AI-related talent needs shift, and AI’s workforce effects are expected to be substantial

Our latest survey results show changes in the roles that organizations are filling to support their AI ambitions. In the past year, organizations using AI most often hired data engineers, machine learning engineers, and Al data scientists—all roles that respondents commonly reported hiring in the previous survey. But a much smaller share of respondents report hiring AI-related-software engineers—the most-hired role last year—than in the previous survey (28 percent in the latest survey, down from 39 percent). Roles in prompt engineering have recently emerged, as the need for that skill set rises alongside gen AI adoption, with 7 percent of respondents whose organizations have adopted AI reporting those hires in the past year.

**The findings suggest that hiring for AI-related roles remains a challenge** but has become somewhat easier over the past year, which could reflect the spate of layoffs at technology companies from late 2022 through the first half of 2023. Smaller shares of respondents than in the previous survey report difficulty hiring for roles such as AI data scientists, data engineers, and data-visualization specialists, though responses suggest that hiring machine learning engineers and AI product owners remains as much of a challenge as in the previous year.

## 4. With all eyes on gen AI, AI adoption and impact remain steady

While the use of gen AI tools is spreading rapidly, the survey data doesn’t show that these newer tools are propelling organizations’ overall AI adoption. The share of organizations that have adopted AI overall remains steady, at least for the moment, with 55 percent of respondents reporting that their organizations have adopted AI. Less than a third of respondents continue to say that their organizations have adopted AI in more than one business function, suggesting that AI use remains limited in scope. Product and service development and service operations continue to be the two business functions in which respondents most often report AI adoption, as was true in the previous four surveys. And overall, just 23 percent of respondents say at least 5 percent of their organizations’ EBIT last year was attributable to their use of AI—essentially flat with the previous survey—suggesting there is much more room to capture value.

## About the research

The online survey was in the field April 11 to 21, 2023, and garnered responses from 1,684 participants representing the full range of regions, industries, company sizes, functional specialties, and tenures. Of those respondents, 913 said their organizations had adopted AI in at least one function and were asked questions about their organizations’ AI use. To adjust for differences in response rates, the data are weighted by the contribution of each respondent’s nation to global GDP.

args.key_excerpts: "Less than a year after many of these tools debuted, one-third of our survey respondents say their organizations are using gen AI regularly in at least one business function."
args.summary:
This McKinsey Global Survey article (published August 1, 2023) examines the state of AI following the explosive growth of generative AI (gen AI) tools. The survey was conducted April 11-21, 2023, with 1,684 participants, of whom 913 reported their organizations had adopted AI in at least one function.

Key findings include:
- One-third of respondents say their organizations are using gen AI regularly in at least one business function, meaning 60% of organizations with reported AI adoption are using gen AI.
- Nearly one-quarter of surveyed C-suite executives personally use gen AI tools for work; more than one-quarter of respondents from companies using AI say gen AI is on their boards' agendas.
- 40% of respondents say their organizations will increase their AI investment overall due to advances in gen AI.
- 79% of all respondents have had at least some exposure to gen AI; 22% regularly use it in their own work.
- Three-quarters of respondents expect gen AI to cause significant or disruptive change in industry competition within three years.
- The most common business functions using gen AI are marketing and sales, product and service development, and service operations—areas that together with software engineering could deliver ~75% of the total annual value from gen AI use cases.

Risk management gaps: Only 21% of organizations with AI adoption have policies governing employees' gen AI use. Just 32% say they mitigate inaccuracy (the most-cited gen AI risk), lower than the 38% mitigating cybersecurity risks. Less than half of respondents report mitigating even the risk they consider most relevant (inaccuracy).

AI high performers (organizations attributing at least 20% of EBIT to AI) are outpacing others in gen AI adoption, using it in more business functions, and are twice as likely to focus on creating new revenue rather than cost reduction. They invest over five times more in AI (spending >20% of digital budgets) and face model/tools challenges rather than strategy challenges faced by others.

Workforce impact: Nearly 40% of respondents expect more than 20% of their workforces to be reskilled over three years, while only 8% expect workforce decreases of more than 20%. Service operations is the only function where most respondents expect workforce decreases from gen AI. Gen AI increased the estimated percentage of automatable worker activities from 50% to 60-70%. AI high performers are over three times more likely to plan reskilling of more than 30% of their workforces.

Overall AI adoption remains steady at 55% of organizations, with less than a third adopting AI in more than one business function. Just 23% say at least 5% of EBIT was attributable to AI use—flat versus prior surveys. However, more than two-thirds expect their organizations to increase AI investment over the next three years.

This is a McKinsey & Company newsletter email (published in 2023) announcing and listing the "Top 10 articles of 2023," compiled by Liz Hilton Segel, chief client officer and managing partner for global industry practices, and Homayoun Hatami, managing partner for global client capabilities. The newsletter opens by noting that generative AI (gen AI) burst onto the scene in early 2023 and became a major topic in boardrooms, with the hype "well deserved" given gen AI's potential to fundamentally disrupt industries. More than half of the top 10 articles of 2023 touch on gen AI.

The top 10 articles are:
1. "The economic potential of generative AI: The next productivity frontier" — McKinsey's best-read piece of the year, authored by Michael Chui, Eric Hazan, Roger Roberts, Alex Singla, Kate Smaje, Alex Sukharevsky, Lareina Yee, and Rodney Zemmel, revealing how gen AI could unlock trillions of dollars in value across sectors from banking to life sciences.
2. "What is generative AI?" — Explaining algorithms (such as ChatGPT) that can create new content including audio, code, images, text, simulations, and videos.
3. "McKinsey Technology Trends Outlook 2023" — Analysis by the McKinsey Technology Council highlighting development, uses, and industry effects of advanced technologies.
4. "What every CEO should know about generative AI" — Generative AI essentials covering business value and risks of the technology.
5. "The State of Organizations 2023: Ten shifts transforming organizations" — Ten significant shifts facing organizations today.
6. "The state of AI in 2023: Generative AI's breakout year" — Survey findings on rapidly deployed gen AI tools and their expected effects on industries and workforces.
7. "2023 summer reading guide" — McKinsey's book picks from influential leaders and editors.
8. "What is AI?" — Artificial intelligence defined as a machine's ability to perform cognitive functions usually associated with human minds.
9. "What is Gen Z?" — Generation Z defined as people born between 1996 and 2010, shaped by the digital age, climate anxiety, shifting financial landscape, and COVID-19.
10. "Stepping up: Becoming a high-potential CEO candidate" — Four keys to succeeding on the path to becoming CEO.

The newsletter also directs readers to McKinsey Publishing's 2023 "Insights to Impact" highlights and the McKinsey Insights mobile app for iOS and Android.

URL: https://www.deloitte.com/global/en/about/press-room/global-gen-ai-simulation-center-of-excellence.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On March 25, 2025, Deloitte announced the significant scaling of its Global Artificial Intelligence (AI) Simulation Center of Excellence (CoE), building on its global investment of US$3 billion in Generative AI (GenAI) through fiscal year 2030. The CoE was first launched in Bengaluru, India to serve Deloitte's global network, aiming to accelerate clients' decision-making, mitigate risks, and maximize ROI. It leverages real-time insights, advanced visualizations, simulations, scenario modeling, digital twins, and multi-agent systems.

The Simulation CoE is newly integrated into existing Deloitte Experience Centers to offer immersive client experiences and augments Deloitte's Global GenAI Market Incubator. The CoE focuses on four simulations designed to help executives accelerate and improve decision-making and serves as a dynamic hub orchestrated with regional centers globally. Deloitte has applied the CoE to create enterprise simulations for the power and utilities sector, addressing use cases such as real-time monitoring, preventive maintenance, and hazard sensing.

Deloitte provides leading professional services to nearly 90% of the Fortune Global 500 and thousands of private companies, spans more than 150 countries and territories, and employs over 470,000 people worldwide, building on its 180+ year history.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Global AI Simulation Center of Excellence will help revolutionize the way clients approach strategy development," says Deloitte Global Strategy, Risk & Transactions leader Nicolai Andersen. ## Deloitte's 2025 Tech Value Survey: AI Dominance and Portfolio Imbalance

**Published:** 2025 (fielded May–June 2025)

**Authors:** Tim Smith, Gregory Dost, Garima Dhasmana, Parth Patwari, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, Iram Parveen

**Overview:** This report, based on a survey of nearly 550 business and technology leaders across five industries (consumer; energy/resources/industrials; financial services; life sciences/healthcare; technology/media/telecom), analyzes how AI investments are consuming an outsized share of digital budgets, potentially leaving other critical technology areas underfunded.

### Key Findings:

**1. AI is Dominating Digital Budgets:**
- 74% of surveyed organizations invested in AI and gen AI over the past year — nearly 20 percentage points higher than the next most popular technologies (data management, cloud, IoT, ERP at ~55% and below).
- More than half of respondents allocate 21% to 50% (average 36%) of digital initiative budgets to AI — about US$700M for a company with US$13B revenue.
- Digital budgets rose from 7.5% of revenue (2024) to 13.7% (2025). If growth continues at this pace, budgets could reach 32% of revenue by 2028.
- Cybersecurity investment is lagging: only 25% to 32% invested in identity management, zero trust, or federated security.
- Emerging areas: 39% invested in agentic AI, 23% in robotics.

**2. Value Creation is Real but Fragmented:**
- 84% of AI/gen AI investors report gaining ROI. However, a cited MIT study found only 5% of gen AI pilots deliver sustained value at scale.
- Over 95% say digital initiatives lifted market cap or return on equity.
- Nearly 60% believe 21% to 50% of enterprise value remains latent.
- Paradox: AI investors were less likely to see significant market cap gains (43%) than those investing in data (65%) or security (66%).
- Data monetization strategy adoption grew from 16% (2023) to 65% (2025).

**3. C-Suite Alignment is Critical:**
- CFOs, CIOs, and CTOs often define success differently (ROI vs. EBITDA vs. KPIs), creating misalignment.
- Strategy innovation leaders — organizations that implement 4+ of 7 strategic innovation actions — outperform peers across all value measures and attribute over 40% of enterprise value to digital initiatives.

**4. Persistent Challenges:**
- Top barriers: misaligned incentives, legacy systems, lack of technical expertise (grew from 52% to 58%), security concerns, lack of strategy, insufficient funding.
- 60% cite data privacy/security as a major hurdle to AI automation.
- Success hinges on three factors: cyber strategy, tech strategy alignment, and dedicated leadership.

### Recommendations:
- Raise digital budgets to match ambition.
- Establish spending minimums for foundational technologies (platforms, data architecture, identity/zero trust, ERP) so AI doesn't starve the portfolio.
- Measure value beyond ROI — use a shared value scorecard.
- Align leadership incentives around enterprisewide outcomes.
- Shift from AI pilots to learning-capable systems integrated into core workflows.

However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. KEY STATISTICS AND PREDICTIONS FROM MCKINSEY (Lari Hämäläinen):

- Two modes of enterprise change: Kaizen (continuous improvement, immediate priority) and Kakushin (radical change/step-change).

PANEL DISCUSSIONS:
1. ThoughtSpot (Ketan Karkhanis): Describes AI shift as "cloud 2.0" - the next AI agentic BI platform is a "smartphone version" not an incremental "flip phone" upgrade of legacy BI tools like Tableau/Power BI. **Gen AI potential and challenges**: McKinsey research estimates gen AI could generate between $2.6 trillion and $4.4 trillion annually. Challenges to adoption include: large data requirements with unstructured data sources that need preprocessing, difficulty selecting the right models (usually multiple models of varying size/complexity), time-consuming training and optimization with rapid version changes, and need for suitable infrastructure to deploy and maintain AI solutions.

- **MLOps/LLMOps tools**: Iguazio (faster model deployment with production-readiness and integrated monitoring), MLRun (manages AI applications lifecycle), Nuclio (automates deployment, minimizes maintenance)

Horizon is designed to complement existing data and analytics technology rather than replace it, functioning as an "end-to-end factory for analytics development and deployment." Bain & Company is a privately held American management consulting firm headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, and is one of the "Big Three" management consultancies (alongside McKinsey and BCG). Founded in 1973 by Bill Bain (former Group Vice President of Boston Consulting Group) and Patrick F. Graham, the firm was spawned from an internal competition at BCG in which Bain led the winning "blue team"; most of that team followed him when he left. The firm grew rapidly through word-of-mouth, reaching $150 million in revenues by 1986 and 800 staff by 1987.

Corporate history: Bain faced turmoil in the late 1980s, including a PR crisis over its work with Guinness (following the Guinness share-trading fraud scandal, though Bain itself was not charged), financial problems from leveraged ESOP buyouts, and layoffs of about 30% of staff. Mitt Romney was brought back as interim CEO in January 1991 and saved the firm from bankruptcy by renegotiating debt, restructuring ownership, and convincing founding partners to give up $100 million in equity. Orit Gadiesh became chairman (a role she has held since) and Thomas Tierney became worldwide managing director in 1993, helping the firm rebound with 25% annual growth from 1992–1999. Recent leaders include managing directors John Donahoe, Robert Bechek, and Manny Maceda; Christophe De Vusser became global CEO in July 2024, the first European to hold the post. In 2025 the firm reported revenue of $14 billion and 22,000 employees, having ~64 offices worldwide. Bill Bain spun off Bain Capital (an investment firm led by Mitt Romney) in 1984.

Controversies: Bain was embroiled in a major scandal in South Africa involving its 2015 consulting work with the South African Revenue Service (SARS), where it billed $11 million for work later deemed bad advice. The Zondo Commission found Bain worked with President Jacob Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to facilitate the takeover of SARS, partly to prevent corruption investigations, and that Bain tried to bribe a former employee (Athol Williams) to "bury the truth." Consequences included: Bain's resignation from Business Leadership South Africa (Jan 2022); a three-year ban from UK government contracts (Aug 2022, later overturned/lifted in March 2023); and a 10-year ban from South African state contracts (Sept 2022). In July 2025, Bain announced it was winding down its consulting operations in South Africa entirely.

Consulting services: Bain primarily advises Fortune 500 CEOs on private equity investments, M&A, corporate strategy, finance, and operations. It developed the Net Promoter Score (sold since 2006), has a large private equity practice (by 2018 over 3x the size of its nearest PE consulting competitor, representing 25% of global business), created the Bridgespan Group for nonprofits, and pledged $1 billion in pro bono consulting by 2025. It also does "AI diligence work" using vibe coding to create prototype replications of commercial software to inform M&A decisions.

Reception and culture: A Price Waterhouse audit found Bain client market value increased 456% from 1980–1989 vs. 192% for the Dow. Bain operates on a non-competition model requiring long-term client engagement, which critics say can make the firm "unfirable." Known for secrecy (dubbed the "KGB of Consulting"), employees sign confidentiality contracts, and clients are given codenames. Bain consistently ranks among top workplaces (Glassdoor, Consulting Magazine) and has a highly ranked LGBT employee group called Pride. Employees are sometimes called "Bainies."

--- SOURCE 1: Bain Vector Interview: Complete Guide (2026) ---
URL: https://www.hackingthecaseinterview.com/pages/bain-vector-interview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This guide by Taylor Warfield (Former Bain Manager and interviewer, updated May 18, 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of the Bain Vector interview process. Bain Vector is Bain & Company's digital delivery platform with 1,500+ specialists in AI, data science, engineering, design, and product management, combining two practice areas: AI, Insights & Solutions (AIS) and Enterprise Technology (ET). 

The interview process has 5-7 stages over 4-6 weeks: resume screen (~90% of applicants filtered), online assessment (TestGorilla, SOVA, or HireVue video, 60-90 minutes), recruiter screen, technical interview (SQL, Python, statistics, A/B testing, ML, generative AI varying by role), traditional business case interview with data/AI elements, behavioral interview (STAR method, Bain's operating principles), and final round with senior managers/partners.

Key details include: The process is very difficult (Glassdoor rating 3.67/5, ~68.5% positive experience, ~1-2% acceptance rate, 35 days average from application to offer). Technical skills tested span five areas: Python/SQL, statistics/A-B testing, machine learning, generative AI/RAG, and business framing. Compared to peers, Bain Vector is more business case-heavy than BCG X (balanced) and McKinsey QuantumBlack (technical-heavy/deep).

The article includes 10 preparation tips: master Bain case format (2 of 6 rounds are pure cases, practice 25-50 cases), drill SQL window functions, perfect the "Why Bain Vector" answer, study A/B testing tradeoffs (not just p<0.05), practice explaining technical concepts to non-technical audiences, prepare 6-8 STAR stories, read Bain's two free practice cases (Coffee Shop Co. and FashionCo.), practice generative AI questions, mock interview with current consultants, and maintain physical/stamina health.

Common Vector behavioral questions focus on using data to change stakeholder minds, balancing speed and accuracy, taking initiative, disagreeing on analytical approaches, and communicating technical findings to non-technical audiences. Entry-level roles require bachelor's/master's degrees; senior roles need 5-10 years experience, with PhDs common but not required at senior levels. The most common mistake candidates make is treating Vector like a tech company data science loop rather than recognizing the emphasis on traditional business case interviews.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This guide from Road to Offer (updated July 27, 2026) explains what Bain Vector is and how its interview process works. Key points:

**What Vector Is:** Vector is the brand name for Bain & Company's digital and technology consulting practice. It lives at bain.com/vector-digital/ (titled "Digital Consulting Services") and includes named practices like AI, Insights, and Solutions (AIS) and Enterprise Technology. Crucially, Bain's careers site does not list "Vector" as a career path—candidates apply into work areas such as Analytics, Data & Research; Technology & Engineering; Design; and Product Management & Innovation.

**Scale and Structure:** The digital practice reports 9,500+ projects, 1,500+ in-house team members, and 700+ ecosystem partners. AIS comprises four integrated capability groups (design/research, engineering, product management/innovation, data science/ML engineering) with 200+ deep analytics experts, 1,500+ partnering analytics/software engineers, and 2,500+ projects. Enterprise Technology covers tech strategy, architecture modernization, operating models, cost management, cybersecurity, and more, reporting 300+ dedicated technology partners and ~2,000 tech due diligence assessments in the last five years.

**How Vector Differs from Core Bain Consulting:** While core Bain consultants decide what clients should do (producing recommendations), Vector candidates build and deliver what the decision requires (models, products, platforms, architectures). The interview center of gravity for Vector is a technical screen or take-home plus a "build-flavored" case, versus the business case for generalist roles.

**Interview Process:** Bain states there is "no one Vector loop"—each role has its own process. The survey was conducted April 11-21, 2023, with 1,684 participants, of whom 913 reported their organizations had adopted AI in at least one function.

Key findings include:
- One-third of respondents say their organizations are using gen AI regularly in at least one business function, meaning 60% of organizations with reported AI adoption are using gen AI.
- Nearly one-quarter of surveyed C-suite executives personally use gen AI tools for work; more than one-quarter of respondents from companies using AI say gen AI is on their boards' agendas.
- 40% of respondents say their organizations will increase their AI investment overall due to advances in gen AI.
- 79% of all respondents have had at least some exposure to gen AI; 22% regularly use it in their own work.
- Three-quarters of respondents expect gen AI to cause significant or disruptive change in industry competition within three years.
- The most common business functions using gen AI are marketing and sales, product and service development, and service operations—areas that together with software engineering could deliver ~75% of the total annual value from gen AI use cases.

Risk management gaps: Only 21% of organizations with AI adoption have policies governing employees' gen AI use. Just 32% say they mitigate inaccuracy (the most-cited gen AI risk), lower than the 38% mitigating cybersecurity risks. Less than half of respondents report mitigating even the risk they consider most relevant (inaccuracy).

AI high performers (organizations attributing at least 20% of EBIT to AI) are outpacing others in gen AI adoption, using it in more business functions, and are twice as likely to focus on creating new revenue rather than cost reduction. They invest over five times more in AI (spending >20% of digital budgets) and face model/tools challenges rather than strategy challenges faced by others.

Workforce impact: Nearly 40% of respondents expect more than 20% of their workforces to be reskilled over three years, while only 8% expect workforce decreases of more than 20%. Service operations is the only function where most respondents expect workforce decreases from gen AI. Gen AI increased the estimated percentage of automatable worker activities from 50% to 60-70%. AI high performers are over three times more likely to plan reskilling of more than 30% of their workforces.

Overall AI adoption remains steady at 55% of organizations, with less than a third adopting AI in more than one business function. Just 23% say at least 5% of EBIT was attributable to AI use—flat versus prior surveys. However, more than two-thirds expect their organizations to increase AI investment over the next three years.

URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/the-economic-potential-of-generative-ai-the-next-productivity-frontier

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This McKinsey & Company report (published June 14, 2023) examines the economic potential of generative AI as "the next productivity frontier." The report defines generative AI as applications built on foundation models—large artificial neural networks that can process vast unstructured data and perform multiple tasks across text, images, video, audio, and code. It provides a comprehensive first assessment of where business value from generative AI could accrue and its potential workforce impacts.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Generative AI could add the equivalent of $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion annually across 63 use cases analyzed across 16 business functions—roughly the size of the UK's entire 2021 GDP ($3.1 trillion). This would increase the impact of all AI by 15 to 40 percent, and could roughly double when including embedding generative AI into existing software.
- About 75 percent of the value falls across four areas: customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering, and R&D.
- Netting out overlap, total economic benefits of generative AI—including use cases and productivity gains across knowledge workers—amount to $6.1 trillion to $7.9 trillion annually.
- Generative AI could automate work activities absorbing 60 to 70 percent of employees' time (up from a previous estimate of 50 percent), largely due to its enhanced natural-language understanding, which affects 25 percent of total work time.
- Half of today's work activities could be automated between 2030 and 2060, with a midpoint in 2045—roughly a decade earlier than previous estimates.
- Generative AI could enable labor productivity growth of 0.1 to 0.6 percent annually through 2040; combined with all other technologies, automation could add 0.5 to 3.4 percentage points annually to productivity growth.

INDUSTRY AND FUNCTION IMPACTS:
- Banking: $200 billion to $340 billion in additional annual value.
- Retail and consumer packaged goods: $400 billion to $660 billion per year (1.2 to 2.0 percent of annual revenues), with retail generating roughly $310 billion alone.
- High tech: value driven primarily by faster software development.
- Customer operations: productivity gains of 30 to 45 percent of function costs; one study showed 14 percent increase in issue resolution per hour and 9 percent reduction in handling time at a 5,000-agent company.
- Marketing: 5 to 15 percent productivity increase of total marketing spending.
- Sales: 3 to 5 percent increase in sales productivity.
- Software engineering: 20 to 45 percent of annual function spending; GitHub Copilot users completed tasks 56 percent faster.
- Product R&D: 10 to 15 percent of R&D costs, including generative design for drug and materials development.

The report highlights notable examples: ChatGPT (released November 2022), GPT-4 (released March 2023), Anthropic's Claude (expanded to 100,000 tokens by May 2023), and Google's PaLM 2. It emphasizes that generative AI's impact is greater on knowledge work, particularly higher-wage and higher-education occupations. The era of generative AI is "just beginning," with leaders facing challenges around risk management, workforce skill development, and rethinking core business processes. Realizing full benefits requires investment in worker support, skill transitions, and managing risks such as intellectual property infringement, adversarial attacks, and bias in training data.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Generative AI's impact on productivity could add trillions of dollars in value to the global economy. Our latest research estimates that generative AI could add the equivalent of $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion annually across the 63 use cases we analyzed—by comparison, the United Kingdom's entire GDP in 2021 was $3.1 trillion."
</key_excerpts>

# Deloitte: As Generative AI Gains Ground, Consumers Choose the Innovators They Trust

## Tech innovation alone isn’t enough; consumers often demand privacy, clarity and ethical security from tech providers in today's AI-driven world

[Print](javascript:window.print(); "Print")

[Share](# "Share")

**New York, Sept. 25, 2025**

**Key takeaways**

* **GenAI goes mainstream**: Over half (53%) of surveyed U.S. consumers use or experiment with GenAI, and usage at work has surged more than fivefold since 2023, rising from 6% to 34%.
* **Despite rapid adoption, GenAI raises concerns**: 82% of users surveyed say the technology could be misused (up from 74% in 2024).
* **Privacy concerns run high**: 70% of respondents worry about data privacy and security when using digital services, and only around 1 in 10 consumers say they are very willing to share certain types of sensitive information, such as financial, communication or biometric data.
* **Responsible innovation can pay off**: Surveyed consumers who view their tech providers as excelling in both innovation and data responsibility spend 62% more annually on tech devices compared to consumers who view their providers as lagging on both aspects. Even among companies seen as innovative, those that are also trusted see 25% higher spending annually on tech devices—proof that trust isn’t just a ‘nice to have,’ it’s a competitive edge.

**Why this matters**

For six years, the Deloitte Center for Technology, Media & Telecommunications has surveyed consumers to help understand their attitudes toward digital life. In its 2025 “Connected Consumer” survey, Deloitte examines how Generative AI (GenAI) has entered the mainstream. Forty-two percent of surveyed GenAI users say it has a “very positive” effect on their lives — outpacing perceptions of both devices (36%) and apps (29%). While enthusiasm is high for many and household tech spending continues to rise, concerns about data security and transparency are escalating for those surveyed. For tech companies, the challenge seems clear: Innovation paired with responsible practices can help to earn trust and drive growth in an AI-driven world.

GenAI is having an early internet-era moment — the excitement is real, and adoption is accelerating fast. It’s driving massive momentum across the tech ecosystem. But as usage surges, consumer trust isn’t keeping pace. Many consumers want intelligent, personalized experiences — but preferably from companies that protect their data and empower their choices. That’s the new threshold for earning loyalty.

— [China Widener](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/about/people/profiles.china-widener+98060309.html), vice chair and technology, media and telecommunications industry leader, Deloitte

**Buying habits: Digital spending stays strong**  
 Many U.S. consumers continue to invest in their connected lifestyles — despite ongoing concerns for some about affordability — with 70% of surveyed households expected to increase their device spending or keep it steady.

* Respondents’ households are spending approximately 17% more on average on connected devices this year — $896 in 2025 compared to $764 in 2024.
* Monthly household spending on digital services and subscriptions was $183 in this year’s survey, slightly up from a monthly spend of $175 in 2024.
* Among regular GenAI users, about four in 10 surveyed say their households pay for GenAI-infused tools and services, while half of non-payers say that free tools meet their needs.

**AI in the workplace: From experimentation to expectation**  
 GenAI is rapidly becoming a powerful tool in the workplace, transforming how many employees work and learn. While most GenAI users report meaningful gains in efficiency, decision-making and creativity, some organizations are still playing catch-up when it comes to setting clear policies and providing the right tools.

* Among surveyed consumers who are using GenAI at work, almost half (46%) report that these tools substantially boost their productivity.
* While many say their organizations encourage use of the technology (55%) and provide training (40%), nearly seven in 10 say they use their own GenAI tools on the job—“shadow AI” — which could raise compliance and governance risks.
* Employee demand for GenAI tools is likely to rise: More than half (53%) of surveyed workers agreed they can see GenAI serving as a valuable assistant in their future roles.

**Security and privacy: The trust gap widens**  
 As GenAI becomes increasingly integrated into daily life, concerns about security and transparency are rising. Despite rapid adoption of the technology, skepticism persists: Nearly three-quarters (74%) of respondents familiar or experimenting with GenAI — and even 62% of regular users — say the increasing popularity of GenAI makes it harder for them to trust what they see online. Many respondents also worry about devices or digital accounts being hacked, data breaches, identities being stolen, and their location being tracked.

* Almost half (47%) of respondents experienced at least one kind of security failure in the past year, with over one-quarter (27%) reporting two or more. And 58% encountered at least one scam attempt in the past year, including phishing, fake profiles, chatbots impersonating real people, deepfake videos, ransomware/malware attacks, and voice cloning.
* Willingness to share sensitive data (financial, biometric, communication) remains low, with over half of respondents unwilling to share — even for better experiences.
* Eighty-two percent of surveyed GenAI users and experimenters are concerned GenAI could be misused by “bad actors.”

**From innovation to impact: Why trust could decide the winners**  
 Deloitte’s analysis reveals that respondents who view their tech providers as both innovative and responsible with their data spend 62% more annually on devices and 26% more per month on services compared to those who see their providers as lagging in both areas. Even among companies seen as innovative, those that also excel at data responsibility see almost four times as much trust, and 25% higher tech device spending annually—proof that data responsibility and trust aren’t just a ‘nice to have,’ but a competitive edge.

* While most respondents (75%) strongly or somewhat agree that new features improve their lives, nearly as many (69%) strongly or somewhat agree that tech companies innovate too quickly without paying enough attention to mitigating risks.
* Fewer than half (48%) of respondents indicated that the benefits they get from online services outweigh their privacy concerns — a steep drop from 58% in 2024, and the lowest level since Deloitte began surveying this sentiment in 2019.
* Many surveyed consumers who expressed security concerns fear not only bad actors like hackers (71%) but also worry that tech companies themselves may not protect data adequately (64%). The majority (60%) of these respondents fear unauthorized use of their information by tech companies.
* Only 20% of survey respondents say tech providers are very clear about what data they collect, and only about one-quarter (27%) have high/very high confidence that their data is protected.

Trust isn’t just a value — it’s a powerful growth engine. While consumers are naturally drawn to innovation, they deepen their engagement and loyalty with companies that prioritize responsible data stewardship. By combining cutting-edge technology with strong data ethics, companies can do more than just lead the market, they can cultivate lasting customer relationships.

— [Steve Fineberg](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/about/people/profiles.steve-fineberg+ae873f4f.html), vice chair and U.S. technology sector leader, Deloitte

**About this survey**  
 Deloitte surveyed 3,524 U.S. consumers in Q2 2025. All data was weighted to the most recent U.S. Census to arrive at a representative view of U.S. consumers’ opinions and behaviors. To gain a more detailed understanding of various consumer groups, Deloitte also segmented respondents into generational groups defined by their birth year: Generation Z (1997–2011), Millennials (1983–1996), Generation X (1966–1982), Boomers (1947–1965), and Matures (1946 and prior).

args.summary: This webpage (published 3 December 2025 by Mackay Goodwin, a professional services firm, via their MG Academy podcast) discusses the key lessons from a Deloitte AI incident in 2025. The incident involved a consulting report sent to the Australian federal Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, which assessed whether an automated system that stops government benefits under certain criteria was working as intended. An expert academic reviewer found that some references and a summary of a legal case in the report contained AI-fabricated material. The podcast, featuring Edmund Tadros from the Australian Financial Review, emphasizes that the publisher (Deloitte) bears responsibility for the report's content regardless of whether AI was used. Key lessons highlighted: organizations should not abandon AI but must know exactly where it was used and apply extra scrutiny to those sections; AI output should be checked more carefully (comparing AI to a well-intentioned intern whose work requires extra review); human judgment, context, and careful review remain essential for high-stakes work; and clients are likely to increasingly ask firms to disclose how AI was used in their reports. The episode treats the incident as a normal part of AI's learning process from which organizations can draw lessons for 2026.

# Two futures for jobs in an AI era

 Research 15 June 2026

![Image 2: Hero image](https://assets.pwc.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:2da73d7c-d9dd-48b9-9978-c0f6e7cf7789/as/ces-pwc_gx_primary_1600x900_gettyimages-1182958427.jpg)

## PwC’s 2026 AI Jobs Barometer: AI boosts productivity, wages, and hiring—while rewarding judgement and leadership.

## Introduction

![Image 3: 40 percent](https://assets.pwc.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:ea82f7b8-54c4-4bae-9a8f-31c34748b6ea/as/callout_40.png?width=640&preferwebp=true)

Productivity growth is 40% higher at companies most exposed to AI versus least.

![Image 4: 2 times](https://assets.pwc.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:f9926ac3-4ba1-4779-9251-a85628b2106a/as/callout_2x.png?width=640&preferwebp=true)

Skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing more than twice as fast as for the least AI-exposed jobs.

![Image 5: 42 percent](https://assets.pwc.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:04708aa9-5787-4839-866b-82a41c21df29/as/callout_42.png?width=640&preferwebp=true)

Two-track jobs market: jobs ‘professionalised’ by AI are growing twice as fast as jobs ‘democratised’ by AI with 42% faster wage growth since 2021.

![Image 6: 7 times](https://assets.pwc.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:543a0ce5-4b84-40a4-8c08-464e515c6526/as/callout_7x.png?width=640&preferwebp=true)

The most AI-exposed junior roles are 7x more likely (than the least AI-exposed junior roles) to demand traditionally senior skills like leadership.

[Video 1](https://download.pwc.com/gx/ai/two-futures-for-jobs-in-an-ai-era.mp4)![Image 7: Video thumbnail](https://assets.pwc.com/adobe/assets/urn:aaid:aem:bf44c7ed-f3b6-4f8c-b665-8e92b133fba2/as/video-still-two-futures-for-jobs-in-an-ai-era.jpeg)

### AI links directly to significant productivity gains

Since 2022 when AI adoption soared, the most AI-exposed companies have tripled their lead in workforce productivity growth compared to the least exposed companies. There is a pronounced ‘super-star’ effect; the top fifth of most-exposed companies achieve stellar 163% productivity growth on average.

### Perhaps surprisingly, AI is linked to rising wages and headcount

The companies achieving the biggest productivity gains from AI are not using it only to cut costs. Instead, they use AI to amplify human performance and create new forms of value. Headcount growth at the most AI-exposed companies is outpacing that at the least exposed companies. Far from being a job killer, AI may actually be a job expander when used to unlock growth and enter new markets. Wages too are growing faster at the most AI-exposed companies, suggesting gains are shared with workers.

### AI is creating a two-track labour market

AI is ‘professionalising’ some jobs by reshaping them to require even more human expertise. AI ‘democratises’ other jobs by making them even easier for non-experts to perform. Professionalised jobs are thriving; numbers of professionalised jobs are growing twice as fast as democratised ones, and with 42% higher wage growth. Our data suggests a bright future for workers in professionalised roles as AI makes them even more valuable.

### AI accelerates skills transformation

The skills needed for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing more than twice as fast as those for the least exposed roles. This is a 75% increase over the gap we saw last year.

Crucially, the new tasks added to AI-exposed roles are 2.5 times more likely to rely on skills like empathy, judgement, and creativity that become even more valuable as AI absorbs some routine work.

### AI transforms entry level work

The traditional career ladder is compressing. AI-exposed junior roles are seven times more likely to demand traditionally senior skills such as leadership and strategic thinking (compared to the least exposed junior roles).

While overall early-career job postings have flatlined in highly AI exposed sectors, 'seniorised' entry level roles are thriving, showing 35% growth since 2019. Organisations must rethink how they mentor and train junior staff, helping them step up to complex decision-making much earlier in their careers.

### Next steps for business leaders

*   **Use AI to pursue growth over efficiency alone**, using it to unlock new revenue, enter new markets, and create new forms of value, especially by [**partnering across traditional industry lines**](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/1/issues/tech-data-ai/ai-performance.html).

*   **Consider how AI is changing the human expertise needed for job roles** to guide talent investment and skills development.

*   **Invest in agentic AI, the ultimate complement to human expertise.** With a team of [**AI agents**](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-agents.html) at their command, workers can use their uniquely human expertise to deliver value at much greater scale.

*   **Reinvent early career pathways.** Redesign onboarding, mentorship, and training programmes to accelerate development of advanced skills like leadership, stakeholder management, and strategic decision-making.

*   **Invest in human-intensive skills alongside AI skills** such as empathy, judgement, creativity, and leadership.

PwC's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, published 15 June 2026, examines the impact of AI on the global labor market, finding that AI drives productivity, wage growth, and hiring rather than job losses. Key findings include:
- Productivity growth is 40% higher at companies most exposed to AI versus least exposed. Since 2022, the most AI-exposed companies have tripled their lead in workforce productivity growth, with the top fifth achieving 163% average productivity growth (a "super-star" effect).
- The most AI-exposed companies use AI to amplify human performance and create new value, with headcount growth outpacing less exposed companies. AI is described as a potential "job expander" rather than a "job killer."
- AI is creating a two-track labor market: jobs "professionalised" by AI (requiring more human expertise) are growing twice as fast as jobs "democratised" by AI, with 42% faster wage growth since 2021.
- Skills for the most AI-exposed jobs are changing more than twice as fast as for least exposed roles — a 75% increase over the gap in the prior year. New tasks added to AI-exposed roles are 2.5 times more likely to rely on skills like empathy, judgement, and creativity.
- The traditional career ladder is compressing: AI-exposed junior roles are 7x more likely to demand traditionally senior skills like leadership. "Seniorised" entry-level roles show 35% growth since 2019, while overall early-career postings have flatlined in highly AI-exposed sectors.

Next steps for business leaders include: using AI to pursue growth over efficiency alone, considering how AI changes human expertise needs, investing in agentic AI as a complement to human expertise, reinventing early-career pathways with accelerated development of advanced skills, and investing in human-intensive skills (empathy, judgement, creativity, leadership).

The report includes sector-specific insights for Consumer Markets (highest AI wage premiums of any sector), Energy Utilities & Resources (lower AI exposure but hiring more AI-skilled workers with strong wage premiums), Financial Services, Government & Public Sector (AI reshaping roles without adding more), Healthcare (slower adoption but acute need), Manufacturing (higher percentage of ads requiring AI skills than more AI-exposed industries), Professional Services, and Technology Media & Telecoms (leads all sectors in AI hiring intensity, with nearly 1 in 8 new roles AI-related).

Contact points include Joe Atkinson (Global Chief AI Officer, PwC Network of Firms) and Peter Brown (Global Workforce Leader, PwC). Related reports include the 2025 AI Jobs Barometer and content on worker attitudes toward AI, redesigning roles, and decoding AI ROI (noting only 20% of companies capture 74% of all AI-driven value).

# AI reshapes global labour market into two distinct paths, rewarding human skills: PwC 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer

**LONDON, 15 June 2026** – AI is rapidly reshaping the skills employers want most from workers – increasing the emphasis on human skills such as judgement, creativity and leadership – as companies most able to use AI continue to expand hiring faster than their peers, according to PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, released today.

The Barometer, which analysed more than one billion job ads across six continents, also finds that AI is driving a ‘two-track’ global labour market in which ‘professionalised’ roles – in which AI automates routine tasks so human judgement and expertise are emphasized – are growing faster than roles ‘democratised’ by AI – in which AI makes the role itself easier for non-experts to perform.

‘Professionalised’ roles (such as radiologists or recruiters) are seeing twice the growth in available jobs and 42% faster salary growth than those categorised as ‘democratised’ (such as IT service managers or medical secretaries).

At the entry level, AI appears to be increasing demand for more ‘senior’ skills from junior workers. Based on 2.4 million entry-level jobs analysed in the US, entry-level roles most exposed to AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level ‘human-intensive’ skills like leadership, creativity or face-to-face interactions.

Job openings for these ‘seniorised’ entry-level roles have grown 35% since 2019, while other entry-level roles shrank 10%.

“Across the global economy, we’re beginning to see a new divide emerge between different models for talent and value creation. The companies seeing the greatest returns on AI are using it to amplify human expertise, accelerate innovation and create entirely new sources of value. As a result, they are pulling further ahead on productivity and growth than companies that focus primarily on automation.”

## AI is driving a productivity boom – and “super-star” companies most able to use AI are pulling ahead significantly

The report finds widening divergence between companies most and least exposed to AI. Companies operating in the most AI-exposed sectors recorded 34% productivity growth in 2025 relative to 2018, compared to 24% for the companies least able to use AI.

Within this group, a pronounced “super-star” effect is emerging. The top 20% of the most AI-exposed companies achieved average labour productivity growth of 163% relative to 2018 – nearly five times higher than the most AI-exposed companies overall.

Perhaps most surprisingly, headcount growth at the most AI-exposed companies is outpacing growth at the least AI-exposed companies – 52% relative to 36% in 2025, based on 2018 baseline levels.

## Average wage premium for AI skills hits 62% as AI job postings eclipse broader labour market growth

As companies continue to boost productivity with AI, the average wage premium for workers with AI skills continued to surge higher – hitting 62%, up from 57% last year.

The wage premium varies by industry: as high as 118% in some sectors, such as consumer markets, and 16% in government and public sector work.

Jobs requiring specific AI skills – such as prompt engineering or machine learning – have also soared, growing roughly eight times (69%) as fast as the overall jobs market, at 9%. The number of AI jobs is almost twice as high as 2024, with growth in AI jobs outpacing all jobs since 2015.

Sectors including technology, media and telecommunications (11%) and professional services (6%) sectors saw the highest share in AI job growth – with health at the lowest end (less than 1%)

“The traditional relationship between experience and expertise is changing. AI is removing some of the routine work that once acted as an apprenticeship, while increasing demand for judgement, leadership and adaptability much earlier in careers. Organisations need to rethink how they develop talent if they want people to thrive in this new environment.”

***–* ENDS *–***

**About PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer**

PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer analysed more than one billion jobs advertisements in 27 countries and territories. The Barometer combines large-scale labour market, company financial and occupational task data to understand how AI is reshaping jobs, skills, wages and productivity across the global economy. Additionally, this year’s Barometer includes targeted analysis of entry-level roles, including how the skill requirements of early-career jobs are changing in highly AI-exposed occupations. You can read the full report and learn more about the methodology and key takeaways at [www.pwc.com](/gx/en.html).

[See the full findings](/gx/en/services/ai/ai-jobs-barometer.html)

args.summary:
PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, released in London on 15 June 2026, analyzed more than one billion job ads across six continents (27 countries/territories) to examine how AI is reshaping the global labour market. The report finds AI is driving a 'two-track' global labour market: 'professionalised' roles (where AI automates routine tasks to emphasize human judgement, e.g., radiologists, recruiters) are growing twice as fast and seeing 42% faster salary growth than 'democratised' roles (where AI makes roles easier for non-experts, e.g., IT service managers, medical secretaries).

Key findings include: At entry level, AI-exposed roles are seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level 'human-intensive' skills (leadership, creativity, face-to-face interactions), based on 2.4 million US entry-level jobs. 'Seniorised' entry-level roles grew 35% since 2019 while other entry-level roles shrank 10%. The average wage premium for AI skills hit 62% (up from 57% last year), varying by industry from 118% in consumer markets to 16% in government/public sector. AI jobs are growing roughly eight times faster (69%) than the overall jobs market (9%), with the number of AI jobs almost twice as high as 2024. Technology, media, and telecommunications (11%) and professional services (6%) saw the highest share of AI job growth, while health was lowest (less than 1%).

A 'super-star' effect is emerging: the top 20% of most AI-exposed companies achieved 163% average labour productivity growth relative to 2018—nearly five times higher than AI-exposed companies overall (34% vs 24% for least-exposed companies). Headcount growth at most AI-exposed companies (52%) outpaced least-exposed companies (36%) in 2025. The report highlights that AI is removing routine work that served as apprenticeship, increasing demand for judgement and leadership earlier in careers, requiring organisations to rethink talent development.

Just released: [PwC](https://uk.linkedin.com/company/pwc?trk=public_post-text)'s 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, drawing on over a billion job ads across six continents. As many hiring specialists and job seekers are finding, AI is creating a two-track labour market: some jobs are being professionalised (reshaped to require deeper human expertise as AI handles routine elements), while others are being democratised (made easier for non-experts to perform as AI lowers the skill floor). Companies most exposed to AI show 40% higher productivity growth. And the bit I love the most: these companies are hiring more AND paying more - not cutting headcount or wages. Interestingly for early-career professionals, junior roles in AI-exposed sectors are seven times more likely to demand senior skills such as leadership and strategic thinking - which are traditionally seen later down the career track. And new tasks in AI-exposed roles are 2.5x more likely to require empathy, judgement, and creativity. So what does this mean for job seekers and career developers? The study indicates that AI is not erasing human value -rather, the skills that make you irreplaceable are increasingly the ones hardest to automate. Practically, this means actively building and evidencing your capacity for judgement, leadership, and complex decision-making, regardless of your career stage. Until recently, the guidance was to focus almost 100% on hard skills in your resume/CV. Now, it’s about authentically framing both hard and key soft skills prominently in your resume/CV and LinkedIn to stand out. Check out more study findings in the link below.

args.summary:
This LinkedIn page centers on PwC's launch of its 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer, based on analysis of over a billion job listings worldwide. PwC's core finding is that AI is not simply automating tasks, but fundamentally redefining roles and skill requirements, creating a widening gap between those who harness AI for growth and those left behind. The report is available at https://pwc.to/4uxKUmR and has been widely shared and discussed across LinkedIn.

Key findings highlighted across the various shares and comments on the post include:
- AI-exposed jobs require skills that are changing 66% faster (up to 75% faster per one commenter) than other roles—more than twice as fast as least-exposed roles, a significant increase over the previous year.
- AI-skilled workers command a wage premium of up to 56%.
- Companies most exposed to AI show significantly higher productivity growth—between 34% and 40% higher than least-exposed companies—and these firms are hiring more and paying more rather than cutting headcount or wages.
- A pronounced "super-star" effect is emerging: the top 20% of the most AI-exposed companies achieved average labour productivity growth of 163% relative to 2018, nearly five times higher than the most AI-exposed companies overall.
- Headcount growth at the most AI-exposed companies (52%) outpaces growth at the least exposed (36%) based on 2018 baselines.
- The labour market is becoming two-track: some jobs are being "professionalised" (reshaped to require deeper human expertise as AI handles routine elements) while others are being "democratised" (made easier for non-experts as AI lowers the skill floor).
- Junior roles in AI-exposed sectors are seven times more likely to demand traditionally senior skills such as leadership and strategic thinking, which were previously expected later in careers.
- New tasks in AI-exposed roles are 2.5x more likely to require empathy, judgement, and creativity.

Major comments on the post emphasize that the real divide will be between those who effectively integrate AI into learning, analysis, and decision-making versus those who use it superficially. Commenters note that human skills—judgement, empathy, creativity, critical thinking, and collaboration—are becoming more valuable as technical tasks become easier, and that the career ladder is compressing rather than disappearing. There are also concerns about the equity dimension, with entry points into high-growth careers narrowing precisely as skill requirements rise.

# 2026 AI Business Predictions

![AI Predictions Desktop Hero](/us/en/tech-effect/assets/ai-predictions-hero-desktop.jpg)
![AI Predictions Mobile Hero](/us/en/tech-effect/assets/ai-predictions-hero-mobile.jpg)

Only a few companies are realizing extraordinary value from AI today, things like surging top-line growth and significant valuation premiums. Many others are also experiencing measurable ROI, but their outcomes are often modest—some efficiency gains here, some capacity growth there, and general but unmeasurable productivity boosts. These results can pay for themselves and then some. But they don’t add up to transformation.

The picture’s starting to shift. It’s still hard to use AI to drive transformative value, and the technology continues to evolve at speed. That’s not changing. But what’s new is this: Success is becoming visible. We can now see what it looks like to use AI to build a leading-edge operating or business model. From mature systems to emerging tools like AI agents, examples of impact are multiplying—across strategy, operations, workforce, trust, tech stacks, and sustainability.

Companies now have enough evidence to build benchmarks, measure performance, and identify levers to accelerate value creation in both the business and functions like finance and tax so they can become nimbler, faster-growing organizations.

Why, then, has this kind of success—the kind that drives revenue growth and opens up new markets—been concentrated in so few? Too often, organizations spread their efforts thin, placing small sporadic bets. Because AI feels easy to use, early wins can mask deeper challenges.

But real results take precision in picking a few spots where AI can deliver wholesale transformation in ways that matter for the business, then executing with steady discipline that starts with senior leadership. After success in your priority areas, the rest of the company can follow.

We’ve seen that discipline pay off.

Across industries and regions, our work with clients reveals how deliberate and sustained efforts can turn AI experiments into engines of growth and innovation.

Our own AI transformation at PwC has given us this perspective from the inside too. Combined with nearly a decade of research through our executive surveys and annual AI predictions, we’ve built a clear view of what drives success—and what holds it back.

Our forecasts are grounded in real experience and focused on practical impact—so you can take confident steps to turn AI ambition into transformative business value in 2026 and beyond.

###### Explore the predictions

![]()

## 1. The disciplined march to value begins

With AI, many companies make an understandable mistake. Instead of leadership calling the shots with a top-down program, they take a ground-up approach, crowdsourcing initiatives that they then try to shape into something like a strategy. The result: projects that may not match enterprise priorities, are rarely executed with precision, and almost never lead to transformation.

Crowdsourcing AI efforts can create impressive adoption numbers, but it seldom produces meaningful business outcomes.

In 2026, we expect more companies to follow the lead of AI front-runners, adopting an enterprise-wide strategy centered on a top-down program. Senior leadership picks the spots for focused AI investments, looking for a few key workflows or business processes where payoffs from AI can be big. Leadership then applies the right “enterprise muscle”—talent, technical resources, and change management. Often, this program is executed through a centralized hub that we call an “[AI studio](/us/en/services/ai/agentic-ai-reinvention.html).” It brings together reusable tech components, frameworks for assessing use cases, a sandbox for testing, deployment protocols, and skilled people. This structure links business goals to AI capabilities so you can surface high-ROI opportunities.

Agentic AI looks to play an increasingly important role. AI agents can go beyond analysis and automate parts of complex, high-value workflows. Especially ripe areas for agents include demand sensing and forecasting, hyper-personalization, product design, and functions like [finance](/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-agents-for-finance.html), [HR](/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/agentic-ai-in-hr.html), [IT,](/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/agentic-ai-in-it.html)[tax](/us/en/services/tax/library/tax-ai-agents.html), and [internal audit](/us/en/services/consulting/cybersecurity-risk-regulatory/internal-audit/ai-internal-audit.html).

#### What to do now

**Have leadership pick the spots.** Top leadership picks a few areas for focused AI investments, often where business priorities, evidence of AI’s value, and availability of talent and data align. Then, leadership focuses on execution.

**Go narrow and deep.** After you identify the right high-value workflow, aim for wholesale transformation. Instead of cutting a few steps, rethink the workflow, which an AI-first approach may turn into a single step. That often starts by asking not how AI can fit into a workflow but how it can create a new one.

**Send your A-team.** Assign top talent to those areas where you’ve decided to focus on AI. These business leads can both work with company leadership to define target outcomes and drive progress with process owners and AI specialists.

![]()

## 2. Proof points and real-world benchmarks set the pace for agentic AI

There is—rightfully—little patience for “exploratory” AI investments. Each dollar spent should fuel measurable outcomes that accelerate business value. But many agentic deployments last year didn’t deliver much value. If you looked under the hood, many weren’t using agents in ways that matter. If you asked for a demo—to see an agent at work delivering value—you often couldn't get it because there wasn’t anything to see.

We expect that to change in 2026. We now know what good agentic AI looks like. It has proof points like benchmarks that track value that matters to the business, whether that’s financial (P&L impact), operational (market differentiation), or related to workforce and trust. Instead of siloed efforts, it has a centralized platform for deployment and oversight that draws on a shared library of agents, templates, and tools. Before each deployment, agents are tested, with flaws corrected and working demos created for future users to try—so they can offer feedback and start to trust what agents can do.

Agents are rolled out as part of all-new workflows, with clearly-articulated steps for human initiative, review, and oversight—and with people who have the training and incentives to work with agents and provide that oversight.

Built-in monitoring also includes different agents checking each other’s work, and for higher-risk scenarios, these agents come from different model providers.

Since agents can automatically document their decisions and actions, continuous monitoring can be highly effective in tracking adoption and performance, fixing errors quickly, and building stakeholder trust.

Agents today are imperfect, but new technologies generally are. Now that companies know how to proceed—with focused, centralized implementation guided by real-world benchmarks—2026 could be the year when agents shine.

#### What to do now

**Create metrics that drive outcomes.** For AI that delivers the value that your business wants, set concrete outcomes for it to deliver, select suitable “hard” metrics, and stand up a capability (with a mix of tech and people) that can help make those metrics timely and reliable.

**Follow the 80/20 rule.** Technology delivers only about 20% of an initiative’s value. The other 80% comes from redesigning work—so agents can handle routine tasks and people can focus on what truly drives impact.

**Spell it out.**As you design a new agentic workflow, map it step-by-step, specifying where agents own the work, where people do, where people and agents collaborate, and how oversight can take place for each step.

![]()

## 3. Rise of the AI generalist: A new workforce emerges

AI could soon end a shift that has marked most of the industrial era—the ever-increasing specialization of work. Agents can increasingly do the specialized tasks that fill the workdays of experienced, mid-tier employees. In IT, for example, you may no longer need coders specialized in specific languages. Instead, you may want engineers who understand both tech architecture and how to manage and oversee the agents that do know these languages. In finance functions, as agents do tasks like invoice processing, purchase order matching, reconciliation, and anomaly detection, people with general finance skills can focus on growing revenue and expanding margins, engaging with vendors on payment terms, working with sales on dynamic pricing models, and conducting more scenario planning.

Across functions, demand may grow for generalists who understand a wide range of tasks well enough to oversee agents and align their work with business goals.

In knowledge work, many of these roles can be filled by entry-level employees who tend to be AI savvy. As agents—available for anyone to buy or rent—take on more “midlevel” work, differentiation comes from senior professionals who excel at strategy and innovation. With more talent concentrated at the junior and senior levels, and a smaller mid-tier, the knowledge workforce may look like an hourglass. But for front-line employee-based task work, agents could replace entry-level workers with more mid-level people needed to orchestrate and manage these agents—creating a workforce more like a diamond.

#### What to do now

**Look for all-around athletes.** Evolve recruitment to look not just for people who are leading but also ones who are AI-forward and open-minded enough to be generalists and agent orchestrators.

**Start on workforce redesign.** As agents spread, your workforce may need new skills (like agent orchestration), new incentives (aligned to business outcomes, as agents do intermediate steps), and new roles (often related to oversight and strategy). And don’t underestimate the importance of having a culture that encourages change, evolution, and adoption of the future of work.

**Measure what matters.**With agents, iterations move quickly, but you may need more to allow for the back and forth required. Still, if an outcome that once took five days and two iterations now takes fifteen iterations but only two days, you’re ahead.

![]()

## 4. Responsible AI moves from talk to traction

Executives know what Responsible AI (RAI) is worth. In our [2025 Responsible AI survey](/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/responsible-ai-survey.html), 60% said that it boosts ROI and efficiency, and 55% reported improved customer experience and innovation. Yet, nearly half of respondents also said that turning RAI principles into operational processes has been a challenge.

2026 could be the year when companies overcome this challenge and roll out repeatable, rigorous RAI practices.

The acceleration of adoption leaves companies little choice, and agentic workflows are spreading faster than governance models can address their unique needs. In many cases, agents can do roughly half of the tasks that people now do—but that requires a new kind of governance, both to manage risks and improve outputs.

The good news: The proliferation of new, tech-enabled AI governance approaches brings new techniques to the challenge. Automated red teaming, deepfake detection, AI enabled inventory management, and other advancements can help make continuous assessment and monitoring a reality.

These tools are powerful and nimble, but to support effective (and cost-effective) RAI, also depends on suitable upskilling and user expectations, risk tiering (with protocols for human intervention), and clarified documentation requirements and tools. RAI can then deliver the value you want like performance, innovation, and a reduction in the costs and delays that come with governance models built for another time.

#### What to do now

**Integrate early.** The faster and deeper you can align IT, risk, and AI specialists—with clear responsibilities and expectations—the easier it can be to operationalize an RAI framework that can help grow business value and stakeholder trust.

**Add assurance.** Unless you have unlimited data science resources, independent assessments may be needed to fill gaps. For higher-risk and higher-value systems, an independent opinion can be critical for performance and risk management.

![]()

## 5. From vibe to value: Orchestration that accelerates impact

AI agents make possible “vibe” coding—where people write software without technical expertise—and other “vibe” work, where almost anyone can invent and test new ideas. But you usually need tech teams to “industrialize” this innovation, putting ideas into production with continuous monitoring. That’s why an [orchestration layer](/us/en/services/ai/agent-os.html) is so important. Its unified “command center” view helps you catch mistakes and track and fine-tune performance. It can also help end-user innovation enhance your top-down strategy.

You can spot valuable ideas and operationalize them quickly, manage risks, and keep everything aligned with your enterprise priorities.

A good AI orchestration layer should be easy even for non-techies to use, with intuitive dashboards and commands that let you drag-and-drop agents into new workflows—even for complex, high-value tasks. It should enable you to combine AI tools from different vendors into unified processes. It should integrate real-time data and natural language. And it should be built for centralized governance and security, with integrated code reviews and tools like encrypted credential vaults and sandboxes for prototyping. Most of all, it should put you in charge, enabling you to control AI anywhere in your company.

#### What to do now

**Create orchestrators.**As orchestrating agents becomes a part of people’s workdays, you’ll want your employees to know how to spot and correct agents’ mistakes, connect them into teams, and find new tasks for them to do.

**Help IT help you.**To help run your orchestration layer and execute your AI agenda, IT likely needs new resources and skills. Agentic AI for IT can help create new capacity by automating or assisting in many common IT tasks.

**Stay practical.** Durable, scaled, industrial-strength deployments depend on practical actions which your orchestration layer can enable, things like testing before release, constant monitoring, and protocols for patches and quick rollbacks if needed.

![]()

## 6. The demand for business returns drives AI for sustainability

Whether AI is a boon or a burden for sustainability in 2026 is up for grabs—but we lean toward boon. That’s not to understate the challenges. Even as AI quickly gets more energy efficient, its use is growing even faster. In fact, its fast-rising efficiency—by making AI cheaper—could accelerate its use even more. That could impact emissions, water supplies, and energy prices. But companies can become more efficient in AI use by approving token usage only when it delivers significant value and using methods like carbon scheduling to further cut emissions and costs.

And, as AI starts to drive a productivity boom, more efficient operations could compensate for AI’s environmental impact.

But there’s another reason that AI could boost sustainability—the quest for sales growth and margin expansion. AI agents, by gathering and analyzing customer data, can identify which customers would pay what premium for what kind of sustainability in products. Or they can measure and document that sustainability to strengthen your brand and grow your markets. AI can also help manage transport and electricity use to lower travel and power bills. Its simulations can show how to grow resilience against natural disasters. And it can cost-effectively help trace products across your value chain to reduce both environmental impacts and costly product recalls. These and other AI solutions can create financial value for you while making your operations more sustainable.

#### What to do now

**Be deliberate—and use what you have.** If you design AI with sustainability value as a goal, that value can come quickly. Since sustainability data is business data, for example, you can cost-effectively add AI use cases for Scope 3 indirect carbon emissions as you modernize supply chain data for AI.

**Follow your customers.** AI to personalize products, marketing, and pricing for customer sustainability wishes can deliver quick returns. You may even discover that you’re already meeting those expectations—you just haven’t been communicating or pricing for it.

**Act now to fend off rising costs.** As the grid struggles to meet AI-driven demand, you may face higher energy bills and even scarcity. Prepare to diversify energy sources or build your own, with renewables often the most affordable long-term option. You can also realize cost savings by integrating sustainability (such as carbon scheduling or protocols for when to use AI) into architecture.
