--- SOURCE 1: AI Upskilling Strategy - IBM ---
URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/ai-upskilling

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This IBM Think article (published October 15, 2024, updated July 2, 2026) defines AI upskilling as the process of building employees' knowledge and capabilities so they can effectively work alongside artificial intelligence in their day-to-day roles. Effective AI upskilling helps employees understand what AI can and can't do, direct AI tools productively, and integrate AI into existing workflows while retaining human judgment and creativity.

**Market context and data:** According to LinkedIn, 75% of US workers expect their roles to shift by 2029, but only 45% have received recent upskilling. Demand for AI literacy skills increased 70% between 2024 and 2025. The World Economic Forum's January 2026 report projects AI and related trends will displace ~92 million jobs by 2030 while creating 170 million new positions. IBM Institute for Business Value research found executives expect 53% of their workforces to require upskilling for their current roles.

**Key components of AI upskilling:** (1) AI literacy—understanding how AI works, its limitations (hallucinations, bias), and critically evaluating output; (2) Prompt engineering—structuring clear requests and breaking complex tasks into AI-handleable steps; (3) AI adoption—identifying where AI adds value and integrating tools into existing workflows; (4) Human-AI collaboration—knowing when to defer to or override AI suggestions while maintaining human accountability; (5) Problem-solving and innovation skills—critical thinking and creativity, which an IBM IBV survey of 2,690 executives found are becoming the most important employee competencies.

**Upskilling vs. reskilling:** Upskilling improves existing skill sets (e.g., customer care reps learning to use generative AI assistants), while reskilling involves learning entirely new skills for a new job (e.g., data processing workers learning web development).

**Benefits of AI upskilling:** Increased productivity (faster routine tasks, more creative work), improved employee retention and internal mobility, better decision-making and innovation, and improved employee experience (84% of employees say learning adds purpose to their work, per LinkedIn).

**Critical tools:** Agentic AI (65% of organizations actively deploying agentic AI operating models, 60% planning integrated AI agent workflows), Generative AI (watsonx, ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot), Machine learning, Natural language processing, and Robotic process automation.

**How AI can be used to upskill:** Customized online learning and development; skills gap analysis and talent matching (per IBM's Sarah Damenti); mentorship matching; and career path development.

**Best practices:** Design a lasting, updateable upskilling strategy aligned with organizational goals; map real use cases first; communicate clearly to address employee concerns; deploy hands-on sandboxes with real tools; drive mentorship networks with internal champions; carve out dedicated learning time; reimagine KPIs as AI reshapes work; and prioritize human-machine collaboration.

The article was written by Keith O'Brien (IBM Consulting), Amanda Downie (IBM Think), and Molly Hayes (IBM Think), with a quote from Sarah Damenti, associate partner for HR talent transformation at IBM.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"75% of US workers expect their roles to shift by 2029. But only 45% have received recent upskilling to meet those new shifts." — LinkedIn special report, "According to the World Economic Forum's January 2026 report, a convergence of disruptive economic trends, most notably AI, is projected to displace around 92 million jobs by 2030. But the same forces are forecast to create 170 million new positions across the globe." "Executives expect 53% of their workforces to require upskilling to perform their current role more effectively." — IBM Institute for Business Value, "By using nuanced skills data, businesses and talent development teams can develop targeted training programs and upskilling initiatives, preparing employees for success," says Sarah Damenti, associate partner for HR talent transformation at IBM. "As with any aspect of the change management process, skills management is an active and iterative process." — Sarah Damenti of IBM, "The most effective forms of AI upskilling allow employees to retain the judgement and creativity that make their work valuable while increasing their capabilities and productivity."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: How IBM Uses AI Upskilling to Shape Its Workforce ---
URL: https://staffing.com/ibm-ai-upskilling-workforce

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published September 10, 2025 on Staffing.com, is authored by Kitty Chaney Reed, IBM's Chief Leadership, Culture, and Inclusion Officer, who has over 20 years of leadership and team-building experience. The piece argues that as AI and automation reshape the workplace, companies must future-proof their workforces through continuous learning and skill development, and that the same AI tools changing work can be leveraged to keep employee skills relevant.

Key statistics cited include: a 2025 IBM Institute for Business Value survey finding CEOs say 31% of the workforce will require retraining or reskilling within three years; McKinsey research estimating up to 30% of hours worked across the US economy could be automated by 2030 and 60% of jobs significantly altered by AI tools; and 54% of CEOs hiring for AI-related roles that didn't exist a year ago.

IBM's AI learning ecosystem centers on "Your Learning," its in-house digital learning platform adopted in 2016. All IBM employees must complete at least 40 hours of learning per year (the average employee completes 85 hours). Since 2018, the platform has used AI to provide personalized learning recommendations based on each user's current skills, job history, and preferences. Employees earn badges for acquiring knowledge or demonstrating hands-on application of skills, and can access credentials from strategic third parties.

The article highlights how AI-driven upskilling boosts inclusion, noting IBM's AI Ethics Board (around 30 professionals) upholds responsible AI principles, with the author serving on it. Real-world benefits include: more meaningful manager-employee conversations driven by data; higher employee engagement (Gallup research shows employees using strengths daily are six times more likely to be engaged); higher productivity (skill development is one of two dimensions of IBM's performance management matrix alongside outcomes); and higher retention (with AI used to identify skills acquisition to inform promotion, rewards, and compensation).

The author outlines how to gain employee buy-in for AI tools, noting a 2025 Pew Research report found 52% of workers worry about AI's workplace impact while only 36% feel hopeful. Key recommendations include: ensuring AI tools align with company culture, identifying skills gaps first, ensuring technology is trusted (via boards or governing bodies for ethical guidelines), being transparent about data use so employees can opt out, and putting humans first by emphasizing AI augments rather than replaces human intelligence.

The article concludes that annual one-size-fits-all training is obsolete; employees need continuous, data-driven, personalized upskilling, with soft skills like adaptability and collaboration increasingly important. It cites LinkedIn's Global Talent Trends showing 69% of US executives plan to prioritize hiring candidates with soft skills that allow them to move nimbly across roles. HR and L&D leaders have an opportunity to equip people with tomorrow's skills and prove to anxious workers that AI can improve their careers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"According to a 2025 global survey by the IBM Institute for Business Value, CEOs say 31% of the workforce will require retraining or reskilling within three years."
</key_excerpts>

**AI:** IBM and Red Hat unveiled InstructLab (open-source LLM fine-tuning), launched Granite 3.0 models (8B and 2B, trained on 12 trillion tokens in 12 languages) in October, and Granite 3.1 models in December with 128K context length. They released Granite Guardian safety models, Granite Time Series models (TTM downloaded 5M+ times on Hugging Face), and the next-gen watsonx Code Assistant (improved code explanation speed by 90%). A new open-source agent framework called Bee was released. The AI Alliance (co-founded with Meta) grew to 140 members in 23 countries. **Semiconductors:** IBM unveiled Spyre, an AI accelerator chip for Z and Power systems with 32 cores and 25.6 billion transistors (5nm process), designed to bring generative AI to mainframes handling ~70% of global transactions by value. The brain-inspired NorthPole chip achieved LLM inference at <1ms per token (47x faster and 73x more energy-efficient than GPUs). Researchers created the world's first polymer optical waveguide for co-packaged optics (50-micron pitch, 80% size reduction), potentially cutting 70B-parameter LLM training from 3 months to 3 weeks. IBM and Rapidus reached a 2nm process milestone using nanosheet multi-Vt technology, and IBM demonstrated EUV lithography metallization down to 21nm pitch.

**Quantum:** IBM extended its quantum roadmap to 2033, unveiled a 156-qubit Heron chip (2Q gate error rates of 8x10^-4, 240x speed improvement to 240K CLOPS), and demonstrated accurate results on Heron out to 5,000 gate operations. Achieved m-coupler (Crossbill) and l-coupler (Flamingo) milestones. Released Qiskit v1.0, benchmarked as the world's most performant quantum SDK (29x faster transpiling than TKET, 54% fewer two-qubit gates), plus Qiskit Functions, Transpiler Service, and AI Code Assistant. --- SOURCE 10: IBM’s AI Strategy: Dominance of Enterprise Solutions - Klover.ai ---
URL: https://www.klover.ai/ibm-ai-strategy-dominance-of-enterprise-solutions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This report by Dany Kitishian of Klover.AI analyzes IBM's strategy to dominate the enterprise Artificial Intelligence (AI) market. Rather than competing head-to-head with consumer-focused hyperscalers over model size, IBM has pivoted to focus on governance, hybrid cloud integration, and full-stack optimization—the "how" of AI deployment in high-value, regulated industries rather than the "what" of ever-larger language models.

The analysis is structured around four strategic pillars:

1. **The "AI First" Doctrine**: IBM focuses on the enterprise B2B market, embedding AI as the central pillar for business model reinvention. CEO Arvind Krishna has stated "the era of AI experimentation is over." Central to this approach is the Red Hat OpenShift hybrid cloud foundation, which lets enterprises keep sensitive data on-premises while leveraging AI capabilities across any cloud. IBM Consulting (160,000 employees, 75,000+ trained on generative AI) drives approximately 80% of AI-related bookings, with consultants called "purple squirrels" possessing dual business/technical fluency.

2. **The watsonx Triad**: A three-part platform designed to address enterprise AI barriers:
   - **watsonx.ai**: An integrated development studio for training, tuning, and deploying models. It's model-agnostic, supporting IBM's Granite models plus open-source options from Meta's Llama and Hugging Face. The "Tuning Studio" enables customization with proprietary data.
   - **watsonx.data**: An open data lakehouse managing trusted data from any source, addressing the fact that 80-90% of enterprise data is unstructured. Includes vector indexes for RAG patterns.
   - **watsonx.governance**: Automates AI governance, risk management, and regulatory compliance—the direct strategic lesson from the Watson Health failure.

3. **The Full-Stack Moat**: From custom silicon (including the AI Hardware Center aiming for 1000-fold AI performance efficiency gains) to the IBM Telum II processor and the re-engineered IBM z17 mainframe capable of processing 450 billion inference operations per day. IBM is also a quantum computing leader with a roadmap for fault-tolerant quantum computers by 2029 and over 70 systems deployed globally.

4. **The Open Ecosystem Offensive**: IBM open-sources its Granite models under Apache 2.0 licenses, positioning watsonx as the commercial "last mile" platform. Co-launched InstructLab with Red Hat for community-driven LLM development. Partners pragmatically with AWS, Microsoft, SAP, Adobe, Salesforce, and others for integration rather than displacement.

**Financial evidence**: IBM's generative AI book of business surpassed $5 billion by Q4 2024 and $6 billion by Q1 2025. Analysts project total AI revenue could reach $15 billion by 2027. A Forrester study found 337% ROI for Watson Assistant customers over three years. IBM has realized approximately $3.5 billion in internal productivity savings since early 2023, with 94% of HR queries handled by AI and contract drafting 80% faster.

**Risks**: Notable past failure of Watson Health (oversold immature technology, struggled with real-world clinical data, poor workflow integration). Current risks include execution complexity, aggressive hyperscaler competition (Microsoft Copilot has a significant enterprise seat-count lead), declining legacy hardware revenues, and internal organizational silos—"the biggest competition for IBM is IBM itself."

**Competitive comparison**: IBM's strategy is described as "asymmetric warfare" against Microsoft Azure AI, Google Vertex AI, and Amazon SageMaker—changing the competitive rules from model scale to hybrid cloud integration, governance, and trust. The report concludes IBM is positioning itself as the "master architect" of enterprise AI rather than a "builder" of AI engines, making its leadership in the regulated enterprise segment "a strategic inevitability."
</summary>

## Deloitte's 2025 Tech Value Survey: AI Dominance and Portfolio Imbalance

**Published:** 2025 (fielded May–June 2025)

**Authors:** Tim Smith, Gregory Dost, Garima Dhasmana, Parth Patwari, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, Iram Parveen

**Overview:** This report, based on a survey of nearly 550 business and technology leaders across five industries (consumer; energy/resources/industrials; financial services; life sciences/healthcare; technology/media/telecom), analyzes how AI investments are consuming an outsized share of digital budgets, potentially leaving other critical technology areas underfunded.

### Key Findings:

**1. AI is Dominating Digital Budgets:**
- 74% of surveyed organizations invested in AI and gen AI over the past year — nearly 20 percentage points higher than the next most popular technologies (data management, cloud, IoT, ERP at ~55% and below).
- More than half of respondents allocate 21% to 50% (average 36%) of digital initiative budgets to AI — about US$700M for a company with US$13B revenue.
- Digital budgets rose from 7.5% of revenue (2024) to 13.7% (2025). If growth continues at this pace, budgets could reach 32% of revenue by 2028.
- Cybersecurity investment is lagging: only 25% to 32% invested in identity management, zero trust, or federated security.
- Emerging areas: 39% invested in agentic AI, 23% in robotics.

**2. Value Creation is Real but Fragmented:**
- 84% of AI/gen AI investors report gaining ROI. However, a cited MIT study found only 5% of gen AI pilots deliver sustained value at scale.
- Over 95% say digital initiatives lifted market cap or return on equity.
- Nearly 60% believe 21% to 50% of enterprise value remains latent.
- Paradox: AI investors were less likely to see significant market cap gains (43%) than those investing in data (65%) or security (66%).
- Data monetization strategy adoption grew from 16% (2023) to 65% (2025).

**3. C-Suite Alignment is Critical:**
- CFOs, CIOs, and CTOs often define success differently (ROI vs. EBITDA vs. KPIs), creating misalignment.
- Strategy innovation leaders — organizations that implement 4+ of 7 strategic innovation actions — outperform peers across all value measures and attribute over 40% of enterprise value to digital initiatives.

**4. Persistent Challenges:**
- Top barriers: misaligned incentives, legacy systems, lack of technical expertise (grew from 52% to 58%), security concerns, lack of strategy, insufficient funding.
- 60% cite data privacy/security as a major hurdle to AI automation.
- Success hinges on three factors: cyber strategy, tech strategy alignment, and dedicated leadership.

### Recommendations:
- Raise digital budgets to match ambition.
- Establish spending minimums for foundational technologies (platforms, data architecture, identity/zero trust, ERP) so AI doesn't starve the portfolio.
- Measure value beyond ROI — use a shared value scorecard.
- Align leadership incentives around enterprisewide outcomes.
- Shift from AI pilots to learning-capable systems integrated into core workflows.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an analysis post from Implicator.ai (published October 6, 2025) analyzing Anthropic's deployment of its Claude AI to 470,000 Deloitte employees across 150+ countries. The post argues this is not merely a software contract but a strategic "distribution machine" and channel play for the AI era.

Key points:
- Deloitte serves nearly 90% of the Fortune Global 500, allowing a single systems integrator to seed hundreds of accounts with certified staff recommending Claude by default.
- Deloitte is certifying 15,000 practitioners on Claude as implementation specialists, creating consulting infrastructure with switching costs that lock in clients.
- This deployment exceeds most AI vendors' entire customer bases by seat count, signaling that heavyweight enterprise wins outweigh consumer buzz in 2025.
- The central strategic contrast: OpenAI chases 200+ million weekly consumer users through ChatGPT, while Anthropic bets on deep integration with fewer partners, embedding inside consulting firms.
- The Deloitte alliance started in 2024 and expanded to global staff access, role-specific configurations (tax research, code generation, proposal drafts), and a push into regulated industries.
- Competitive moat: Anthropic's "safety-first" posture is now a commercial wedge, as regulated industries need audit trails, policy enforcement, explainability, and named controls that general-purpose chatbots can't compete with.
- Timing context: In September 2024, Anthropic closed $13 billion at a $183 billion valuation, launched Claude Sonnet 4.5 as its flagship coding/agent model, and committed to tripling its international workforce.
- The Deloitte internal deployment (live sandboxes, benchmarks, Claude artifacts) provides credibility—"we use what we sell"—plus billable follow-ons like persona design, red-teaming, data-guardrail tuning, and agent workflow rewrites, creating recurring revenue with lock-in.

--- SOURCE 3: What can we learn from Deloitte's AI incident of 2025? ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a29kqInpbos

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage (published 3 December 2025 by Mackay Goodwin, a professional services firm, via their MG Academy podcast) discusses the key lessons from a Deloitte AI incident in 2025. The incident involved a consulting report sent to the Australian federal Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, which assessed whether an automated system that stops government benefits under certain criteria was working as intended. An expert academic reviewer found that some references and a summary of a legal case in the report contained AI-fabricated material. The podcast, featuring Edmund Tadros from the Australian Financial Review, emphasizes that the publisher (Deloitte) bears responsibility for the report's content regardless of whether AI was used. Key lessons highlighted: organizations should not abandon AI but must know exactly where it was used and apply extra scrutiny to those sections; AI output should be checked more carefully (comparing AI to a well-intentioned intern whose work requires extra review); human judgment, context, and careful review remain essential for high-stakes work; and clients are likely to increasingly ask firms to disclose how AI was used in their reports. The episode treats the incident as a normal part of AI's learning process from which organizations can draw lessons for 2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The key takeaway: AI can definitely speed things up when it comes to repetitive tasks, but you still need human judgment, context and careful review when the stakes are high.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: 2026 AI Business Predictions ---
URL: https://www.pwc.com/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-predictions.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
PwC's "2026 AI Business Predictions" (published as part of their Tech Effect and AI services content) outlines six key forecasts for how companies can turn AI ambition into transformative business value in 2026. The central thesis is that only a few companies are currently realizing extraordinary value from AI, while many others achieve only modest ROI. The article argues that success in AI requires precision, discipline, and top-down leadership rather than spreading efforts thin across small sporadic bets.

The six predictions are:
1. **The disciplined march to value begins** - Companies will shift from ground-up crowdsourcing to top-down, enterprise-wide AI strategies where senior leadership picks the spots for focused AI investment. Execution happens through centralized "AI studios" that link business goals to AI capabilities, with agentic AI playing an increasingly important role in workflows like demand sensing, hyper-personalization, product design, finance, HR, IT, tax, and internal audit.
2. **Proof points and real-world benchmarks set the pace for agentic AI** - While many agentic deployments failed to deliver value in 2025, 2026 could be the year agents shine, using real-world benchmarks that track business-value metrics (financial P&L impact, operational differentiation, workforce/trust). Guidance includes the 80/20 rule (technology delivers only ~20% of an initiative's value; the rest comes from redesigning work) and step-by-step workflow mapping with human oversight.
3. **Rise of the AI generalist** - AI agents will reduce specialization, causing demand to grow for generalists who oversee agents and align their work with business goals. Knowledge workforces may become hourglass-shaped (talent concentrated at junior and senior levels), while front-line workforces may become diamond-shaped (more mid-level orchestrators).
4. **Responsible AI moves from talk to traction** - Companies will roll out repeatable RAI practices, driven by acceleration of adoption and agentic workflows outpacing governance models. New tools like automated red teaming, deepfake detection, and AI-enabled inventory management will help. PwC's 2025 Responsible AI survey found 60% said RAI boosts ROI/efficiency, and 55% reported improved customer experience and innovation, but nearly half said operationalizing RAI principles was challenging.
5. **From vibe to value: Orchestration that accelerates impact** - "Vibe" coding and innovation require an orchestration layer ("command center") to industrialize ideas into production with continuous monitoring, centralized governance, and security. The layer should be easy for non-techies to use with drag-and-drop workflows, integrate AI tools from different vendors, and put companies in charge of controlling AI anywhere.
6. **The demand for business returns drives AI for sustainability** - AI use is growing faster than its energy efficiency improvements, potentially impacting emissions, water, and energy prices. However, AI can boost sustainability through productivity gains, customer sustainability analysis, supply chain tracing, and carbon scheduling. The article advises being deliberate with sustainability goals, following customer sustainability wishes, and preparing for rising energy costs by diversifying energy sources (renewables often most affordable long-term).

Each prediction includes practical "What to do now" action items for business leaders. The article is grounded in PwC's nearly a decade of executive survey research and its own internal AI transformation experience.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation ---
URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This McKinsey Global Survey article, published November 5, 2025, examines the state of AI adoption across organizations. Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, while revenue benefits are reported in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development.

The survey identifies "AI high performers" (about 6% of respondents who attribute 5%+ EBIT impact and report significant value) as distinguished by several factors: they are more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; more likely to set growth and/or innovation objectives (not just efficiency); nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows (identified as one of the strongest contributing factors via a relative weights analysis of 31 variables); three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to have senior leaders demonstrating ownership and commitment; more likely to have defined human-validation processes; and more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI (one-third of high performers do so, versus about three-quarters scaling AI overall). Successful practices align with McKinsey's Rewired research across six dimensions: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption/scaling.

On workforce impact, expectations vary: 32% of respondents expect enterprise-wide workforce decreases of 3% or more in the coming year, 43% expect no change, and 13% expect increases. A median of 17% of respondents report declines in function workforce sizes in the past year due to AI, but a median of 30% expect decreases next year. Larger organizations and high performers are more likely to expect meaningful workforce changes. The article identifies three centers of innovation in the AI market:
1. **High end (hyperscalers/CSPs):** The biggest cloud providers lead in R&D, talent, and innovation, developing larger, more powerful models requiring more compute. This will push data center scale from today's ~100 megawatts to gigawatts, straining power grids and supply chains (GPUs, substrates, silicon photonics, power generation equipment).
2. **Enterprises and sovereigns:** Generative AI inference is becoming the killer app for edge computing. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) and vector embeddings help reduce latency, costs, and keep data private. Small language models (open-source: Meta's Llama, Mistral, Falcon; proprietary: Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini) will become increasingly important for domain-specific, cost-efficient tasks.
3. **Independent software vendors (ISVs):** LLM-enabled SaaS (Adobe, Microsoft, Salesforce) is creating a flood of new AI capabilities within existing application suites.

The article also discusses industry disruption and verticalization. Technology vendors are optimizing stacks vertically—hyperscalers like Amazon (Trainium, Graviton), Google (TPU), and Meta (MTIA) have developed their own silicon. Nvidia has expanded its "unit of compute" beyond the GPU to include fabrics, hybrid memory, DGX, and cloud offerings. Apple is developing on-device LLM silicon.

Key segment disruptions include:
- **LLMs:** OpenAI's ChatGPT held near monopoly until 2023, but open-source and proprietary models now offer diversified options.
- **Storage:** Advancements for generative AI needs, including data silo consolidation, object vs. file/block storage, and vectorized databases.
- **Data management:** Growing need for data preparation and mobility as data-hungry AI apps mobilize public cloud data.
- **Tech services:** High demand in the medium term while clients lack AI skills, though significant portions will eventually be replaced by software.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stated: "Generative AI is the largest TAM [total addressable market] expansion of software and hardware that we've seen in several decades." AI workloads are projected to grow 25% to 35% per year through 2027. The article concludes that AI's disruptive growth will spread beyond hyperscalers to smaller CSPs, enterprises, sovereigns, and software vendors, requiring companies to adapt rapidly to capture share of this potential trillion-dollar market.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Bain & Company is a privately held American management consulting firm headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, and is one of the "Big Three" management consultancies (alongside McKinsey and BCG). Founded in 1973 by Bill Bain (former Group Vice President of Boston Consulting Group) and Patrick F. Graham, the firm was spawned from an internal competition at BCG in which Bain led the winning "blue team"; most of that team followed him when he left. The firm grew rapidly through word-of-mouth, reaching $150 million in revenues by 1986 and 800 staff by 1987.

Corporate history: Bain faced turmoil in the late 1980s, including a PR crisis over its work with Guinness (following the Guinness share-trading fraud scandal, though Bain itself was not charged), financial problems from leveraged ESOP buyouts, and layoffs of about 30% of staff. Mitt Romney was brought back as interim CEO in January 1991 and saved the firm from bankruptcy by renegotiating debt, restructuring ownership, and convincing founding partners to give up $100 million in equity. Orit Gadiesh became chairman (a role she has held since) and Thomas Tierney became worldwide managing director in 1993, helping the firm rebound with 25% annual growth from 1992–1999. Recent leaders include managing directors John Donahoe, Robert Bechek, and Manny Maceda; Christophe De Vusser became global CEO in July 2024, the first European to hold the post. In 2025 the firm reported revenue of $14 billion and 22,000 employees, having ~64 offices worldwide. Bill Bain spun off Bain Capital (an investment firm led by Mitt Romney) in 1984.

Controversies: Bain was embroiled in a major scandal in South Africa involving its 2015 consulting work with the South African Revenue Service (SARS), where it billed $11 million for work later deemed bad advice. The Zondo Commission found Bain worked with President Jacob Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to facilitate the takeover of SARS, partly to prevent corruption investigations, and that Bain tried to bribe a former employee (Athol Williams) to "bury the truth." Consequences included: Bain's resignation from Business Leadership South Africa (Jan 2022); a three-year ban from UK government contracts (Aug 2022, later overturned/lifted in March 2023); and a 10-year ban from South African state contracts (Sept 2022). In July 2025, Bain announced it was winding down its consulting operations in South Africa entirely.

Consulting services: Bain primarily advises Fortune 500 CEOs on private equity investments, M&A, corporate strategy, finance, and operations. It developed the Net Promoter Score (sold since 2006), has a large private equity practice (by 2018 over 3x the size of its nearest PE consulting competitor, representing 25% of global business), created the Bridgespan Group for nonprofits, and pledged $1 billion in pro bono consulting by 2025. It also does "AI diligence work" using vibe coding to create prototype replications of commercial software to inform M&A decisions.

Reception and culture: A Price Waterhouse audit found Bain client market value increased 456% from 1980–1989 vs. 192% for the Dow. Bain operates on a non-competition model requiring long-term client engagement, which critics say can make the firm "unfirable." Known for secrecy (dubbed the "KGB of Consulting"), employees sign confidentiality contracts, and clients are given codenames. Bain consistently ranks among top workplaces (Glassdoor, Consulting Magazine) and has a highly ranked LGBT employee group called Pride. Employees are sometimes called "Bainies."

--- SOURCE 1: Bain Vector Interview: Complete Guide (2026) ---
URL: https://www.hackingthecaseinterview.com/pages/bain-vector-interview

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This guide by Taylor Warfield (Former Bain Manager and interviewer, updated May 18, 2026) provides a comprehensive overview of the Bain Vector interview process. Bain Vector is Bain & Company's digital delivery platform with 1,500+ specialists in AI, data science, engineering, design, and product management, combining two practice areas: AI, Insights & Solutions (AIS) and Enterprise Technology (ET). 

The interview process has 5-7 stages over 4-6 weeks: resume screen (~90% of applicants filtered), online assessment (TestGorilla, SOVA, or HireVue video, 60-90 minutes), recruiter screen, technical interview (SQL, Python, statistics, A/B testing, ML, generative AI varying by role), traditional business case interview with data/AI elements, behavioral interview (STAR method, Bain's operating principles), and final round with senior managers/partners.

Key details include: The process is very difficult (Glassdoor rating 3.67/5, ~68.5% positive experience, ~1-2% acceptance rate, 35 days average from application to offer). Technical skills tested span five areas: Python/SQL, statistics/A-B testing, machine learning, generative AI/RAG, and business framing. Compared to peers, Bain Vector is more business case-heavy than BCG X (balanced) and McKinsey QuantumBlack (technical-heavy/deep).

The article includes 10 preparation tips: master Bain case format (2 of 6 rounds are pure cases, practice 25-50 cases), drill SQL window functions, perfect the "Why Bain Vector" answer, study A/B testing tradeoffs (not just p<0.05), practice explaining technical concepts to non-technical audiences, prepare 6-8 STAR stories, read Bain's two free practice cases (Coffee Shop Co. and FashionCo.), practice generative AI questions, mock interview with current consultants, and maintain physical/stamina health.

Common Vector behavioral questions focus on using data to change stakeholder minds, balancing speed and accuracy, taking initiative, disagreeing on analytical approaches, and communicating technical findings to non-technical audiences. Entry-level roles require bachelor's/master's degrees; senior roles need 5-10 years experience, with PhDs common but not required at senior levels. The most common mistake candidates make is treating Vector like a tech company data science loop rather than recognizing the emphasis on traditional business case interviews.
</summary>

The report defines generative AI as applications built on foundation models—large artificial neural networks that can process vast unstructured data and perform multiple tasks across text, images, video, audio, and code. It provides a comprehensive first assessment of where business value from generative AI could accrue and its potential workforce impacts.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Generative AI could add the equivalent of $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion annually across 63 use cases analyzed across 16 business functions—roughly the size of the UK's entire 2021 GDP ($3.1 trillion). - About 75 percent of the value falls across four areas: customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering, and R&D.

Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, while revenue benefits are reported in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development.

The survey identifies "AI high performers" (about 6% of respondents who attribute 5%+ EBIT impact and report significant value) as distinguished by several factors: they are more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; more likely to set growth and/or innovation objectives (not just efficiency); nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows (identified as one of the strongest contributing factors via a relative weights analysis of 31 variables); three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to have senior leaders demonstrating ownership and commitment; more likely to have defined human-validation processes; and more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI (one-third of high performers do so, versus about three-quarters scaling AI overall). Successful practices align with McKinsey's Rewired research across six dimensions: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption/scaling.

On workforce impact, expectations vary: 32% of respondents expect enterprise-wide workforce decreases of 3% or more in the coming year, 43% expect no change, and 13% expect increases. A median of 17% of respondents report declines in function workforce sizes in the past year due to AI, but a median of 30% expect decreases next year. Larger organizations and high performers are more likely to expect meaningful workforce changes. Most organizations hired for AI-related roles in the past year, with software and data engineers most in demand.

Risk mitigation efforts are becoming more common. Respondents report acting to manage an average of four AI-related risks today versus two in 2022. Fifty-one percent of respondents from organizations using AI report at least one negative consequence, with nearly one-third reporting consequences from AI inaccuracy—the most commonly experienced and mitigated risk. Explainability is the second-most-reported risk but is not among the most commonly mitigated. High performers report more negative consequences (particularly IP infringement and regulatory compliance) but also protect against more risks.

The survey was in the field June 25 to July 29, 2025, with 1,993 respondents from 105 nations, weighted by GDP contribution. Thirty-eight percent work for organizations with over $1 billion in annual revenues. Authors include Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, and Tara Balakrishnan from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey.

--- SOURCE 2: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation ---
URL: https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This McKinsey Global Survey article, published November 5, 2025, examines the state of AI adoption across organizations. Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, while revenue benefits are reported in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development.

The survey identifies "AI high performers" (about 6% of respondents who attribute 5%+ EBIT impact and report significant value) as distinguished by several factors: they are more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; more likely to set growth and/or innovation objectives (not just efficiency); nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows (identified as one of the strongest contributing factors via a relative weights analysis of 31 variables); three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to have senior leaders demonstrating ownership and commitment; more likely to have defined human-validation processes; and more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI (one-third of high performers do so, versus about three-quarters scaling AI overall). Successful practices align with McKinsey's Rewired research across six dimensions: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption/scaling.

On workforce impact, expectations vary: 32% of respondents expect enterprise-wide workforce decreases of 3% or more in the coming year, 43% expect no change, and 13% expect increases. A median of 17% of respondents report declines in function workforce sizes in the past year due to AI, but a median of 30% expect decreases next year. Larger organizations and high performers are more likely to expect meaningful workforce changes. Most organizations hired for AI-related roles in the past year, with software and data engineers most in demand.

Risk mitigation efforts are becoming more common. Respondents report acting to manage an average of four AI-related risks today versus two in 2022. Fifty-one percent of respondents from organizations using AI report at least one negative consequence, with nearly one-third reporting consequences from AI inaccuracy—the most commonly experienced and mitigated risk. Explainability is the second-most-reported risk but is not among the most commonly mitigated. High performers report more negative consequences (particularly IP infringement and regulatory compliance) but also protect against more risks.

The survey was in the field June 25 to July 29, 2025, with 1,993 respondents from 105 nations, weighted by GDP contribution. Thirty-eight percent work for organizations with over $1 billion in annual revenues. Authors include Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, and Tara Balakrishnan from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a video panel discussion from The Montgomery Summit (March 7, 2025) presented by QuantumBlack AI by McKinsey, featuring a prelude by Lari Hämäläinen, Senior Partner at McKinsey & Company, followed by a panel discussion with three CEOs: Priya Vijayarajendran (Chief Executive Officer & President Technology, ASAPP), Matan Grinberg (Founder & CEO, Factory AI), and Ketan Karkhanis (CEO, ThoughtSpot).

KEY STATISTICS AND PREDICTIONS FROM MCKINSEY (Lari Hämäläinen):
- McKinsey believes by 2030, 50-70% of tasks in the economy can be automated, translating to roughly $25 trillion in global economic impact (out of ~$100 trillion global economy, a 25% productivity uplift), with software industry expected to double by adding ~$500 billion in revenue.
- Even assuming job creation matches losses, unemployment is projected to increase by 5%.
- Compute efficiency of training LLMs triples every year (compute needed to reach the same level drops to one-third annually); 4.5x more compute was spent training models in the past year compared to the year before.
- Only ~25% of companies feel they've made meaningful progress on GenAI; of those, only 10% have truly scaled GenAI, and only 5% have done end-to-end workflow implementations.
- GitHub Copilot retention drops to nearly zero at the 3-4 month mark at one of the world's largest software companies due to tool-focused scaling, limited integration, individual reluctance (80% of developers feel it doesn't meaningfully change their job, some fear displacement), and lack of management/incentive systems.
- The total economic impact potential of AI remains ~$17-25 trillion (unchanged), but adoption speed and the adoption curve are accelerating, though enterprise-wide scale is not yet proven and legacy enterprises haven't yet seen concrete revenue increases.

KEY CONCEPTS:
- Hämäläinen divides agents into transactional agents (individual augmentation/co-pilots, task & workflow automation platforms like Salesforce Agentforce and Microsoft Copilot Studio, domain-specific journey/workflow redesign) and transformative agents (rethinking how companies run, becoming AI-native).
- Copilots haven't generated a single dollar of revenue at any company he knows; workflow automation solutions can deliver 3-5% annual productivity benefits.
- Two modes of enterprise change: Kaizen (continuous improvement, immediate priority) and Kakushin (radical change/step-change).
- Enterprise transformation is 3-5 years away for AI-native organizations.

PANEL DISCUSSIONS:
1. ThoughtSpot (Ketan Karkhanis): Describes AI shift as "cloud 2.0" - the next AI agentic BI platform is a "smartphone version" not an incremental "flip phone" upgrade of legacy BI tools like Tableau/Power BI. Replacing 10,000 dashboards with one agentic AI analyst. Examples: EasyJet completely replacing Tableau; Bank of America as a customer. Notably, regulated industries (financial services, health) are embracing this faster than tech companies. Every AI conversation is an ROI conversation. Focus areas: becoming an AI company (targeting 30-35% productivity gains from using AI in every function), training (rolling out AI certification for every employee), trust as the "killer AI feature" of the future, and consultative customer education.

2. Factory AI (Matan Grinberg): Software development's biggest opportunity is not the coding itself but the understanding/planning/migration work (right order of operations, testing, verification). Large enterprises are most eager to adopt agentic AI for software development, partly due to "scars from being late to mobile" and the large stakes with tens of thousands of developers. Key challenge is behavior change among stubborn developers and net-new workflows; takes a strong stance that developers will remain essential with more leverage. Sees differentiation in ruthlessly focusing on less flashy, less sexy enterprise problems (e.g., migrations done in 2 weeks vs. 6 months) and has found success working with consulting firms.

3. ASAPP (Priya Vijayarajendran): Customer care/contact centers serve ~70% of customer care through voice costing $7-8 per call; IVR is four decades old; digital channels cost ~$4. ASAPP promises containment improvement (e.g., 30-point improvement) with 5-7% reduction in agents, converting cost centers into profit centers. Product promise: seamless real-time natural language autonomous agents (voice, chat, SMS, email) that act like humans and scale like software, triaging and performing actions across complex backend systems. Scaling focus is frictionless onboarding and bite-size adoption; customers who start typically consume ~200% more automation within a year.

The panel also discusses scaling strategies at different company stages and answers a question clarifying that McKinsey's total AI impact figure (~$17-25 trillion) hasn't tripled—rather, the boundary between traditional AI and GenAI has blurred and adoption speed has accelerated.
</summary>

3. **Independent software vendors (ISVs):** LLM-enabled SaaS (Adobe, Microsoft, Salesforce) is creating a flood of new AI capabilities within existing application suites.

- **Data management:** Growing need for data preparation and mobility as data-hungry AI apps mobilize public cloud data.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Bain & Company is a privately held American management consulting firm headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts, and is one of the "Big Three" management consultancies (alongside McKinsey and BCG). Founded in 1973 by Bill Bain (former Group Vice President of Boston Consulting Group) and Patrick F. Graham, the firm was spawned from an internal competition at BCG in which Bain led the winning "blue team"; most of that team followed him when he left. The firm grew rapidly through word-of-mouth, reaching $150 million in revenues by 1986 and 800 staff by 1987.

Corporate history: Bain faced turmoil in the late 1980s, including a PR crisis over its work with Guinness (following the Guinness share-trading fraud scandal, though Bain itself was not charged), financial problems from leveraged ESOP buyouts, and layoffs of about 30% of staff. Mitt Romney was brought back as interim CEO in January 1991 and saved the firm from bankruptcy by renegotiating debt, restructuring ownership, and convincing founding partners to give up $100 million in equity. Orit Gadiesh became chairman (a role she has held since) and Thomas Tierney became worldwide managing director in 1993, helping the firm rebound with 25% annual growth from 1992–1999. Recent leaders include managing directors John Donahoe, Robert Bechek, and Manny Maceda; Christophe De Vusser became global CEO in July 2024, the first European to hold the post. In 2025 the firm reported revenue of $14 billion and 22,000 employees, having ~64 offices worldwide. Bill Bain spun off Bain Capital (an investment firm led by Mitt Romney) in 1984.

Controversies: Bain was embroiled in a major scandal in South Africa involving its 2015 consulting work with the South African Revenue Service (SARS), where it billed $11 million for work later deemed bad advice. The Zondo Commission found Bain worked with President Jacob Zuma and SARS head Tom Moyane to facilitate the takeover of SARS, partly to prevent corruption investigations, and that Bain tried to bribe a former employee (Athol Williams) to "bury the truth." Consequences included: Bain's resignation from Business Leadership South Africa (Jan 2022); a three-year ban from UK government contracts (Aug 2022, later overturned/lifted in March 2023); and a 10-year ban from South African state contracts (Sept 2022). In July 2025, Bain announced it was winding down its consulting operations in South Africa entirely.

Consulting services: Bain primarily advises Fortune 500 CEOs on private equity investments, M&A, corporate strategy, finance, and operations. It developed the Net Promoter Score (sold since 2006), has a large private equity practice (by 2018 over 3x the size of its nearest PE consulting competitor, representing 25% of global business), created the Bridgespan Group for nonprofits, and pledged $1 billion in pro bono consulting by 2025. It also does "AI diligence work" using vibe coding to create prototype replications of commercial software to inform M&A decisions.

Reception and culture: A Price Waterhouse audit found Bain client market value increased 456% from 1980–1989 vs. 192% for the Dow. Bain operates on a non-competition model requiring long-term client engagement, which critics say can make the firm "unfirable." Known for secrecy (dubbed the "KGB of Consulting"), employees sign confidentiality contracts, and clients are given codenames. Bain consistently ranks among top workplaces (Glassdoor, Consulting Magazine) and has a highly ranked LGBT employee group called Pride. Employees are sometimes called "Bainies."
</summary>

Interview types drawn from a menu include behavioral interviews, portfolio walkthroughs, case interviews, coding/case problem challenges, take-home assignments (typically 3 days), and online assessments (including named SOVA and TestGorilla screens). The page also provides a two-week prep plan and notes that Road to Offer covers the consulting half of a Vector loop (cases, structure, math, chart reading, synthesis) but does not simulate SQL screens or coding assessments.

This is a video panel discussion from The Montgomery Summit (March 7, 2025) presented by QuantumBlack AI by McKinsey, featuring a prelude by Lari Hämäläinen, Senior Partner at McKinsey & Company, followed by a panel discussion with three CEOs: Priya Vijayarajendran (Chief Executive Officer & President Technology, ASAPP), Matan Grinberg (Founder & CEO, Factory AI), and Ketan Karkhanis (CEO, ThoughtSpot).

KEY STATISTICS AND PREDICTIONS FROM MCKINSEY (Lari Hämäläinen):
- McKinsey believes by 2030, 50-70% of tasks in the economy can be automated, translating to roughly $25 trillion in global economic impact (out of ~$100 trillion global economy, a 25% productivity uplift), with software industry expected to double by adding ~$500 billion in revenue.
- Even assuming job creation matches losses, unemployment is projected to increase by 5%.
- Compute efficiency of training LLMs triples every year (compute needed to reach the same level drops to one-third annually); 4.5x more compute was spent training models in the past year compared to the year before.
- Only ~25% of companies feel they've made meaningful progress on GenAI; of those, only 10% have truly scaled GenAI, and only 5% have done end-to-end workflow implementations.
- GitHub Copilot retention drops to nearly zero at the 3-4 month mark at one of the world's largest software companies due to tool-focused scaling, limited integration, individual reluctance (80% of developers feel it doesn't meaningfully change their job, some fear displacement), and lack of management/incentive systems.
- The total economic impact potential of AI remains ~$17-25 trillion (unchanged), but adoption speed and the adoption curve are accelerating, though enterprise-wide scale is not yet proven and legacy enterprises haven't yet seen concrete revenue increases.

KEY CONCEPTS:
- Hämäläinen divides agents into transactional agents (individual augmentation/co-pilots, task & workflow automation platforms like Salesforce Agentforce and Microsoft Copilot Studio, domain-specific journey/workflow redesign) and transformative agents (rethinking how companies run, becoming AI-native).
- Copilots haven't generated a single dollar of revenue at any company he knows; workflow automation solutions can deliver 3-5% annual productivity benefits.
- Two modes of enterprise change: Kaizen (continuous improvement, immediate priority) and Kakushin (radical change/step-change).
- Enterprise transformation is 3-5 years away for AI-native organizations.

PANEL DISCUSSIONS:
1. ThoughtSpot (Ketan Karkhanis): Describes AI shift as "cloud 2.0" - the next AI agentic BI platform is a "smartphone version" not an incremental "flip phone" upgrade of legacy BI tools like Tableau/Power BI. Replacing 10,000 dashboards with one agentic AI analyst. Examples: EasyJet completely replacing Tableau; Bank of America as a customer. Notably, regulated industries (financial services, health) are embracing this faster than tech companies. Every AI conversation is an ROI conversation. Focus areas: becoming an AI company (targeting 30-35% productivity gains from using AI in every function), training (rolling out AI certification for every employee), trust as the "killer AI feature" of the future, and consultative customer education.

2. Factory AI (Matan Grinberg): Software development's biggest opportunity is not the coding itself but the understanding/planning/migration work (right order of operations, testing, verification). Large enterprises are most eager to adopt agentic AI for software development, partly due to "scars from being late to mobile" and the large stakes with tens of thousands of developers. Key challenge is behavior change among stubborn developers and net-new workflows; takes a strong stance that developers will remain essential with more leverage. Sees differentiation in ruthlessly focusing on less flashy, less sexy enterprise problems (e.g., migrations done in 2 weeks vs. 6 months) and has found success working with consulting firms.

3. ASAPP (Priya Vijayarajendran): Customer care/contact centers serve ~70% of customer care through voice costing $7-8 per call; IVR is four decades old; digital channels cost ~$4. ASAPP promises containment improvement (e.g., 30-point improvement) with 5-7% reduction in agents, converting cost centers into profit centers. Product promise: seamless real-time natural language autonomous agents (voice, chat, SMS, email) that act like humans and scale like software, triaging and performing actions across complex backend systems. Scaling focus is frictionless onboarding and bite-size adoption; customers who start typically consume ~200% more automation within a year.

The panel also discusses scaling strategies at different company stages and answers a question clarifying that McKinsey's total AI impact figure (~$17-25 trillion) hasn't tripled—rather, the boundary between traditional AI and GenAI has blurred and adoption speed has accelerated.

KEY FINDINGS:

- About 75 percent of the value falls across four areas: customer operations, marketing and sales, software engineering, and R&D.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This McKinsey Global Survey article, published November 5, 2025, examines the state of AI adoption across organizations. Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. However, most organizations remain in the experimentation or piloting phase, with approximately two-thirds not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. AI agents (systems based on foundation models that can plan and execute multi-step workflows) are generating high interest: 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents, and 23% report scaling an agentic AI system, though no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors.

Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI, with most saying less than 5% of EBIT is attributable to AI use. However, qualitative benefits are reported: 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, while revenue benefits are reported in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development.

The survey identifies "AI high performers" (about 6% of respondents who attribute 5%+ EBIT impact and report significant value) as distinguished by several factors: they are more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; more likely to set growth and/or innovation objectives (not just efficiency); nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows (identified as one of the strongest contributing factors via a relative weights analysis of 31 variables); three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to have senior leaders demonstrating ownership and commitment; more likely to have defined human-validation processes; and more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI (one-third of high performers do so, versus about three-quarters scaling AI overall). Successful practices align with McKinsey's Rewired research across six dimensions: strategy, talent, operating model, technology, data, and adoption/scaling.

On workforce impact, expectations vary: 32% of respondents expect enterprise-wide workforce decreases of 3% or more in the coming year, 43% expect no change, and 13% expect increases. A median of 17% of respondents report declines in function workforce sizes in the past year due to AI, but a median of 30% expect decreases next year. Larger organizations and high performers are more likely to expect meaningful workforce changes. Most organizations hired for AI-related roles in the past year, with software and data engineers most in demand.

Risk mitigation efforts are becoming more common. Respondents report acting to manage an average of four AI-related risks today versus two in 2022. Fifty-one percent of respondents from organizations using AI report at least one negative consequence, with nearly one-third reporting consequences from AI inaccuracy—the most commonly experienced and mitigated risk. Explainability is the second-most-reported risk but is not among the most commonly mitigated. High performers report more negative consequences (particularly IP infringement and regulatory compliance) but also protect against more risks.

The survey was in the field June 25 to July 29, 2025, with 1,993 respondents from 105 nations, weighted by GDP contribution. Thirty-eight percent work for organizations with over $1 billion in annual revenues. Authors include Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, and Tara Balakrishnan from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey.

## CROSS-FIRM COMPARISONS AND NOTABLE DIFFERENCES

**MBB vs. Big Four/technology services firms.** The Medium article identifies several structural differences:
1. **Investment disclosure:** PwC US: $1 billion AI investment over three years with firm-wide training; Accenture: $3 billion investment, doubling AI workforce from 40,000 to 80,000; KPMG: $2 billion partnership with Microsoft for AI integration, including in "Clara" audit platform; IBM: 160,000+ consultants automating repetitive tasks; EY and Deloitte expanding AI specialists and in-house AI units. MBB firms' investments are evidenced through acquisitions (QuantumBlack, Iguazio, Formation, Max Kelsen), partnerships (OpenAI, Microsoft, AWS, Google, Anthropic, etc.), and internal AI tooling rather than large fixed-dollar public commitments [17].
2. **Business model evolution:** The pyramid-to-diamond shift—firms are reducing junior MBA hiring (BCG limiting "generalist MBA" hires per Poets&Quants research) while recruiting engineering/AI talent; revenue model transformation from billable hours to value-based, success-fee, and subscription pricing; "productizing" AI platforms [17].
3. **Competitive positioning:** OpenAI's Frontier Alliances divide roles—BCG and McKinsey serve as strategy and operating model partners; Accenture and Capgemini take end-to-end systems integration roles (data architecture, cloud infrastructure, connecting Frontier to enterprise systems) [19].
4. **Consulting model ceiling:** Both McKinsey and BCG X follow the advisory consulting model with "9–24 months to production" timelines; charge by the hour; separate strategy from execution; are "fundamentally advisory (strategists, not builders)"; create consulting dependency; and add a coordination layer. Nexus contrasts this with its own FDE model (4 weeks to production) [5].
5. **Deloitte (from Virtasant):** Deloitte emphasizes partnership with Google Cloud (expanded decade-long collaboration in 2023; April 2025 expansions with Google Cloud and ServiceNow for agentic AI), works with AWS, Anthropic, and NVIDIA, acquired OpTeamizer (February 2024) for NVIDIA GPU AI expertise, serves ~90% of Fortune 500 companies, and differentiates through its "Trustworthy AI™" framework and "AI Factory as a Service" platform with NVIDIA and Oracle [20].
6. **Accenture (from Virtasant):** In mid-2023 became the first consulting firm to follow a multi-cloud generative AI strategy with simultaneous AWS, Microsoft, and Google Cloud collaborations; committed $3 billion to its Data & AI practice, planning to double its AI workforce to 80,000 specialists; offers AI Navigator for Enterprise platform and Center for Advanced AI [20].

**Firm-level partnership differences.** McKinsey is "The Ecosystem Orchestrator" (1,000+ partners, academia/startups/all cloud providers, Iguazio acquisition) [20]; BCG is "The Strategic AI Alliance Builder" (exclusive partnerships with OpenAI and Anthropic, NASA GenAI labs, Formation acquisition, stakes in Solution Seeker) [20]; Bain is "The OpenAI Power Player" (first major consulting firm to partner with OpenAI in February 2023, flagship Coca-Cola client, OpenAI Center of Excellence, 12 internal AI tools including Sage, Max Kelsen acquisition) [20].

**AI adoption findings (QuantumBlack State of AI 2025).** Nearly nine out of ten (88%) survey respondents say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function, up from 78% a year ago. Approximately two-thirds are not yet scaling AI across the enterprise. 62% of respondents are at least experimenting with agents; 23% report scaling an agentic AI system; no more than 10% report scaling agents in any individual function. Agent use is most common in IT and knowledge management, and most widely reported in technology, media/telecommunications, and healthcare sectors. Only 39% of respondents attribute any level of EBIT impact to AI. 64% say AI is improving innovation, and nearly half report improvement in customer satisfaction and competitive differentiation. Cost benefits are most commonly seen in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT; revenue benefits in marketing/sales, strategy/corporate finance, and product/service development. "AI high performers" (~6% of respondents) are: more than three times more likely to intend transformative change via AI; nearly three times more likely to fundamentally redesign workflows; three times more likely to scale AI agents; more likely to invest over 20% of digital budgets in AI. Risks: 51% report at least one negative consequence, with nearly one-third reporting consequences from AI inaccuracy. Survey: June 25 to July 29, 2025, 1,993 respondents from 105 nations. Authors: Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, Tara Balakrishnan (QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey) [2]. Work published November 5, 2025 [2].

**State of AI 2023 findings.** One-third of survey respondents report their organizations regularly use gen AI in at least one business function; 40% plan to increase overall AI investment due to gen AI; 79% of all respondents have had at least some exposure to gen AI; 22% regularly use it in their own work; three-quarters expect gen AI to cause significant or disruptive change in industry competition within three years; 60% of organizations with reported AI adoption are using gen AI; only 21% of organizations with AI adoption have policies governing employees' gen AI use; only 32% mitigate inaccuracy (the most-cited gen AI risk), lower than the 38% mitigating cybersecurity (Survey April 11-21, 2023, 1,684 participants) [66].

**Economic impact figures.** McKinsey's generative AI economic potential: $2.6 trillion to $4.4 trillion annually across 63 use cases; $6.1 trillion to $7.9 trillion including productivity gains [68]. McKinsey's Lari Hämäläinen: up to $25 trillion global impact by 2030 [4]. $23 trillion annually by 2040 (later report) [65]. BCG's "From Potential to Profit": only one-quarter of executives report significant value from AI initiatives; 10-20-70 principle [10]. BCG 2025 report: only 5% of companies seeing real returns [7]. Bain Technology Report 2025: AI leaders improving EBITDA by 10-25% [12]. Bain's AI TAM: $780 billion to $990 billion by 2027 [13].

## Deloitte's 2025 Tech Value Survey: AI Dominance and Portfolio Imbalance

**Published:** 2025 (fielded May–June 2025)

**Authors:** Tim Smith, Gregory Dost, Garima Dhasmana, Parth Patwari, Diana Kearns-Manolatos, Iram Parveen

**Overview:** This report, based on a survey of nearly 550 business and technology leaders across five industries (consumer; energy/resources/industrials; financial services; life sciences/healthcare; technology/media/telecom), analyzes how AI investments are consuming an outsized share of digital budgets, potentially leaving other critical technology areas underfunded.

### Key Findings:

**1. AI is Dominating Digital Budgets:**
- 74% of surveyed organizations invested in AI and gen AI over the past year — nearly 20 percentage points higher than the next most popular technologies (data management, cloud, IoT, ERP at ~55% and below).
- More than half of respondents allocate 21% to 50% (average 36%) of digital initiative budgets to AI — about US$700M for a company with US$13B revenue.
- Digital budgets rose from 7.5% of revenue (2024) to 13.7% (2025). If growth continues at this pace, budgets could reach 32% of revenue by 2028.
- Cybersecurity investment is lagging: only 25% to 32% invested in identity management, zero trust, or federated security.
- Emerging areas: 39% invested in agentic AI, 23% in robotics.

**2. Value Creation is Real but Fragmented:**
- 84% of AI/gen AI investors report gaining ROI. However, a cited MIT study found only 5% of gen AI pilots deliver sustained value at scale.
- Over 95% say digital initiatives lifted market cap or return on equity.
- Nearly 60% believe 21% to 50% of enterprise value remains latent.
- Paradox: AI investors were less likely to see significant market cap gains (43%) than those investing in data (65%) or security (66%).
- Data monetization strategy adoption grew from 16% (2023) to 65% (2025).

**3. C-Suite Alignment is Critical:**
- CFOs, CIOs, and CTOs often define success differently (ROI vs. EBITDA vs. KPIs), creating misalignment.
- Strategy innovation leaders — organizations that implement 4+ of 7 strategic innovation actions — outperform peers across all value measures and attribute over 40% of enterprise value to digital initiatives.

**4. Persistent Challenges:**
- Top barriers: misaligned incentives, legacy systems, lack of technical expertise (grew from 52% to 58%), security concerns, lack of strategy, insufficient funding.
- 60% cite data privacy/security as a major hurdle to AI automation.
- Success hinges on three factors: cyber strategy, tech strategy alignment, and dedicated leadership.

### Recommendations:
- Raise digital budgets to match ambition.
- Establish spending minimums for foundational technologies (platforms, data architecture, identity/zero trust, ERP) so AI doesn't starve the portfolio.
- Measure value beyond ROI — use a shared value scorecard.
- Align leadership incentives around enterprisewide outcomes.
- Shift from AI pilots to learning-capable systems integrated into core workflows.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Our analysis identifies key insights that can help maximize value: rethinking digital initiative budgets, expanding value measurements beyond tech return on investment, gaining leadership alignment on priorities, and overcoming a rising tide of challenges through proven success factors—cyber resilience, an aligned digital strategy, and dedicated leadership., AI is consuming digital budgets at a significant rate compared to the rest of the tech estate. Leadership must determine where human oversight is essential, design modern talent architectures with new hiring/performance/compensation strategies, and HR must ensure skilled individuals are available through strategic workforce planning, L&D, change management, and transformative leadership. --- SOURCE 10: 2026 AI Business Predictions ---
URL: https://www.pwc.com/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/ai-predictions.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
PwC's "2026 AI Business Predictions" (published as part of their Tech Effect and AI services content) outlines six key forecasts for how companies can turn AI ambition into transformative business value in 2026. The central thesis is that only a few companies are currently realizing extraordinary value from AI, while many others achieve only modest ROI. The article argues that success in AI requires precision, discipline, and top-down leadership rather than spreading efforts thin across small sporadic bets.

The six predictions are:
1. **The disciplined march to value begins** - Companies will shift from ground-up crowdsourcing to top-down, enterprise-wide AI strategies where senior leadership picks the spots for focused AI investment. Execution happens through centralized "AI studios" that link business goals to AI capabilities, with agentic AI playing an increasingly important role in workflows like demand sensing, hyper-personalization, product design, finance, HR, IT, tax, and internal audit.
2. **Proof points and real-world benchmarks set the pace for agentic AI** - While many agentic deployments failed to deliver value in 2025, 2026 could be the year agents shine, using real-world benchmarks that track business-value metrics (financial P&L impact, operational differentiation, workforce/trust). Guidance includes the 80/20 rule (technology delivers only ~20% of an initiative's value; the rest comes from redesigning work) and step-by-step workflow mapping with human oversight.
3. **Rise of the AI generalist** - AI agents will reduce specialization, causing demand to grow for generalists who oversee agents and align their work with business goals. Knowledge workforces may become hourglass-shaped (talent concentrated at junior and senior levels), while front-line workforces may become diamond-shaped (more mid-level orchestrators).
4. **Responsible AI moves from talk to traction** - Companies will roll out repeatable RAI practices, driven by acceleration of adoption and agentic workflows outpacing governance models. New tools like automated red teaming, deepfake detection, and AI-enabled inventory management will help. PwC's 2025 Responsible AI survey found 60% said RAI boosts ROI/efficiency, and 55% reported improved customer experience and innovation, but nearly half said operationalizing RAI principles was challenging.
5. **From vibe to value: Orchestration that accelerates impact** - "Vibe" coding and innovation require an orchestration layer ("command center") to industrialize ideas into production with continuous monitoring, centralized governance, and security. The layer should be easy for non-techies to use with drag-and-drop workflows, integrate AI tools from different vendors, and put companies in charge of controlling AI anywhere.
6. **The demand for business returns drives AI for sustainability** - AI use is growing faster than its energy efficiency improvements, potentially impacting emissions, water, and energy prices. However, AI can boost sustainability through productivity gains, customer sustainability analysis, supply chain tracing, and carbon scheduling. The article advises being deliberate with sustainability goals, following customer sustainability wishes, and preparing for rising energy costs by diversifying energy sources (renewables often most affordable long-term).

Each prediction includes practical "What to do now" action items for business leaders. The article is grounded in PwC's nearly a decade of executive survey research and its own internal AI transformation experience.
</summary>

## Notable Differences: Big Four vs. Management Consulting and Technology Services Firms

- **Enki AI analysis (August 12, 2026):** The Big Four are being fundamentally reshaped by AI, forcing them to pivot from a human-led, billable-hour model to an AI-driven, human-supervised approach. Collectively, the Big Four have directed over $10 billion toward AI technology and talent. KPMG has committed $2 billion (targeting $12 billion in new revenue); KPMG is exploring acquisitions of AI startups in Silicon Valley. Deloitte announced its largest enterprise deployment of Anthropic's AI models in October 2025. Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by end of 2026 (up from less than 5% in 2025). Organization-wide AI use in professional services nearly doubled to 40% in 2026 (Thomson Reuters report). The AI advisory market is projected to reach $349 billion by 2034, with a CAGR of over 35%. SWOT highlights: strengths—massive capital reserves ($10B+), C-suite access, global reach; weaknesses—rigid billable-hour model that conflicts with AI efficiency, entrenched culture resistant to change; opportunities—exploding AI advisory market, new AI governance/compliance service lines, automating low-value audit/tax work; threats—agile AI-native competitors, 95% failure rate of AI projects creating reputational risk, erosion of traditional audit/tax margins. The critical 2027 signal: whether Big Four successfully shift to outcome-based pricing models rather than billable hours. [20]

--- SOURCE 1: IBM Introduces Granite 3.0: High Performing AI Models Built for Business - Oct 21, 2024 ---
URL: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2024-10-21-ibm-introduces-granite-3-0-high-performing-ai-models-built-for-business

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On October 21, 2024, IBM announced the release of Granite 3.0, its most advanced family of AI models, at its annual TechXchange event in Armonk, NY. The third-generation Granite flagship language models outperform or match similarly sized models from leading providers on many academic and industry benchmarks while showcasing strong performance, transparency, and safety. Released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license, the models are unique in combining performance, flexibility, and autonomy for enterprise clients.

The Granite 3.0 family includes: (1) 8B and 2B language models designed as "workhorse" models for enterprise AI tasks including RAG, classification, summarization, entity extraction, and tool use; (2) Granite 3.0 1B-A400M and 3B-A800M Mixture of Experts (MoE) models for low-latency and CPU-based deployments; (3) updated pre-trained Granite Time Series models trained on 3x more data that outperform 10x larger models from Google and Alibaba; and (4) new Granite Guardian 3.0 8B and 2B safety models providing the most comprehensive risk and harm detection capabilities available, including RAG-specific checks (groundedness, context relevance, answer relevance).
